PSI-10.one_line: On the space station, small ball-shaped flames of ethylene gas were burned for minutes around a porous sphere, either as fuel blowing into oxygen-rich air or as oxygen blowing into a fuel atmosphere, to learn when such flames make soot and when they go out.
PSI-10.summary: ACME/Flame Design burned ethylene spherical diffusion flames on a 6.35 mm porous sphere in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS. In 2019, fuel (pure or nitrogen-diluted) flowed into oxygen/nitrogen atmospheres of 21-40% O2 near 1 atm (normal flames). In 2021-22, oxygen/nitrogen with up to 85% O2 flowed into ethylene/nitrogen atmospheres at 0.43-3 atm (inverse flames); one day used propane. The tables list 327 tests. Flows were held constant while cameras, thin-filament pyrometry, thermocouples and photomultipliers tracked each flame. In the 2019 tests flames grew, cooled by gas radiation, oscillated and went out after 28-336 s. At 1 atm all ethylene flames extinguished near 1130 K, at a fuel flux through the flame of 0.2 g/m2/s (normal) or an oxygen flux of 0.68 g/m2/s (inverse). Small flames burned steadily for up to 870 s. Sustained soot appeared only at 40% O2 with concentrated fuel. For fire safety, quiescent microgravity flames persist far below the about 1500 K extinction temperature typical on Earth, although these gas-burner limits are not material flammability limits.

question.text: Flame Design asked how the internal structure of a non-premixed (diffusion) flame, set by the stoichiometric mixture fraction Z_st, controls soot inception and extinction, separately from the direction of convection across the flame. Moving nitrogen from the oxidizer to the fuel stream raises Z_st at fixed adiabatic flame temperature, and in normal-gravity work this produced 'permanently blue' flames that never soot, with much higher extinction strain. Buoyancy and strain make those results ambiguous, and spherical flames on Earth are impossible, so the team used microgravity spherical flames, normal (fuel out of the burner) and inverse (oxygen out of the burner), to measure sooting limits, extinction limits (radiative and kinetic) and their temperatures as functions of flow rate, Z_st, dilution and pressure. It also asked whether truly steady spherical diffusion flames can exist despite radiative loss, and whether a 'pseudo-flammability limit' exists for non-premixed flames. The stated hypotheses were that soot needs a region of high enough local C/O ratio and temperature at low strain, that spherical flames extinguish when peak temperature falls below 1130 K, and that steady spherical flames are possible.

sources.quote: The method involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad.

By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts.
the pseudo-flammability limit represents the limiting condition where a nonpremixed flame can exist for a given fuel burning with an inert and oxygen.

physics.text: In a diffusion flame, fuel and oxidizer meet by diffusion at a thin reaction zone near the stoichiometric surface, Z = Z_st. For ethylene in air Z_st is about 0.064. Diluting the fuel and enriching the oxidizer (for example 1 mol C2H4 with 11.28 mol N2 burning in pure O2) gives the same adiabatic temperature but Z_st near 0.78. The flame then sits on the fuel side of the mixing layer, where hot gas contains free oxygen and little fuel, so soot precursors cannot grow. On Earth, a burner flame is dominated by buoyancy: the Richardson number for these flames is about 1000. Making it much less than 1 needs gravity reduced by about four orders of magnitude, and the team's analysis required about 10 micro-g. In microgravity the porous-sphere flame is one-dimensional. The radial velocity falls as 1/r^2, so at a few burner radii transport is purely diffusive, the diffusion time r^2/D reaches tens of seconds, and the hot zone keeps growing. As it grows, CO2 and H2O accumulate and radiate. Radiative loss scales with flame surface area, while the reactant flux per unit flame area falls, so the peak temperature drops until the flame undergoes radiative extinction. This occurs at a much lower temperature (about 1100-1130 K) than the kinetic (strain or blow-off) extinction familiar on Earth (about 1500 K). Near that limit, low-temperature 'warm flame' chemistry involving HO2 appears. Normal and inverse flames reverse the direction of convection relative to the flame. Soot formed in a normal flame is carried toward the oxidizer and burned; in an inverse flame it is carried toward the fuel and can grow.

equations.meaning: Stoichiometric mixture fraction. Y_{F,inf}, Y_{O,inf}: fuel and oxygen mass fractions in the fuel and oxidizer supply streams (-); W_F, W_O: molecular weights (kg/kmol); nu_F, nu_O: stoichiometric coefficients. Z_st is the mixture fraction (0 = pure oxidizer stream, 1 = pure fuel stream) at which the flame sits. Low Z_st (~0.06 for C2H4/air) puts the flame on the oxidizer side and favours soot. High Z_st (~0.7-0.8, diluted fuel into O2) gives soot-free 'permanently blue' flames. In the experimental tables, Z_st ranges over 0.06-0.76.

equations.meaning: Diffusion time scale of the spherical flame. r: radial distance from burner centre (m); D: gas diffusivity (m^2/s). Because the convective velocity decays as 1/r^2, transport beyond a few burner radii is diffusive. tau_d is tens of seconds at a few cm, and the investigators found the time for an unbounded spherical flame to reach steady state is of order 10^5 s. This is why drop towers (2-5 s) cannot reach quasi-steady conditions.

equations.meaning: Sooting-limit correlation (drop-tower spherical flames). Fitted line through the sooting-limit flames from 2.2 s drop-tower tests (ethylene, 1.5 mg/s fuel consumption, normal and inverse flames; Sunderland et al. 2004). Flames with T_ad below the line at a given Z_st were soot-free at the end of the drop ('permanently blue' regime). It is valid only for these transient 2 s flames; the longest-residence-time flames (>0.5 s) were excluded from the fit.

equations.latex: r_{f,ext} = \sqrt{\frac{\dot m_R}{4\pi\,\dot m''_{crit}}},\quad \dot m''_{crit} \approx 0.2\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{normal, fuel}),\ 0.68\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{inverse, } O_2)
equations.meaning: Flame radius at radiative extinction from the critical mass flux. dot m_R: mass flow of the burner reactant (fuel for normal flames, O2 for inverse flames) (g/s); dot m''_crit: reactant mass flux through the flame sphere at extinction (g/m^2/s); r_f,ext: radius of peak temperature at extinction (m). This is a mass-conservation reconstruction (steady flux through a sphere) of the 'simple equation' the investigators say estimates extinction flame size from reactant flow rate alone. The published form was not available. Valid for 1 atm ethylene flames whose peak temperature reaches 1130 K. For example, 1 mg/s of fuel gives r_f,ext of about 2 cm.

apparatus.text: Tests ran in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS using the ACME chamber insert. The chamber is a constant-volume vessel with about 83-90 L of free volume, so pressure and composition drift during a test day (vitiation). The burner was a 6.35 mm (0.25 in) porous sphere of sintered stainless steel (10 micron pores), fed by a single supply tube. Burner serial 1002 was replaced by 1003 in June 2019 because flames were off-centre at high flows. Three mass-flow controllers metered fuel or oxidizer and ISS nitrogen, allowing on-orbit dilution. A retractable hot-wire igniter lit the flame. Diagnostics were: the ACME colour DataCam (12-bit, 1360x1024, up to 30 frame/s, with filters for colour, BG7 pyrometry, CH* at 430 nm and formaldehyde); an analog ops camera; the CIR HiBMs monochrome camera with backlight, for soot extinction; an intensified CFI camera, generally with a CH* filter; three PMTs (OH* at 310 nm, CH* at 430 nm, and broadband); a thermopile radiometer array; a crew-replaceable array of 14 micron SiC fibres spaced 5 mm apart for thin-filament pyrometry (TFP); a burner-surface thermocouple; far (45, 60, 100, 100 mm) or near (13, 25, 50, 100 mm) thermocouple rakes, plus two thermocouples at 200 mm; and chamber pressure transducers. Non-imaging data were logged at 125 Hz. The CIR gas chromatograph was used occasionally.

procedure.text: The ISS crew configured the hardware, swapping gas bottles, MFCs, igniter tips, burners, rakes and fibre arrays. Tests were then commanded from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center. Each test ran from uplinked script and parameter files in a nominally automated mode, without manual flow changes during a test except halting after extinction. A typical sequence was: pre-ignition data and images, igniter preheat, flow priming, ignition with automatic detection (usually by the OH* PMT) and igniter retraction, then a stabilisation period. The flow was then held constant, or in some tests ramped, for up to a few minutes, with test end on detected extinction or flow timeout. A burner-temperature limit (for example 500 C) protected the sphere. About 16 tests were run per test day, with a couple of failed or unsustained ignitions. The chamber was vented and refilled between days, and recirculated through a sorbent filter mid-day in normal-flame testing. Round 1 (Apr-Jul 2019, Increments 59/60) used normal flames in roughly 21%, 30% and 40% O2. Round 2 (Oct 2021-Feb 2022, Increment 66) began with one propane normal-flame day using the near thermocouple rake to calibrate TFP. It then ran inverse flames with 85% O2 bottle gas diluted on orbit into 8-65% C2H4 atmospheres. From January 2022, after the chamber limit was raised from 1.5 to 3 atm, these included tests at about 0.5, 2 and 3 atm. The same constant-flow flames give soot-inception limits (yellow luminosity disappearing as the flame cools) and radiative-extinction limits (flame growth until extinction). Extinction diameter and burn time come from the ops video and the PMTs.

psi_data.summary: PSI holds 3,807 files (about 2.18 TB) for PSI-10. The two experimental tables (327 tests with conditions: mole fractions, mass flows, pressure, Z_st, T_ad) and the documents are small and immediately usable. They are the Final Report (2023, 92+ pages), the SRD (2010), the ACME ISRD and SORD, the Engineering Implementation report and 16 years of NASA Task Book reports. Per-test raw data are complete but heavy. Per test there are a 125 Hz data CSV (raw channel voltages for MFCs, pressure transducers, PMTs, thermocouples and radiometers, not engineering units), an MFC set-point CSV, the as-run parameter file, a test-point timeline (TP) with extinction-detection time, comments on missing images, and daily 'flow traces' PDFs with operator notes. Imagery is 1,183 zip archives (about 2.1 TB: DataCam raw and converted TIFFs, intensified and HiBMs images) and 317 ops-video .ts recordings (75 GB); none is downloaded here. Burn time, flame diameter and temperatures are not tabulated anywhere in PSI.

findings.claim: At about 1 atm, every ethylene spherical flame that extinguished radiatively did so at a peak temperature of about 1130 K. The reactant mass flux through the flame sphere at extinction was about 0.2 g/m^2/s of fuel for normal flames and 0.68 g/m^2/s of oxygen for inverse flames. This held across normal flames with ambient X_O2 0.20-0.38, burner X_fuel 0.13-1, total flow 0.6-12.2 mg/s and T_ad 2000-2800 K, and inverse flames with ambient X_C2H4 0.08-0.12, burner X_O2 0.40-0.85, 2.3-11.3 mg/s and T_ad 2080-2590 K.

sources.quote: Despite this broad range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2 - s for normal flames, and an oxygen- based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.

For normal flames, the ambient oxygen mole fraction was varied from 0.2 to 0.38, burner supply fuel mole fraction from 0.13 to 1, total mass flow rate, mtotal , from 0.6 to 12.2 mg/s, and adiabatic flame temperature, Tad , from 2000 to 2800 K.
For inverse flames, the ambient fuel mole fraction was varied from 0.08 to 0.12, burner supply oxygen mole fraction from 0.4 to 0.85, mtotal from 2.3 to 11.3 mg/s, and Tad from 2080 to 2590 K.

findings.claim: At constant burner flow, the normal ethylene flames at 1 atm grew monotonically after ignition while their peak gas temperature generally fell. Burn times were 28-336 s. Radiative extinction occurred when the growing flame's radiative loss approached its chemical heat release. Just before total extinction, many flames entered an oscillatory mode, partially extinguishing and re-forming with growing amplitude.

sources.quote: Burn times range from 28 –336 s. All flames grow monotonically after ignition. Peak gas temperature generally decreases with time.
Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release.
Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms.

findings.claim: Steady-state spherical diffusion flames can exist despite radiative loss. This requires the steady flame to be smaller than the radiative-extinction size, and the flame to develop fast enough that radiation does not first drive its temperature below 1130 K. Flames showing steady behaviour burned for up to 870 s on the ISS. In an unbounded domain, the diffusion-controlled approach to steady state takes of order 10^5 s.

relevance.text: In quiescent microgravity, with no buoyant flow to strain or blow off a flame, gaseous diffusion flames survive until radiative loss cools them to about 1130 K. That is several hundred kelvin below normal-gravity extinction temperatures. Spherical ethylene flames burned for minutes (up to 870 s) at constant fuel supply. For spacecraft fire safety this means: (1) a small, slow fuel leak can sustain a weak, possibly dim flame much longer than ground experience suggests; (2) extinction criteria based on a ~1500 K limit temperature are non-conservative in microgravity; (3) larger flames self-extinguish sooner, by radiation, than smaller ones at the same atmosphere; and (4) the critical flux of about 0.2 g/m^2/s fuel (1 atm, ethylene) offers a simple test for whether a diffusion flame fed at a given rate can persist. The PI explicitly cited pressure-dependent extinction data as valuable for spacecraft fire safety. The ACME documents themselves state that ACME was not designed as a fire-safety project. These are gas-burner flames, not material flammability limits.

PSI-20.one_line: A flat gas burner on the Space Station imitated small burning patches of plastics and liquids in still air, showing that such flames can burn steadily for minutes without any air flow when oxygen is raised to about 26.5% or more, but go out within tens of seconds at 21%.
PSI-20.summary: ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) used flat porous gas burners, 25 and 50 mm across, in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the International Space Station to imitate small burning patches of solids and liquids in still air. Ethylene, nitrogen-diluted ethylene or methane was fed at a fixed mass flux (about 1-12 g/(m2 s)) into nitrogen-oxygen atmospheres of 21-40% O2 at 56-100 kPa; embedded heat-flux gauges, radiometers and cameras gave the effective heat of gasification of each flame, its radiative loss and its size. Over 18 test days in 2019-2021, 194 flames were ignited. All 25 mm flames at 21% O2 self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas at 26.5, 34 and 40% O2 many burned steadily for 2-5 minutes until shut down. Larger, higher-flow and methane flames extinguished sooner; radiative heat loss drove the oscillation and extinction. Models built on these data suggest common plastics could burn steadily at about 1-3 g/(m2 s) in microgravity, and that low-pressure, oxygen-enriched cabin atmospheres widen the burning range. Stopping ventilation may therefore not quickly put out a small fire at elevated oxygen.

question.text: Can a small condensed-fuel (solid or liquid) fire burn steadily in quiescent microgravity, where there is no buoyant or forced flow to bring oxygen in, and if so for which combinations of material properties and cabin atmospheres? Testing dozens of real materials in orbit is too expensive, so BRE emulates them: a porous gas burner fed with ethylene or methane (optionally diluted with nitrogen) is set to match a material's heat of combustion, heat of gasification, surface re-radiation and smoke point. The hypothesis is that a quasi-steady burning regime exists as a function of these properties, and that if so the ground-based cone calorimeter test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2), which measures such properties, could be used to build microgravity flammability maps for real materials. Objectives also named three NASA-considered cabin atmospheres (21% O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5% at 10.2 psia, 34% at 8.2 psia), O2/CO2 ambients (desired) and extinction limits.

sources.quote: Ground-based tests are too short to overcome ignition transients and testing dozens of condensed fuels in orbit is prohibitively expensive.
In this fire safety study, the flammability of solid and liquid materials is simulated by burning gaseous fuels under key conditions corresponding to the solid and liquid materials.

physics.text: On Earth a burning surface is fed by a buoyant plume that brings in fresh air and carries away hot products. In quiescent microgravity there is no buoyancy, so oxygen reaches the flame only by diffusion; the flame becomes a slowly growing, nominally hemispherical blue diffusion flame over the surface. For a steadily burning condensed fuel the mass burning rate equals the net heat flux to the surface divided by the heat of gasification L (energy needed to turn unit mass of solid or liquid into vapour), so L = q''_net / m''. BRE inverts this: the fuel mass flux m'' is imposed through the porous burner, the heat flux to the surface is measured, and the 'effective' L of the emulated material is derived. Stagnant-layer (Spalding B-number) theory gives a purely diffusive burning rate proportional to ln(1+B). Because microgravity flames are large, slow and long-lived, radiative loss from soot and from CO2/H2O becomes a large fraction of the heat release; as the flame grows the flame temperature drops until it oscillates and undergoes radiative extinction. Higher oxygen raises flame temperature; dilution with nitrogen lowers heat of combustion and makes flames smaller and less radiative. A drop-tower test (5 s) is too short for these flames to reach steady state, hence the need for ISS-duration tests.

sources.note: Diffusion-limited quiescent burning, B-number theory and radiative extinction of microgravity diffusion flames are textbook combustion background.

equations.latex: L = \frac{\dot q''_{net}}{\dot m''}, \qquad \dot q''_{net} = \dot q''_{f,c} + \dot q''_{f,r} - \dot q''_{s,r} + \dot q''_{e,r}
equations.meaning: Steady energy balance at a burning surface, used by BRE to define the emulated material. $L$: heat of gasification (kJ/g), energy to turn unit mass of condensed fuel into vapour at the surface; $\dot q''_{net}$: net heat flux into the surface (kW/m2), measured by the burner's heat-flux gauges and slug calorimeter; $\dot m''$: fuel mass flux (g/(m2 s)), imposed through the porous burner. Components: flame convective flux $\dot q''_{f,c}$, flame radiative flux $\dot q''_{f,r}$, surface re-radiation $\dot q''_{s,r}$ and external radiation $\dot q''_{e,r}$ (zero in the ISS tests). Exact for a simply vaporising fuel at steady state; only approximate for real pyrolysis (charring, in-depth heating).

sources.quote: burning of a condensed fuel, the heat of gasification L is given by the ratio of the net heat flux and the burning rate.
the heat of gasification, L, (a material property) is found by Eq. (4.8)
The external radiative heat flux is not present in the experiments but could be included in the theory to follow.
This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions.

equations.latex: B = \frac{Y_{O_2,\infty}(1 - X_r)\,\Delta h_c / S - c_p (T_s - T_\infty)}{L_e}, \qquad L_e = L - \frac{\dot q''_{f,r} + \dot q''_{e,r} - \dot q''_{s,r}}{\dot m''}
equations.meaning: Spalding B number (mass transfer number): ratio of the energy the flame can deliver per unit mass of fuel to the energy needed to gasify it. $Y_{O_2,\infty}$: ambient O2 mass fraction; $\Delta h_c$: heat of combustion of the fuel/diluent stream (kJ/g; 15-47.2 kJ/g in BRE); $S$: mass of O2 consumed per unit mass of fuel stream; $\Delta h_c/S$ is the heat released per unit mass of O2 (taken as 13.76 kJ/g for ethylene); $c_p$: gas specific heat (kJ/(g K), consistent with $L$ and $\Delta h_c/S$); $T_s$, $T_\infty$: surface and ambient temperatures (K); $L$: heat of gasification (kJ/g); $L_e$: effective heat of gasification (kJ/g), $L$ less the net radiative fluxes per unit mass flux (dissertation Eq. 4.6 and 4.7), so that $\dot m'' L_e$ is the convective flux alone. The Dehghani analysis uses this effective B, in which the heat of combustion is reduced by the flame radiative loss fraction $X_r$ (transparent-flame assumption) and the denominator is $L_e$; $X_r$ and $L_e$ belong together. With $X_r = 0$ and no radiative fluxes this is the classical textbook B number. Higher O2 raises B and so the burning rate.

the formulas will be used throughout the paper as modified to include the heat of combustion reduced by a flame radiation loss fraction, Xr, the ratio of radiant energy lost by the flame to its combustion energy.

equations.latex: \dot m'' = \frac{8k}{\pi c_p D}\,\ln(1 + B) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda \equiv \frac{\pi c_p R\,\dot m''}{4k} = \ln(1 + B)
equations.meaning: Steady, purely diffusive burning rate of a flat circular fuel surface in quiescent surroundings (stagnant-layer and oblate-ellipsoid models give the same form); the relation BRE is built on. $\dot m''$: fuel mass flux (kg/(m2 s)); $k$: gas thermal conductivity (W/(m K)); $c_p$: gas specific heat (J/(kg K)); $D = 2R$: burner diameter (m); $\lambda$: dimensionless mass flux (burning eigenvalue); $B$: Spalding B number. Unity Lewis number ($\rho\mathcal{D} = k/c_p$), constant properties, laminar, no buoyancy. Note the rate scales as $1/D$, so small surfaces burn faster per unit area. In BRE $\dot m''$ is prescribed, so the relation is inverted to find the $B$ (and hence $L$) a flame emulates. Neglecting radiation, it over-predicted the measured drop-tower burning rates, and the 25 and 50 mm data followed two distinct curves.

procedure.text: For each test the crew/ground set the chamber atmosphere (diluent, O2 concentration, pressure), started fuel flow at a fixed rate and ignited it with the hot-wire igniter. The flame was observed at constant flow while burner surface temperature and heat flux evolved; a test ended either at self-extinction or, for flames that appeared steady, by commanded fuel shutdown (in practice after about 2-5 min, partly to conserve fuel and keep the atmosphere roughly constant). The planned extinction-limit procedure was to reduce flow stepwise after the burner reached steady temperature. Ignition limits were deliberately not studied in orbit. Several ignitions were made per test day: 194 flames over 18 test days, 2019-02-08 to 2021-01-28 (a 2019 round and a 2020-21 round after a one-year hiatus). Normal-gravity lab tests with gas, liquid and solid fuels, 5.18 s drop-tower tests at NASA Glenn and CFD modelling supported the flight work.

findings.claim: Small (25 mm) emulated condensed-fuel flames burned quasi-steadily for minutes in quiescent microgravity, with no air flow and no flame spread; more than half of round-1 tests (59 analysed ignitions) burned at least 2 and up to 5 minutes, and ~29 flames reached an apparently steady state for 120 s or more before shutdown.

findings.claim: Oxygen threshold for the 25 mm ethylene/N2 flames tested: all flames in 21% O2 (by volume) self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas steady flames were observed at nominal 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2. findings.claim: Simulations of the ISS test conditions in normal air (3-D, transient) reproduce the observed time to extinction; extinction happens when the instantaneous radiative fraction rises to 60-70% of the current heat release rate, a level reached because the low-momentum microgravity flame has a long residence time. After local extinction the flame edge takes a hook-like (bibrachial) form, and on re-ignition a triple flame runs along the stoichiometric surface.

sources.quote: Time to flame extinction predicted in this work agrees with the experimental observations. Extinction occurs due to the excessive radiative losses when the instantaneous radiative fraction grows up to 60–70% of the current heat release rate.
The excessively high level of the radiative losses is facilitated by the long residence time in the low-momentum microgravity flame.

relevance.text: Spacecraft fire response relies partly on stopping ventilation to starve a fire. BRE indicates that a small burning surface can keep burning for minutes in still air in microgravity, particularly in oxygen-enriched atmospheres, so turning off flow may not extinguish a fire quickly at elevated O2. The investigators suggest NASA make more use of the cone-calorimeter-based flammability Test 2, whose measured properties (heat of combustion, heat of gasification) map onto BRE's flammability maps, alongside the upward-flame-spread Test 1. Transferability caveats: BRE is a gas burner with imposed fuel flow; it does not pyrolyse, melt, drip, char or spread, and L is derived as heat flux / mass flux, which is exact only for simply vaporising fuels. Emulation was validated for several materials in 1 g, but its accuracy for real materials in microgravity was not directly verified with real samples on ISS. Sizes were 25 and 50 mm only. The O2 thresholds therefore describe burner flames at the tested flow rates, not material flammability limits.

sources.quote: Significance: Spacecraft fire prevention, including (1) microgravity flammability conditions and (2) assessment of flammability test methods for spacecraft materials.
This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions.

This technique has been demonstrated for a wide variety of materials in normal-gravity and could provide an efficient way to screen and select fire-resistant materials for use in spacecraft, if the technique is similarly effective in microgravity.
Seven condensed fuels were emulated: acetone, ethanol, methanol, polyethylene, polymethylmethacrylate, polypropylene, and polystyrene.

habitat_conditions.text: The test atmospheres bracket the NASA-considered cabin atmospheres named in the objective: 21% O2 at 14.7 psia (101.4 kPa), 26.5% at 10.2 psia (70.3 kPa) and 34% at 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa, the exploration atmosphere). The dissertation describes these nominal pairs as 21% at 1 bar, 26.5% at 0.7 bar and 34% at 0.565 bar. Steady burning was seen at 26.5% and 34% (and at 40%, above any proposed habitat level), while 21% flames self-extinguished; i.e. the exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) falls on the side where these small flames persist. Pressures per test are not in PSI. Against the shared reference atmospheres: the 21% O2 / ~100 kPa tests correspond to Earth sea level (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa), where these flames self-extinguished. The 34% O2 / 56.5 kPa case lies inside the Moon-habitat envelope (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less), and the 40% tests exceed it in O2; the 26.5% / 70.3 kPa case is at the envelope's pressure but below its O2. Steady burning was observed in all three of these enriched conditions. Spacesuit conditions (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa) were far outside the tested range (at most 40% O2, at least ~56 kPa).

sources.quote: Three of the atmospheres are nominal NASA selected atmospheres of pressure and oxygen for human habitat in space flight: 21 % oxygen and 1 bar, 26.5% and 0.7 bar and 34 % and 0.565 bar
All flames burning in 21% by volume oxygen self-extinguished within 40 s. However, steady flames were observed at 26.5, 34, and 40% oxygen.
This is further support of the significant hazards of using enriched oxygen atmospheres in spacecraft.

earth_benefits.text: The emulation approach and its 1-g validation (wick and gas-burner tests on ignition and extinction of small fires) are aimed at fire science generally; NASA states the results could improve fire safety on Earth, but no specific Earth application is documented in the sources reached.

sources.quote: While BRE is focused on improving the process to select fire-resistant spacecraft materials, the research results could yield new understanding that also enables improved fire safety on Earth.

limitations.text: Emulation, not real materials: a gas burner with prescribed fuel flow cannot reproduce pyrolysis chemistry, charring, melting, bubbling, dripping, in-depth heating or flame spread; real-material burning in microgravity was not tested.

PSI-21.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames surrounded by a gentle co-flowing air stream were burned on the Space Station, from very diluted near-extinction flames to very sooty ones, to give computer models clean, buoyancy-free benchmark data; the sooty flames held several times more soot than on Earth and diluted flames survived at lower fuel concentrations.
PSI-21.summary: CLD Flame produced benchmark data on laminar coflow diffusion flames, a fuel jet surrounded by co-flowing air, for testing chemical-kinetic and soot models at both extremes of fuel dilution. On the ISS, in the ACME insert of the Combustion Integrated Rack, a small coflow burner (about 2 mm fuel tube in a 25 mm air nozzle) burned nitrogen-diluted methane (20-100%) and ethylene (10-100%) in air on 32 test days from November 2017 to March 2021, igniting 344 flames. Cameras and pyrometry gave flame shape, lift-off height, CH* chemiluminescence, temperature, soot temperature and soot volume fraction. Preliminary results: sooty microgravity flames were taller and wider and held 5-8 times more soot than equivalent 1 g flames, and dilution limits of both fuels were extended, with lifted flames stable at lower fuel concentrations. Simulations of the ACME ethylene flames showed weaker gravity effects than in a larger burner, and highlighted errors in the predicted temperature field. For fire safety this is fundamental: microgravity flames can be sootier, more radiative and burn closer to dilution limits.

question.text: Can detailed computational models with chemical-kinetic and soot sub-models predict laminar diffusion flames at the extremes of fuel dilution: heavily sooting pure-fuel flames and very dilute flames near extinction? Earlier work, including microgravity work, showed the models fall short there. Buoyancy complicates 1 g flames (it accelerates and narrows them, shortens residence time and causes flicker), so the ISS was used to obtain momentum-dominated, buoyancy-free coflow flames with long residence times as clean benchmark cases. Objective A: characterise weak coflow methane and ethylene flames versus velocity and dilution (flame shape, lift-off height, temperature, extinction limits). Objective B: characterise sooting tendency of long-residence-time flames versus velocity and dilution (shape, gas temperature in soot-free regions, soot luminosity, soot temperature, soot volume fraction). The stated hypothesis is to supply benchmark data to validate the investigators' computational models. Motivation is terrestrial combustion (efficiency, pollutants, design tools); NASA states the work does not serve space applications.

sources.quote: Past research, including that conducted in microgravity, had revealed shortfalls in the ability to accurately model flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.

The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
Improve computational flame models with benchmark quantitative data for sooty and extremely diluted microgravity flames.

The CLD Flame research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing).

physics.text: In a coflow laminar diffusion flame, fuel (here methane or ethylene, often diluted with nitrogen) issues from a central tube into a surrounding stream of air; fuel and oxygen meet by diffusion and burn in a thin sheet roughly where they meet in stoichiometric proportion. On Earth the hot, light products are accelerated upward by buoyancy, which stretches and narrows the flame, pulls in air radially and shortens the time gas spends in the hot sooting region; the flame also flickers. In microgravity the flow is set only by the injection momentum, so flames are longer, wider and more diffuse, residence times are longer, and temperatures are lower. Longer residence time lets soot particles grow, so sooty flames carry several times more soot; more soot means more radiative loss, which cools the flame, which in turn changes soot chemistry - a strongly coupled problem that models struggle with. At the dilute extreme the flame is weak and lifts off the burner, stabilising where the local flow speed matches the propagation speed of its leading (triple-flame) edge; working with lifted flames removes heat loss to the burner rim from the problem. Without buoyancy-induced acceleration, dilute flames survive at lower fuel concentrations. Diluting the fuel with nitrogen lowers flame temperature and moves the stoichiometric surface, so dilution and velocity are the two knobs spanning weak to heavily sooting flames. Drop towers give only ~5 s, too short for soot to reach quasi-steady conditions, hence the need for ISS duration.

equations.meaning: Burke-Schumann/Roper scaling for the length of a laminar jet diffusion flame. $L_f$ flame length (m); $\dot{m}_F$ mass flow rate of the fuel mixture (kg/s); $\rho D$ density times diffusivity of the gas (kg m-1 s-1, roughly temperature-independent); $S$ moles of oxidiser stream needed per mole of fuel stream (dilution changes $S$). Length depends on fuel mass flow, not separately on velocity or burner diameter, to leading order in both buoyant and non-buoyant flames; buoyancy and coflow change the prefactor and the flame width. Consistent with the SLICE finding that luminous flame length is proportional to fuel mass flow in both 1 g and microgravity, with microgravity flames longer.

sources.note: Roper (1977) laminar jet flame length correlations

sources.quote: Buoyant and nonbuoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to the mass flow rate of the fuel mixture; computed and measured nonbuoyant flames are noticeably longer than their 1g counterparts

equations.meaning: Stoichiometric mixture fraction, locating the flame sheet in mixture-fraction space. $Y_{F,1}$ fuel mass fraction in the fuel stream (lowered by N2 dilution); $Y_{O_2,2}$ = 0.233, oxygen mass fraction in air; $s$ stoichiometric oxygen-to-fuel mass ratio (4.0 for CH4, 3.43 for C2H4). Dilution raises $Z_{st}$ and lowers flame temperature and soot formation, which is how the fuel concentrations in the experimental table span sooty to near-extinction flames. Valid for a one-step, equal-diffusivity picture.

sources.note: standard mixture-fraction definition

equations.meaning: Froude number comparing jet momentum to buoyancy for exit velocity $U$ (m/s), tube diameter $d$ (m) and gravity $g$ (9.81 m/s2 on Earth); residence time $t_{res}$ (s) of gas in a flame of length $L_f$ (m). For the ACME burner ($d \approx 2$ mm, $U$ of order 10-100 cm/s) $Fr$ in 1 g is of order 0.5-50, so small slow flames are buoyancy-affected on Earth; in orbit ($g \approx 10^{-6} g_0$) they are momentum-dominated and gas lingers longer, giving more time for soot growth. Order-of-magnitude only.

sources.note: standard dimensional analysis; values are illustrative

equations.meaning: Two-colour (colour-ratio) soot pyrometry used with the calibrated colour camera, in the Wien approximation: $S_1/S_2$ signal ratio of two colour channels at effective wavelengths $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ (m); $\eta_{12}$ instrument calibration factor; $\alpha$ soot dispersion exponent (emissivity $\propto \lambda^{-\alpha}$; 0.9-1.38 assumed for microgravity soot in the SLICE analysis); $C_2$ = 0.014388 m K; $T_s$ soot temperature (K). Soot volume fraction $f_v$ (dimensionless, ppm) then follows from the absolute emission (calibrated against a thermocouple) via spectral emissivity $\varepsilon_\lambda$ over path length $L$ (m) with dimensionless extinction coefficient $K_e$. Assumes optically thin, line-of-sight data after Abel inversion; self-absorption in sooty flames biases temperature (corrections up to 22-75 K).

sources.note: standard two-colour pyrometry

sources.quote: While the true soot dispersion exponent remains unknown in microgravity, a range from 0.9 to 1.38 is estimated based on literature values

with the maximum correction quantified to be 22 K for a flame with a maximum optical depth of 0.31. This correction is as much as 42 and 75 K for simulated flames with the same optical properties, structure, and a factor of two and five increase in soot volume fraction, respectively.

apparatus.text: ACME chamber insert in the CIR combustion chamber (nominally 100 L, ~83 L free volume; constant-volume tests lasting a few minutes). Small coflow burner: two concentric tubes of 2.1 mm (fuel) and 25 mm (air) inner diameter; a 2023 modelling paper gives 2.2 mm inner diameter with 0.1 mm wall. The same burner was later used by E-FIELD Flames. Gas delivery by crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers (fuel, nitrogen diluent, coflow); per test day the fuel MFC full scale was 0.1 or 0.2 slpm and the N2 MFC 0.02-0.2 slpm (nitrogen basis). Diagnostics: a pre-characterised high-definition colour camera (flame shape, lift-off, CH* concentration, flame and soot temperature by pyrometry, soot volume fraction), a gray-scale camera with an opposed collimated light source for soot by light extinction, intensified cameras for OH* and CH*, PMTs for CH*/OH* chemiluminescence, radiometers, and translating 14 micron SiC fibres for thin-filament pyrometry (TFP) of gas temperature. Tests configured by crew and commanded from NASA Glenn.

procedure.text: Each test day the crew set up the burner, fuel bottle and mass flow controllers, and tests were run from the ground. Flames were ignited in an air-filled chamber with an air coflow, fuel and air velocities typically matched; fuel concentration (N2 dilution) and velocity were varied between tests and sometimes during a test, stepping toward lower fuel concentration until extinction for the dilute-limit work. Three ISS rounds: methane, 14 days (2017-11-15 to 2018-02-22, 130 flames); ethylene, 14 days (2018-05-25 to 2018-09-14, 162 flames); 'improved coflow tests', 4 days (2021-02-10 to 2021-03-03; 2 ethylene, 2 methane; 52 flames). Total 32 test days, 344 flames. Normal-gravity comparison flames were burned at Yale, and the investigators' MC-Smooth vorticity-velocity code with sectional soot model was used to compute both. The precursor SLICE experiment (Microgravity Science Glovebox, January-March 2012) used a different burner (76 mm square duct, 5 interchangeable nozzles) to refine the test matrix; most published ISS results in the PSI publication list come from SLICE, not from these ACME test days.

relevance.text: CLD Flame is not a fire-safety experiment (NASA: no space application intended). Its relevance is fundamental: (1) in still or slow flows microgravity flames can carry several times more soot and lose more heat by radiation than the same flames on Earth, which affects smoke production (detection) and radiative heating of nearby surfaces; (2) dilute flames survived to lower fuel concentrations in microgravity, so dilution or inerting margins derived from 1 g flames may be non-conservative for gaseous fuel leaks in orbit; (3) validated soot/radiation models are a prerequisite for predictive spacecraft fire simulation. Transferability caveats: small laminar gas-jet flames in air with nitrogen-diluted fuel; no solid or liquid fuels, no oxygen enrichment or reduced pressure; extinction data are fuel-dilution limits of a burner flame, not material flammability limits.

PSI-22.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames on the Space Station were placed in a strong electric field between the burner and a metal mesh; the field drags the flame's natural ions and the gas around them, creating an adjustable 'ion wind' that can reshape, compact, de-soot or stabilise the flame with no buoyancy present.
PSI-22.summary: E-FIELD Flames studied how a DC electric field changes small laminar diffusion flames when buoyancy is absent. In the ACME insert of the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS, up to 10 kV of either polarity was applied between the burner and a copper mesh about 35-50 mm downstream, while the ion current, flame images, chemiluminescence and radiation were recorded. Nitrogen-diluted methane (40-100%) and ethylene (25-100%) flames were burned on 20 test days between March and November 2018, on a coflow burner (11 days) and a gas-jet burner (9 days), 219 flames. In microgravity the ion current versus voltage curve shows a distinct peak at saturation, where the flame is most compact, and then falls, unlike in 1 g. Fields could suppress soot, stabilise highly diluted flames with very weak fields, and produced corona and arcs at high strength. A drop-tower precursor showed an electric field alone can make microgravity flames resemble 1 g flames; this ion-wind body force is the basis for describing E-FIELD as mimicking partial gravity, but no calibrated partial-gravity tests were reported. Fire-safety relevance is indirect.

question.text: How does an applied DC electric field act on a laminar non-premixed (diffusion) flame once buoyancy is removed? Flames contain a small population of chemi-ions; a field drives them through the gas, and by collisions they drag neutral gas along (the ion wind). On Earth this ion-driven flow is entangled with buoyant convection, which acts in a similar way, so the two are hard to separate. The stated objectives were to (1) relate applied voltage to chemi-ion current (the voltage-current characteristic), (2) analyse the dynamic response of flames to changes in the field, (3) evaluate soot formation, and (4) characterise stabilised near-limit lifted flames. The hypothesis was that fields in microgravity would allow precise manipulation of flame stability, soot and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization. The motivation stated by NASA and the PSI record is terrestrial (cleaner, leaner, more efficient combustion); the record says the work does not serve space applications, although it might aid space-based combustors such as waste processors.

sources.quote: the current measurements represent the first mapping of the effects of an ion-driven wind on flame behavior under an electric field in the absence of the confounding influences of buoyancy
The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame.
Moreover, in earth gravity the hot combustion products are subject to buoyancy effects that are difficult to isolate from those generated by the electric field.

physics.text: Hydrocarbon flames are weak plasmas. Chemi-ionization in the reaction zone (chiefly CH + O -> CHO$^+$ + e$^-$, followed by fast proton transfer that makes H$_3$O$^+$ the dominant positive ion) produces ions and electrons at a rate set by the flame chemistry, but their number density is many orders of magnitude below that of the neutral gas. When a voltage is applied between the burner and a downstream mesh, positive ions drift toward the negative electrode and electrons (which soon attach to form negative ions) toward the positive one. Outside the thin reaction zone each electrode gap carries charge of one sign only. Ions drift at $v = \mu E$ (mobility $\mu$ of order $10^{-4}$ m$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$), colliding constantly with neutrals, so their momentum is handed to the gas: the net force per unit volume on the gas is the electrohydrodynamic (EHD) body force $f = \rho_q E = j/\mu$. This 'ion wind' is a body force like buoyancy, $(\rho_\infty-\rho) g$, and the analogy is the reason E-FIELD is described as able to mimic gravity: a field that drives positive ions downstream pushes hot gas away from the burner much as buoyancy does on Earth, and its strength can be dialled with the voltage. Equating the two forces defines an equivalent gravity $g_{eq} = j/[\mu(\rho_\infty-\rho)]$. In 1 g the field can cancel buoyancy locally (the 'microbuoyant' condition found at ion-current saturation); in microgravity it can add a controllable convection. Illustrative estimate (not an ISS measurement): air at 300 K versus ~1800 K combustion products at 1 atm gives $\rho_\infty-\rho \approx 1.0$ kg/m$^3$, so buoyancy is ~10 N/m$^3$ at Earth gravity, ~3.6 N/m$^3$ at Mars (3.71 m/s$^2$) and ~1.6 N/m$^3$ at Moon gravity (1.62 m/s$^2$). With $\mu \approx 2\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$/(V s), the current densities needed are only ~0.2, ~0.07 and ~0.03 $\mu$A/cm$^2$; ground measurements of EHD body force in a coflow flame were 200-400 N/m$^3$, i.e. 20-40 times 1 g buoyancy. The total ion supply caps the force: once every ion produced is collected (saturation current $I_{sat}$), extra voltage cannot raise $j$. Why this is only an analogue and not true partial gravity: (1) buoyancy acts on every parcel in proportion to its density deficit, everywhere in the flow; the EHD force acts only where ion current flows (between the flame sheet and the electrodes, along field lines) and is independent of temperature; (2) its direction follows the field lines and polarity, not a uniform vector; (3) it is coupled to the flame itself - ion extraction, field-induced changes to the flame position and chemistry, and space charge that reshapes the field; (4) it does nothing to condensed phases (melt flow, dripping, particle settling) or to the cold ambient outside the current path. Microgravity is valuable because it removes buoyancy so that the ion-driven flow can be measured on its own, and because quasi-steady small flames can be held for minutes.

sources.note: Chemi-ionization chemistry, ion drift, EHD body force f = rho_q E = j/mu, buoyancy body force, and the planetary surface gravities (Moon 1.62, Mars 3.71 m/s2) are textbook background; the numerical estimate is the record author's illustration, not an investigator result.

equations.meaning: Electrohydrodynamic (ion-wind) body force per unit volume on the gas. $\rho_q$ net space-charge density (C/m3); $\mathbf{E}$ local electric field (V/m); $\mathbf{j}$ ion current density (A/m2); $\mu$ ion mobility (m2 V-1 s-1, of order 1e-4 for flame ions in air; drop-tower fits gave 2.2-10.3 cm2/(V s) for positive ions). Valid in the unipolar drift regions between the flame and each electrode, where ions move at drift speed $\mu E$ and pass their momentum to neutrals by collisions (ion density tiny compared with gas density). For a spherically symmetric gap the same relation gives $f = I/(4\pi \mu r^2)$. Not valid inside the quasi-neutral reaction zone, where $\rho_q \approx 0$.

equations.meaning: Buoyancy body force per unit volume on hot gas of density $\rho$ in ambient of density $\rho_\infty$ (kg/m3) under gravity $g$ (m/s2), and the 'equivalent gravity' $g_{eq}$ (m/s2) at which the ion-wind force matches it locally. Example: $\rho_\infty-\rho \approx 1.0$ kg/m3 (300 K air vs ~1800 K products at 1 atm) and $\mu = 2\times10^{-4}$ m2/(V s) give $g_{eq}$ = 1.62 m/s2 (Moon) at $j \approx 3.2\times10^{-4}$ A/m2 (0.032 uA/cm2) and 9.81 m/s2 at ~0.2 uA/cm2. The match is local only: buoyancy acts on every hot parcel, the EHD force only where current flows, so $g_{eq}$ varies in space and with polarity. Record author's illustration, not an investigator correlation.

equations.meaning: Saturation ion current (A): all chemi-ions produced in the flame volume $V$ (m3) at volumetric production rate $\dot{\omega}_{ci}$ (ions m-3 s-1, mainly from CH + O -> CHO+ + e-) are collected; $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C. Above saturation extra voltage raises $E$ but not the ion supply, so the total EHD force (and hence any gravity-equivalent) is capped by the flame's ion production unless secondary ionisation (corona) adds carriers. On the ground, the buoyancy-cancelling (microbuoyant) condition for methane coincided with saturation; on the ISS the most compact flame occurred at saturation.

equations.meaning: Space-charge-limited (Mott-Gurney-type) current density for unipolar ions crossing a planar gap of width $d$ (m) at voltage $V$ (V); $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m. Idealised 1-D description of the sub-saturation branch of a flame voltage-current characteristic (current rising roughly with $V^2$) when the flame supplies more ions than the gap can carry. It ceases to apply at saturation ($I = I_{sat}$); the ISS curves then peaked and fell ('parabolic super-saturation region'), behaviour this relation does not describe. Real burner-to-mesh geometries are not planar.

With $j$ = 0.2 uA/cm2 (2e-3 A/m2), $d$ = 0.04 m, $\rho$ = 0.3 kg/m3, $\mu$ = 2e-4 m2/(V s): $U \sim 1$ m/s, i.e. larger than the 3.1 cm/s coflow and comparable to buoyant velocities of small 1 g flames, which is why weak fields visibly reshape microgravity flames. apparatus.text: ACME chamber insert in the CIR combustion chamber (nominally 100 L; ~83 L free volume; constant-volume tests of a few minutes). Two burners were used: the small coflow burner shared with CLD Flame (fuel tube ~2.1-2.2 mm inner diameter inside a 25 mm air nozzle) and a gas-jet burner (ACME gas-jet burners span 0.4-3.2 mm inner diameter; the one used is not identified in sources reached). A crew-removable flat circular copper mesh electrode, orthogonal to the burner axis, was set ~35 or ~50 mm downstream of the electrically insulated burner and driven by a high-voltage supply between +10 and -10 kV (average field up to roughly 2-3 kV/cm, derived). The ion current between burner and mesh was measured from the voltage drop across a known resistor. Other instruments: high-definition colour camera and other CIR cameras (flame shape, luminosity, soot), photomultiplier tubes for CH* and OH* chemiluminescence, thermopile radiometers for flame radiant emission, three mass flow controllers for fuel/nitrogen/coflow, and a hot-wire igniter. Tests were configured by crew and commanded from NASA Glenn.

procedure.text: Each test day the crew installed the appropriate burner, fuel bottle and electrode and the ground team ran pre-programmed scripts. A flame was ignited in the air-filled chamber (with a weak synthetic-air coflow on the coflow burner, or with no coflow), then the voltage was ramped and the ion current and images recorded as a function of field strength, polarity, fuel and dilution; fuel flow rate and coflow velocity were also varied. Fuel was diluted on orbit with nitrogen to span highly stable to near-extinction flames. Mesh polarity (polarity of the supply and copper electrode relative to the burner) was fixed per test day. Round 1 used the coflow burner on 11 days (2018-03-14 to 2018-05-17; 5 negative, 6 positive polarity; 120 flames); round 2 used the gas-jet burner on 9 days (2018-09-26 to 2018-11-15; 5 negative, 4 positive; 99 flames). Total 219 flames on 20 unique test days. In the published coflow-flame example (used for simulation), 70% CH4 issued at 15 or 19 cm/s into 3.1 cm/s air coflow.

psi_data.summary: PSI holds a one-page experimental table (date, test type/burner, mesh polarity, fuel bottle, fuel concentrations, flames ignited for each test day), four representative images and an ISA-Tab metadata zip that repeats the record text. The images are an ACME logo and three uncaptioned flame photographs: a blue, soot-free flame bulging to an almost spherical shape around the burner tip, a blue flame flattened into a low dome over the burner (similar to the NASA poster image captioned as a flame 'pushed' toward the coflow burner), and a teardrop-shaped flame with a yellow (sooty) tip; their test conditions are not given. findings.claim: Polarity sets the ion-wind direction. By electrostatics, with the mesh positive relative to the burner the dominant positive ions are driven back toward the burner, a downward ion wind opposite to Earth buoyancy; with the mesh negative, positive ions move downstream as buoyancy would move hot gas on Earth. A poster caption describes a flame 'pushed' toward the coflow burner, and a JASMAC figure with the mesh negative shows the flame size changing with field strength. The investigators' own wording reads the other way if their field sign means mesh polarity: the UCI group's page links a downward ion wind to negative field strength, and the OSTI modelling report links a positive field to a taller, narrower flame. Their field-sign convention is not given in the sources reached, so the pairing of mesh polarity with flame shape here is inferred, not observed; the sources show images, not velocity data.

findings.claim: What 'mimicking gravity' rests on (precursor, not ISS data): in 2.2 s NASA Glenn drop-tower tests of a jet flame, an electric field alone made microgravity flames resemble 1 g flames. On the ground, ion winds were used to cancel buoyancy locally (a 'microbuoyant' condition), which for methane coincided with ion-current saturation. The investigators proposed as early as 1999 that ion winds allow 'varying gravitational convection equivalents' in reduced gravity. No source reached reports ISS tests calibrated to a specific partial-gravity level (e.g. lunar or Martian).

findings.claim: Size of the force (ground measurements): in a 1 g coflow flame the derived electrical body force was 200-400 N/m^3 (reported as N/m2 in the abstract), roughly 20-40 times the ~10 N/m^3 buoyancy of hot products at 1 g, so modest currents suffice to rival or exceed lunar/Martian buoyancy. In a 2.2 s drop-tower test with a spherical burner the ion wind was negligible: the spherically symmetric force acts like an apparent pressure, and that pressure was about six orders of magnitude below ambient, so the density and velocity changes it causes were negligible. Geometry decides whether the force can be written as a pressure; its size decides whether it matters.

relevance.text: E-FIELD is not a fire-safety experiment: the PSI record states it serves no space application. Its relevance to spacecraft and habitat fire safety is indirect: (1) it is the only PSI investigation that applies a controllable, gravity-like body force to flames in orbit, so it is the nearest PSI has to partial-gravity combustion data, but the force is an ion-wind analogue acting only along the current path, not true buoyancy acting on all hot gas; results cannot be read as lunar or Martian fire behaviour; (2) the strong correlation between ion current and flame state hints at electrical flame sensing in microgravity (detection), not demonstrated for fires; (3) high-voltage fields near flames produced corona and arcs. All flames were small gas-jet or coflow burner flames in air; nothing here is a material flammability limit.

PSI-23.one_line: On the space station, gas fuels (hydrogen, methane, ethylene, diluted with nitrogen or helium) were fed out of a small porous ball into still oxygen-containing gas to make nearly perfect spherical flames, to see how such flames grow, and how they go out when the fuel supply is too small or when the flame becomes so large that it loses too much heat by radiation.
PSI-23.summary: s-Flame burned gaseous fuels issuing from a 6.35 mm porous spherical burner into a quiescent oxygen atmosphere at about 1 atm inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack. The aim was to test detailed chemistry and transport models against a one-dimensional diffusion flame. In 18 test days (Sept. 2019 to July 2020), 276 flames were ignited: 145 with nitrogen dilution of fuel and atmosphere (about 21% or 30% O2) and 131 with helium dilution (about 21%, 30% and 17.5% O2). Fuels were ethylene, methane, hydrogen and hydrogen/methane blends at roughly 1-17.5 cc/s. Nitrogen-diluted ethylene and methane flames showed both extinction branches. Flows of 5-10 cc/s gave flames that grew until radiative loss extinguished them. Flows ramped down toward 1 cc/s gave kinetic extinction. Radiative extinction, never seen in drop towers, was common. No flame was inherently sooty. Helium made ignition much harder and moved the limits. Predicted pulsating instabilities were not clearly seen. For fire safety, the work shows that flame size and residence time set extinction in quiescent microgravity, and that dim hydrogen flames are hard to see.

question.text: s-Flame asked whether detailed chemical-kinetic and transport models, validated mainly on homogeneous systems and premixed flames, also predict diffusion flames. The test case was the simplest diffusion flame there is: a steady, one-dimensional spherical flame around a porous sphere that discharges fuel into a quiescent oxidizer. Such a flame exists only without buoyancy. Three objectives were set. (A) Measure the transient structure (temperature, species) of spherical diffusion flames that start from a non-steady ignition, for H2/CH4/diluent (soot-free) and C2H4/diluent (sooty) mixtures at several flow rates. (B) Find the two quasi-steady extinction limits. The low system Damkohler number limit is convective/kinetic extinction (small flame, short residence time). The high Damkohler number limit is radiative extinction (large flame, large radiating volume). (C) Determine the existence, onset and nature of pulsating instabilities predicted for fuel/diluent mixtures above a critical Lewis number. A second line of work concerned soot onset versus residence time in initially non-steady sooty flames. Ground facilities (2.2 s and 5 s drop towers, parabolic aircraft) were too short or too noisy to observe radiative extinction, which simulations predicted needs more than 2.5 s and up to about 25 s.

sources.quote: For diffusion flames, since a steady mathematical solution does not exist for the planar and cylindrical geometri es in the doubly infinite or semi-infinite domain, the onl y possible steady, one-dimensional flame is the spherical flame

physics.text: Fuel leaving a porous sphere at mass flow rate m moves radially outward, and its velocity falls as 1/r^2. A diffusion flame sits where fuel diffusing outward and oxygen diffusing inward meet in stoichiometric proportion. For a flame sheet the flame radius scales roughly linearly with m. Without buoyancy the problem is one-dimensional: convection, diffusion and net radiation all act along the radius. This removes the flow ambiguities of counterflow and jet flames. After ignition near the burner, the flame front moves outward toward its steady radius while fuel accumulates inside it. Simulations predicted tens of seconds of growth, which only orbit can provide. Extinction of a diffusion flame occurs through reactant leakage when the flame Damkohler number (diffusion time over chemical time) drops too low. That can happen in two ways. At small m the flame is small and residence time is short, giving kinetic (blow-out-like) extinction at low system Da. At large m the flame is large. Radiative loss, a volumetric process, then grows faster than heat release, cools the flame and causes radiative extinction at high system Da. The steady response is therefore a closed 'isola', not an S-curve. Gas-phase reabsorption of radiation (CO2, H2O) reduces net loss and enlarges the flame at extinction. Near either limit, theory predicts that flames with Lewis number Le > 1 can develop pulsating instabilities, which grow until extinction. Le is greater than 1 when the deficient reactant diffuses more slowly than heat. Helium instead of nitrogen as diluent raises thermal conductivity (about 6x) and flame temperature, and changes Le and the Zeldovich number. Visible or CH* luminosity is not a reliable measure of flame strength in these transient flames. CH* emission can fall while temperature rises, so extinction should be judged from temperature or radiometer data.

equations.meaning: Flame Damkohler number of a spherical diffusion flame. d_f flame diameter (m); alpha thermal diffusivity (m^2/s); T_a activation temperature of the overall reaction (K); T_f flame temperature (K). tau_diff ~ d_f^2/alpha is the diffusion (residence) time, tau_chem ~ exp(T_a/T_f) the chemical time. Scaling only, from the s-Flame SRD (its Eqs. 1-2); valid for a quasi-steady flame sheet with one-step Arrhenius kinetics. The flame is extinguished when Da_f falls below a critical value Da_f,e.

sources.quote: let us consider the Damkohler number in the flame region, Daf, which is the ratio of the characteristic diffusion time to the reaction time at the flame, τDiff/τChem.
where df is the flame diameter, Tf the flame temperature, Ta the activation temperature, and α the thermal diffusivity

equations.meaning: Dual (kinetic and radiative) extinction scaling with burner mass flow. mdot burner mass flow rate (kg/s); A a positive constant set by the radiative loss. Radiative loss from a shell of thickness delta at the flame scales with flame volume and lowers T_f. Expanding the exponential for small loss gives Da_f(mdot), which tends to 0 both as mdot -> 0 and as mdot -> infinity. A critical Da_f,e therefore gives two extinction flow rates: m_e,1 (purely kinetic extinction, low system Da) and m_e,2 (radiation-induced extinction, high system Da). Order-of-magnitude scaling from the SRD (its Eqs. 3-6), not a fitted correlation.

sources.quote: This final expression, shown in Fig. 1.4 with Daf plotted versus m, clearly demonstrates the dual extinction nature of the problem.

The lower value corresponds to the m2 in the coefficient term of Eq. (6 ), and hence represents purely kinetic exti nction, in the absence of heat loss. The upper value corresponds to the m2 term in the exponent, and hence represents extinction being induced by radiative heat loss.

equations.meaning: Steady flame-sheet radius of a burner-generated spherical diffusion flame. r_f flame radius (m); mdot total mass flow of the fuel stream from the sphere (kg/s); rho D density times mass diffusivity, taken constant (kg m^-1 s^-1); Y_O,inf ambient oxygen mass fraction; Y_F,0 fuel mass fraction in the supply stream; nu stoichiometric oxygen-to-fuel mass ratio. Textbook Shvab-Zeldovich result for a steady, adiabatic flame sheet with unity Lewis number in an unbounded quiescent oxidizer, neglecting the burner's own surface. It shows why diluted fuels and higher O2 give smaller flames, and why the flame grows linearly with flow. The real flames approach it only slowly (tens of seconds) and radiation keeps them from reaching it at high flow.

Lewis and Zeldovich numbers. alpha thermal diffusivity (m^2/s); D_i mass diffusivity of the deficient reactant (m^2/s); T_a activation temperature (K); T_ad adiabatic flame temperature (K); T_inf ambient temperature (K). Pulsating thermo-diffusive instability is expected for Le sufficiently above 1 and large Ze. Helium dilution raises the flame temperature (lower molar heat capacity than N2), which lowers Ze and is expected to suppress oscillations. CO2 (proposed for a third round) would lower T_ad and raise Ze. Textbook definitions.

sources.quote: However, higher characteristic flame temperatures (given the lower molar heat capacity of monatomic He versus that of diatomic N2) correspond to lower Zeldovich numbers, which would suppress oscillations based on Sivashinsky’s criterion for premixed flames.

equations.meaning: Optically thin radiative heat loss per unit volume. sigma Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67e-8 W m^-2 K^-4); a_P Planck-mean absorption coefficient of the gas mixture (1/m), dominated by CO2 and H2O (and soot if present); T local gas temperature (K). This is the optically thin limit. The s-Flame SRD notes that wide-band Planck-mean coefficients over-predict loss compared with statistical narrow-band (SNB) mean coefficients in the optically thin case, and that SNB computations with gas-phase reabsorption better matched drop-tower flame trajectories. Integrated over the hot shell, it grows with flame volume, which is what drives radiative extinction of large flames.

apparatus.text: Tests ran in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS using the modular ACME chamber insert, a constant-volume chamber of about 83-90 L free volume. The burner was a 6.35 mm diameter porous sphere sintered from 316 stainless steel (10 micron media grade, about 41% porosity) on a supply tube. It carried a slightly embedded type-K surface thermocouple. The same unit (s/n 1003) served the earlier Flame Design and later CFI-G experiments. Three crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers metered fuel, oxidizer/inert and nitrogen. Their ranges were set on a nitrogen basis: 0.1, 0.5 and 1 slpm fuel MFCs were used on different days. A retracting resistive igniter, with a loop tip and later a thicker coil tip, lit the flame and was then withdrawn. Diagnostics, all synchronised by an automated script, were as follows. The ACME colour DataCam (1360x1024, 12-bit, fused-silica 'filter', often long exposures and bracketing, so frame rates near 1-10 fps) also served for thin-filament pyrometry (TFP). The CFI intensified camera (CH*, CH2O or clear filter, about 23 fps). The CIR LLL-UV intensified camera with a 310 nm OH* filter (512x512, 30 fps), used only by s-Flame among the ACME experiments. The CIR HiBMs camera with red backlight (15 fps), of little use for these soot-free flames. An analog ops camera recorded on the ground. A translatable array of 14 micron SiC fibres spaced 5 mm apart for TFP. Thermopile radiometers (0.2-11 micron) and three PMTs (OH* 310 nm, broadband, CH* 430 nm). Far-field thermocouples at 45-200 mm from the burner centre. Chamber pressure transducers. The CIR gas chromatograph sampled the chamber before and after tests. Non-imaging data were logged at 125 Hz. Accelerations were recorded by SAMS, although the rack isolation system was not used.

procedure.text: The crew only configured hardware: they swapped gas bottles, MFCs and igniter tips. Every test was commanded from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center and run automatically by a script with 68 parameters. The script steps were: open the image test point; position the TFP fibre array; preheat the igniter (e.g. 2 s at 3.5-4.49 V); start fuel flow; pulse the igniter (e.g. 0.5 s); retract it once OH* PMT ignition detection fired; then hold a constant flow or run one or more ramps and holds of fuel (and in round 1, on-orbit nitrogen dilution). Two protocols probed the two extinction branches. For radiative extinction, the flame was ignited at a given flow (often 3-17.5 cc/s), or established at about 3 cc/s and ramped up, and allowed to expand. For kinetic extinction, a near-steady flame was established at about 2-3 cc/s and then ramped down toward 1 cc/s. Extinction detection, a burner surface temperature limit of 250 C (held 3 s), or a flow timeout ended each test and stopped the gas. Typical flow times were up to about 45-120 s. An average of 15 flames were ignited per test day. The chamber was rarely vented between tests, so O2 fell and pressure rose slowly through a day ('vitiation'). Sometimes it was scrubbed through a molecular-sieve cartridge, or partly vented and refilled to change O2. The CIR gas chromatograph sampled the stirred chamber on most test days. Data were downlinked between test days so the next day's parameters could be adjusted. No testing took place during thruster firings or dockings.

psi_data.summary: PSI-23 has 4,165 files (782 GB). Almost all of it is raw imagery that is not downloaded: 1,974 per-test zips (770.6 GB) and 287 MP4 ops-camera videos (9.3 GB). The zips hold DataCam HOBJ images (568 zips, 253 GB), CFI intensified TIFFs (550, 329 GB), HiBMs (283, 130 GB), LLL-UV OH* TIFFs (286, 35 GB) and ground-recorded ops video (285, 24 GB). The downloaded raw data (1,795 files, 0.88 GB) are fully usable. They comprise a 125 Hz non-imaging data CSV for 288 test points (raw voltages: MFC flows, chamber pressure, PMTs, thermocouples, radiometers; conversions in ACME-DOC-010 Rev D) and an MFC set-point CSV for each. There are also as-run script parameter files (290) and test-timing files (266), image-completeness comments (276), daily ACME and IPSU-G logs, camera metadata, and 170 raw GC chromatograms (.asc, not reduced). Reference Data holds 48 zips of TFP fibre images (one or two per test day, ten for 20142) and 4 video files, plus the interface document (twice). Documents are rich: SRD (2010), Science Concept Review, ISRD, SORD, a 30-day operations report, a 113-page final report (2021), a data-interpretation guide and the experimental procedure with script. No reduced data (flame radius vs time, extinction flow rates, temperatures) and no ISS-results journal paper are in PSI. The experimental table is an 18-row per-test-day summary (date, atmosphere, fuel bottle, flames ignited).
