findings.claim: For nitrogen-diluted ethylene in air (20% C2H4/80% N2 fuel stream, ~21% O2, ~1 atm), a flow of 3 cc/s produced a quasi-steady spherical flame that lasted until the automated system stopped it at the 250 C burner limit. At 5-10 cc/s the same mixture's flames grew until radiative extinction. Mixtures of 25% and 30% C2H4 also showed radiative extinction at the higher flows.

sources.quote: For a case of fuel-mixture of 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 at a flow rate of 3 cc/s, a seemingly quasi-steady flame is attained for extended duration. For the same mixture, higher flow rates of 5-10 cc/s result in radiative extinctions, corresponding to high system Damköhler number.
The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C.

findings.claim: Both extinction branches were observed for the same nitrogen-diluted ethylene mixtures in air. With 20-30% C2H4, non-sooty spherical flames established at 3 cc/s extinguished kinetically during a ramp down before the flow reached 1 cc/s. They extinguished radiatively during a ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s. A 15% C2H4 mixture could not sustain a quasi-steady flame even at 3 cc/s. Flames at 13.5-15 cc/s were asymmetric and extinguished radiatively. This is the dual-extinction 'isola' behaviour predicted by theory, but the extinction flow rates are given only as brackets.

sources.quote: For mixtures with 20-30% C2H4 content, spherical non-sooty flames are established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions are observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. For the same mixtures, radiative extinctions are observed when the non-sooty flames are established at 3 cc/s and the flow rates are ramped up before reaching 8 cc/s.
The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down.
High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished.

findings.claim: Nitrogen-diluted methane (45% CH4/55% N2) in air at ~21% O2 gave no quasi-steady flame within the 0.5 slpm fuel MFC range: all flows were in the kinetic-extinction regime. In 30% O2/70% N2, the same mixture burned for about 15 s at 2 cc/s and about 10 s at 3 cc/s. At 5 and 9.4 cc/s the flames expanded to large radii and extinguished radiatively. Reducing the flow from 2 to 1 cc/s produced extinction during the ramp, interpreted as kinetic. 30%, 25% and 20% CH4 behaved similarly, while 15% CH4 flames extinguished very quickly after ignition.

sources.quote: The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established.

For 45% CH4 / 55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s are established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and 9.4 cc/s, the flames expand to large radii and then extinguish, demonstrating radiative extinction at high system Damköhler number.
For 15% CH4 / 85% N2, flames are ignited, but extinguish soon after.

findings.claim: Radiative extinction of growing spherical diffusion flames, predicted computationally but never conclusively seen in 2.2 s or 5 s drop towers or on parabolic aircraft, turned out to be a common event on the ISS. Kinetic extinction could also be reached only because a near-steady flame could be established first and then ramped down. The investigators list it first among the flight's initial surprises and discoveries.

sources.quote: Surprisingly, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event in ISS testing, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions.

Initial surprises and discoveries include: (1) Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air seem to demonstrate kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low system Da) and radiative extinction at high flow rates (high system Da).

Although experimental data of good quality were obtained on the transient response of spherical diffusion flames in the 2.2-s drop tower facility, the duration was insufficient to observe radiative extinction.

findings.claim: No inherently sooty flame was produced. This held for ethylene (up to 40-50% C2H4 in N2 after ramping, and 20-30% C2H4 in He), with either diluent, and at ~21% or ~30% O2. Soot appeared only during forced hot-wire ignition and dissipated as the flame grew. The sooty-flame objective (soot onset vs residence time, soot effect on extinction) was therefore not met. The team proposes propane and CO2 dilution for any third round.

sources.quote: (2) Ethylene flames which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred during forced ignition from the hotwire, but soon dissipated. Inherent sooting was also not found for enriched oxidizer conditions or for either of the inerts, i.e., N2 and He, examined.
None of the flames were inherently sooty, so the effect of soot on extinction could not be investigated.
experimentation with C3H8 is of utmost importance if we are to achieve our original objectives with respect to characteristically sooty flames

findings.claim: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames (15-45% H2 in N2, into air, 0.5 slpm fuel MFC) did not extinguish radiatively. At 10 cc/s they appeared quasi-steady until the flow timed out. The investigators conclude that such flames would have to grow much larger than the chamber and flow range allow before radiative loss could extinguish them. Hydrogen produces only H2O as a radiating product. Extinction during flow ramp-down was seen and may be kinetic, but this is unconfirmed.

sources.quote: 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures are investigated, where flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing quasi- steady until time out. The hydrogen flames would likely need to reach a diameter much larger than that accommodated by the experiment to extinguish radiatively.
Additionally, pure H2 only produces H2O as its radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties.

findings.claim: Nitrogen-diluted H2/CH4 blends in air behaved differently with composition. 20% H2/25% CH4/55% N2 flames extinguished radiatively during expansion even at flows as low as 2 cc/s. Some showed wavy oscillation and local extinction and re-ignition before final extinction. 30% H2/15% CH4/55% N2 flames at flows up to 15 cc/s persisted with patchy extinction areas until the flow timed out. Kinetic extinction was not identified for either blend. The authors suggest the kinetic extinction radius may lie within the burner radius (about 3.2 mm for the 6.35 mm spherical burner).

sources.quote: However, it seems that even for very small flow rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction is by the radiative mechanism during flame expansion.
Radiative extinction is difficult to identify conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seem to last, although with patchy extinction areas, until time out.
The characteristic extinction radius may be within the burner radius, precluding experimental identification.
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm

findings.claim: Replacing nitrogen with helium (about 6 times higher thermal conductivity) made ignition much harder with the same hot-wire settings. On the first helium day (20132), 25% H2/20% CH4/He into 21% O2/He, igniter power was raised cautiously and the first ignition came on the ninth test: 7 flames from 15 tests. The team switched to a thicker coil igniter tip and moved part of the matrix to ~30% O2. Even so, 13 attempts with 20% C2H4/80% He in 21% O2/He failed to ignite, and 3 cc/s of 30% C2H4/He in 21% O2/He did not ignite. Methane without hydrogen needed even more ignition energy.

sources.quote: The power level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 (20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63.
Although 13 tests were conducted with the 21% O2/He atmosphere, ignition was not achieved.
Without H2 in the mixture, even larger energy and power were needed to ignite the mixtures.
The 3 cc/s case did not ignite.

findings.claim: Helium-diluted flames had extinction limits shifted relative to nitrogen-diluted ones, and kinetic extinction was hard to isolate. Many helium flames were stopped by the 250 C burner temperature limit before self-extinction: 45% H2/He at 10 and 14 cc/s (the top of that fuel MFC's range) in 30% O2/He; 5 cc/s of 20-30% C2H4/He in 30% O2/He. The authors attribute this to helium carrying heat to the burner. Ramp-down extinctions may thus reflect burner heat loss rather than chemistry. At higher flows (6-17.5 cc/s), helium-diluted CH4, C2H4 and H2/CH4 flames expanded to apparent radiative extinction. In 17.5% O2/82.5% He, 45% H2/He flames appeared to show both radiative and kinetic extinction.

sources.quote: For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the tests produced flames at 10 and 14 cc/s (MFC limit of 1 SLMP) that expanded after ignition, but were extinguished by the automated protocol because the burner reached the 250°C temperature limit before any self-extinction could occur.

(7) The highly thermal conductive nature of He seems to affect various processes, such as ignition and heat transfer to the burner (affecting isolation of kinetic extinction), despite higher characteristic flame temperatures.
Helium-diluted hydrogen displayed radiative extinction and showed kinetic extinction for oxygen-reduced environments. Helium-diluted ethylene and methane exhibited radiative extinction.

findings.claim: Some helium-diluted H2/CH4 flames showed an unexplained 'flash'. With 25% H2/20% CH4/He into 21% O2/He at 5-10 cc/s, and 20% H2/25% CH4/He at 17.5 cc/s, the flame seemed to disappear and then re-ignite with a flash, or to waver, before final extinction. With 20% H2/25% CH4/He at 5 and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignited but extinguished at once with almost no flame-front expansion.

sources.quote: For 5-10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're- ignite' with a "flash" before final extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon.
For 5 cc/s and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but immediately extinguishes, with almost no observable flame-front expansion.

findings.claim: The pulsating (Le > 1) instabilities that theory and simulation predict near both extinction limits were not conclusively observed, at least in the video. Wavy or oscillatory flame behaviour before extinction was common. The investigators attribute much of it to the region near the burner support tube, where fuel is lacking and heat is lost, rather than to intrinsic pulsation. PMT and radiometer records still have to be analysed for oscillations.

sources.quote: However, such instabilities were not conclusively observed in the ISS tests, at least from the video images. Radiometer and PMT data will need to be examined in detail.
Many flames presented unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region, rather than inherent pulsating instability.

findings.claim: Flame luminosity was not a reliable indicator of flame strength. Before flight, simulations showed CH* emission from expanding flames decaying while peak temperature rose, so extinction should be judged from temperature or radiometer data rather than visible light. The flight confirmed this as a finding. Diluted hydrogen flames were barely or not at all visible to the DataCam and ops camera, and were tracked mainly by OH* (310 nm) imaging and PMTs.

sources.quote: (8) Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).
In particular, Fig. 1.13 shows that the peak visible emission from CH* decreases rapidly despit e an ever increasing flame temperature.
A critical challenge for s-Flame was in imaging the pure hydrogen and diluted hydrogen flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the DataCam and analog operations camera.

findings.claim: A fuel-bottle safety error was found during the mission. The first H2/CH4 blend bottle leaked on installation (July 2019). The review showed that the H2/CH4 bottles had been over-filled: a leak into the open CIR rack volume could reach flammable or explosive limits. The safe fill pressure had been set by considering the two fuels separately rather than combining them with Le Chatelier's mixing rule. The final report states the plan to vent each H2/CH4 bottle to a safe pressure before its use.

sources.quote: During the review of the leaked fuel bottle, it was determined that the bottles with the hydrogen/methane blends (H2/CH4) were over-filled in that the flammable and explosive limits could be reached if the fuel were to leak into the open volume of the CIR rack.
The two fuels were considered individually instead of collectively using Le Chatelier's mixing rule.
Therefore, before their use, the plan is to vent each H2/CH4 bottle to a pressure that will be safe if a bottle leaks into the CIR free volume.

relevance.text: s-Flame is fundamental combustion research, not a materials or suppression test, so its fire-safety value is indirect. (1) In quiescent microgravity, a fed diffusion flame need not reach a steady state. If its fuel supply is large it keeps growing until radiative loss kills it. If the supply is small it dies from too short a residence time. This flow-controlled 'isola' is the gas-phase analogue of the low-flow and radiative quenching limits relevant to a leak or a pyrolysing material in a still cabin. Validated chemistry, transport and radiation models from these data would improve predictions of fire size and extinction in spacecraft. The gas-burner results are not material flammability limits. (2) Detection: diluted hydrogen flames were nearly invisible to colour cameras, and the investigators stress that luminosity does not track flame strength. Visual or visible-band detection of hydrogen or lean flames in a cabin could therefore miss a burning flame, whereas OH* (310 nm) UV sensing worked. (3) Prevention: the leaked and over-filled H2/CH4 bottles show that flammability of fuel mixtures leaking into an enclosed rack must be assessed with mixing rules (Le Chatelier), not per component. (4) Helium-diluted atmospheres made ignition much harder and moved extinction limits, a reminder that the inert gas is not a passive participant.

sources.quote: Understanding extinction phenomenon is paramount to revealing basic flame processes, along with highlighting implications in fire safety.
(8) Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).
The two fuels were considered individually instead of collectively using Le Chatelier's mixing rule.
The role of the inerts will be better revealed, as the tests showed that they are far from passive participants in the flame dynamics and responses.

habitat_conditions.text: All tests were near 1 atm. The chamber was filled to about 1 atm (101 kPa) and rose slightly with vitiation; the uncalibrated ACME transducer reads 104-110 kPa. That is close to Earth sea level (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa). Round 1 used ~21% and ~30% O2 in N2; round 2 used ~21%, ~30% and 17.5% O2 in He. The ~30% O2 cases match the oxygen fraction expected for Moon habitats (30% or more), but at about 1.4 times the habitat pressure (70.3 kPa or less). So the oxygen partial pressure (about 30 kPa) was higher than in such a habitat (about 21 kPa or more), and the nitrogen dilution was greater than in a reduced-pressure cabin. Reduced-pressure, elevated-O2 atmospheres such as the 100% O2 / 29.6 kPa spacesuit were not tested. Helium atmospheres are not cabin-relevant: they were chosen to change transport and Lewis number. Results transfer to exploration atmospheres only through the models they are meant to validate.

earth_benefits.text: Better-validated kinetic, transport and radiation models for diffusion flames, the basis of most engines and burners. The investigators cite lean-burn engine development for higher efficiency and lower emissions, plus improved understanding of extinction, ignition in non-premixed flames and the role of diluents.

sources.quote: The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth.

limitations.text: Results are preliminary and largely qualitative. The final report (2021) gives extinction behaviour as flow brackets and descriptive observations. No reduced flame-radius histories, temperature profiles, extinction flow rates or model comparisons are in PSI, and no peer-reviewed paper with ISS results is listed (only conference talks and posters). Several extinction-mode attributions are explicitly 'presumed' or 'seems'.

sources.quote: Currently, detailed analyses of the acquired data, computational simulation, and theoretical analysis are ongoing.

limitations.text: The porous sphere did not produce spherically symmetric flames at high flow. More gas escaped through the sintered joint to the supply tube, so flames shifted toward the tube and became ellipsoidal or even parabolic, with local quenching near the tube. Heat loss to the support tube adds further asymmetry. This limited the flows usable for radiative extinction.

sources.quote: At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube.

limitations.text: Flow-control limits. MFC ranges were often too small (e.g. a 0.1 slpm fuel MFC on 19352) or used at small fractions of full scale, where the delivered flow differed from the set point. Overshoot, undershoot and small flow perturbations showed up in the PMT signals. MFCs are calibrated for nitrogen, and the chamber-calculator estimates of chamber composition ignore gas conversion factors (about 0.6 for ethylene).

sources.quote: The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints.
In Aug. 2021, it was determined that the ACME chamber calculator doesn’t account for gas conversion factors where the Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) were calibrated for nitrogen.

limitations.text: Uncontrolled atmosphere drift. The chamber was rarely vented between tests, so O2 decreased and pressure and combustion products increased over each test day. GC samples exist, but species concentrations have not been reduced because the analysis software runs only on retired Windows versions. The ACME pressure transducer had not been calibrated in years.

sources.quote: NASA plans to analyze the files to determine species concentrations and make those results available, but the agency abandoned use of Windows 7 and earlier operating systems which has thus far prevented the planned analysis.

limitations.text: The test matrix was inconsistent. Ignition problems in round 2 forced part of the helium matrix from the planned ~21% O2 to ~30% O2, which limits planned test-to-test comparisons. The planned 25% H2/20% CH4/N2 blend was lost to a leaking bottle. The burner temperature limit (250 C) cut off many low-flow helium flames before self-extinction, confounding kinetic extinction with burner heat loss.

sources.quote: As a result, tests were conducted with an inconsistent mix of oxygen concentrations, which may yield valuable insights, but limits the planned test-to-test comparisons.

limitations.text: Imaging losses and limits. Much of the image data on 19256 was lost (IPSU-G failure, later replaced). DataCam files were mis-formatted on 19352; both days were repeated. Hydrogen flames were invisible to the colour cameras. The two intensified cameras faced each other, so 3-D symmetry of dim flames cannot be assessed. The TFP fibre arms partly block the intensified cameras' fields of view. Radiation damage causes growing numbers of hot pixels. The DataCam's long exposures cut frame rates to about 1 fps in some tests.

sources.quote: This unfortunately inhibits assessment of three-dimensional flame symmetry because the CFI intensified camera and Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) cameras were opposite of each other.
it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.

limitations.text: The finite chamber (about 83 L, constant volume) limits the largest flames and, through oxygen depletion, the useful test time. The SRD set a 25 s bound for a 20 cm penetration depth. Because radiative reabsorption enlarges flames at extinction, the investigators note that chamber size becomes a parameter. The acceleration environment has not been checked against SAMS data.

sources.quote: Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction, making the chamber size an important parameter.

It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).

open_questions: Extract flame radius vs time (peak CH*/OH*) from the LLL-UV and CFI intensified image zips for the nitrogen-diluted ethylene and methane tests. Compare the trajectories with transient detailed-chemistry simulations with and without radiation reabsorption, which the reports say are underway.

Use the 125 Hz MFC, PMT and burner-thermocouple traces to pin down the actual flow rate and burner temperature at each detected extinction. Classify each extinction as kinetic, radiative or burner-heat-loss, giving a quantitative extinction map (flow vs fuel fraction vs O2 vs diluent).
Look for pulsating instability in the PMT (OH*, CH*) and radiometer time series near extinction (frequency, amplitude, growth rate), comparing N2- vs He-diluted flames as Objective C intended.
Reduce the thin-filament pyrometry images (Reference Data fibre zips and DataCam HOBJ) to radial temperature profiles, especially for the hydrogen flames where the fibres glowed.
Reduce the 170 GC chromatograms to chamber O2/CO2/fuel concentrations, so that test-by-test ambient O2 (vitiation) is known rather than nominal.
Investigate the 'flash' re-ignition events seen in helium-diluted H2/CH4 flames, using synchronized PMT and intensified-camera data.
Check the acceleration environment for each test from PIMS/SAMS archives (not in PSI) for g-jitter effects on flame symmetry.

gaps: No reduced quantitative results (flame radius histories, extinction flow rates, temperatures) and no ISS-results journal paper exist in PSI; the final report lists only conference presentations with ISS results (ASGSR 2019 and 2020, Russian conferences 2019/2021, USNCM 2021 poster). A web search (NASA s-Flame page, general search) found no later peer-reviewed s-Flame ISS paper; the NASA investigation page has no results.

Flow rates are reported only in 'cc/s' without stating whether they are standard or actual volumetric rates or whether they refer to the total fuel-mixture stream; the parameter files give slpm on a nitrogen basis. Values are kept as reported.

Chamber pressure: the CIR chamber calculator workbook named in the data-interpretation guide (the reliable pressure/composition record) was not found among the downloaded files. The 1.03-1.09 atm range was computed from the uncalibrated ACME PTA3 channel of the 288 _data.csv files using the ACME-DOC-010 conversion and should be treated as approximate.
Actual ambient O2 per test is unknown: only nominal ~21%/~30%/17.5% values are given; GC data are unreduced and the chamber calculator is not available.

Data quality (experimental table CSV): the Atmosphere column reads '~21% O2 with N3/N4/N5/N6' and one fuel cell '50% C2H4 with N3' (spreadsheet auto-increment of 'N2'); row 20132 is labelled 'First round of tests with nitrogen-diluted fuel' although it was the first helium (second-round) day; row 20190 lists '35% H2 with He' while the reports say 45% H2 with He; tests.csv parses the H2/CH4 bottles 20006 and 20013 as fuel fraction 1.0 although they were diluted 55% with N2 on orbit. The 30-day report's Table 1 also mislabels the helium round as 'First round of tests, with helium-diluted fuel and oxygen'.

Data quality: the metadata zip is named 'PSI-23_metadata_PSI-99_ACME s-Flame.zip', but PSI-99 is SAFFIRE-II; its content is the PSI-23 record. The two Reference Data PDFs 'ACME-DOC-010_D.pdf' and 'ACME-DOC-010_D Software Interface Design Description.pdf' are identical (same size and text). The 2012 FLEX paper (PSI-23_Presentations_20120015928.pdf) was previously filed under Raw Data.

The PSI record lists only Law (PI), Tse (Co-I) and Stocker (PS); the final report also names Kurt Sacksteder as Co-I and Vladimir Gubernov as lead collaborator. The PSI record end date (2019-11-24) precedes the last test day (2020-07-08).
Objective statements in the 30-day reports are mislabelled (objective C printed as 'A' or 'B'); content is otherwise identical to the SRD.

Documents contain staff work contact details (e-mail, phone) and the GC raw files contain an instrument user-name header field; these were not copied. The ACME-DOC-010 interface document defines FTP login parameter fields (no actual credentials seen). No text addressed to an AI was found.

Raw-data notes were sampled, not read in full: the _Comments.txt files record only image-download completeness (e.g. missing frames on 19256), the as-run/test-point .txt files are script parameter lists, and the daily test-point log spreadsheets hold only image counts for 20164; none contains science observations.
Three drawing/poster PDFs (s1101mfa0100_C, s1101mfa1800_B, PS-01374 ACME poster, PS-03403 ACME on the ISS) have no text layer and were not read; none is a report.

Most ACME presentations in PSI-23 (ASGSR 2012/2013, CSSCI 2014, AIAA 2012, IAC 2008, researcher's guide) predate the s-Flame flight and describe ACME generally; they were used only for hardware context.

Publications pass 2026-11-15: all 44 publications listed in the PSI record were checked (35 by abstract, 2 by full text, 7 not reachable; details in data/publications/PSI-23.json). All date from 1994-2019, before the 2019-2020 flight, and none reports s-Flame ISS results. Six confirm background already in the record (2.2 s too short for steady flames; oscillation before radiative extinction in theory and low-pressure tests; luminosity not tracking flame strength; the porous-sphere configuration).

PSI-25.one_line: Astronauts ran 129 burns of small plastic and fabric samples in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS while lowering the oxygen with nitrogen, to find the weakest airflow and the lowest oxygen at which solids keep burning without gravity, and to compare that with the Earth test NASA uses to approve materials.
PSI-25.summary: BASS-II ran 129 burns of small solid samples (126 in 2014, three in 2016) in a 7.6 cm square flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox. Imposed air flows ranged from below 1 to about 55 cm/s. For the first time on ISS the glovebox was diluted with nitrogen, so oxygen ranged from 22.2% to 13.6%. Five teams studied separate configurations: thin PMMA films and thick PMMA slabs in opposed flow, PMMA rods in opposed and concurrent flow, and a cotton-fibreglass fabric in concurrent flow. Thin-film flames went out from radiative loss at about 1 cm/s in air, whatever their thickness, and at 2.6-4 cm/s near 16% O2. The limit fitted for concurrent rod flames has its minimum at about 13.5% O2 (lowest reading with a flame: 13.6%), against a 15.4% upward-burning limit on Earth. Opposed spread over rods persisted to 17.5% O2, against 19% in normal gravity. Fabric flames quenched at 1-5 cm/s. Most flames released under 100 W and burned fuel-rich, producing much CO. Weak ventilation near spacecraft surfaces can therefore sustain flames where Earth tests show none.

question.text: BASS-II tested the same hypothesis as BASS (PSI-26): a material in microgravity with adequate ventilation burns as well as, or better than, the same material in normal gravity at the same pressure, O2 concentration and temperature. NASA screens spacecraft materials with an upward-burning 1 g test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), considered the worst case on Earth, but it may not be conservative in space. BASS-II set out to (1) study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows; (2) bridge the gap between Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and real flammability in microgravity; (3) give preliminary data to refine the science requirements of the follow-on SoFIE project; and (4) use practical, thicker fuels in realistic geometries (slabs, rods, a spherical section, films and fabrics). Many tests looked for the minimum O2 or minimum flow at which a material still burns in space, to compare with Earth-based limits. Others looked at how fast a fire grows and whether the flame reaches a finite size, which matters for firefighting strategy. The new variable compared with BASS was ambient O2, lowered below 21% by adding nitrogen to the glovebox. Despite the project's name, the PSI documents describe no suppression tests in BASS-II; the nitrogen was used only to dilute the atmosphere.

sources.quote: One objective of the BASS–II tests is to identify what is the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft environments, and how does that compare to the terrestrial upward burning used to screen the materials for safe use aboard spacecraft.
Many of the tests focused on finding a minimum O2 concentration or flow velocity where a material will burn in space, to compare with the Earth-based limits.

Flame growth rates are also of interest, to determine how quickly a fire in space can grow and if the flames reach a finite size or continue to grow. This has implications for firefighting strategies in spacecraft.
GN2 is used to vitiate the MSG working volume to desired O2 levels.
OBJECTIVE: Conduct BASS-2 (Burning and Suppression of Solids-2) operations by adding GN2 to the WV to reduce the O2 partial pressure in order to get a stable blue flame for longer periods of time.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a solid heats the unburnt fuel ahead of it to its pyrolysis temperature. The fuel vapour then mixes with oxygen and burns. In opposed flow (air moving against the spread direction, like downward burning on Earth) the heating comes from a small region at the flame's leading edge. In concurrent flow (air moving with the spread, like upward burning) the whole flame preheats the fuel and can grow. The gas residence time at the leading edge scales as $\alpha_g/V_g^2$. Three regimes follow. At high flow, finite-rate chemistry cannot keep up with the short residence time and the flame blows off (kinetic regime; a small Damkohler number). At moderate flow, the spread rate of a thin fuel is set only by heat conduction and is independent of flow (thermal regime of de Ris). At very low flow, the long residence time lets surface and gas radiation remove a growing fraction of the heat, and the flame quenches (radiative regime). Plotted as O2 against flow, these limits form a U-shaped flammability boundary with a blowoff branch and a quenching branch. On Earth, buoyancy imposes its own flow at the flame: about 0.5 m/s at ignition for the BASS-II rods, and of order 20 cm/s at the base of an upward flame. So the low-flow quenching branch and the bottom of the U, where the minimum oxygen for burning lies, can only be reached in sustained microgravity. For rods and stagnation flames the investigators use a stretch rate $a$ in place of velocity. At about 1-2 cm/s, comparable to a diffusive velocity of 2 cm/s, convection and diffusion supply oxygen at similar rates, and the flame changes from residence-time-limited to diffusion-limited. Thermally thin fuels heat through their whole thickness, so spread rate varies as 1/thickness. Thick fuels such as millimetre PMMA slabs keep a cold core, so ignition and growth are slower and heat loss into the solid and the holder matters.

sources.quote: As the opposed-flow velocity is increased, the residence time being inversely proportional to the square of velocity, finite-rate kinetics in the gas phase becomes important leading ultimately to the blowoff extinction.

Numerical (Refs. 6 and 7) and experimental (Refs. 8 and 9) studies have established the radiative regime in the mild opposed-flow environment in which the flame spread rate decreases as the opposed-flow velocity is reduced leading to flame extinguishment (Ref. 10) if the flow velocity is sufficiently low.
at the point of ignition it is approximately 0.50 m/s, which is an order of magnitude greater than the largest forced-flow velocity tested in the BASS–II experiments

The normal-gravity upward limiting O2 concentration of 15.4 percent O2 (Ref. 23) is plotted for comparison, assuming linear superposition of the buoyant flow velocity at the base of the flame (20 cm/s (Ref. 32)) and the 4-cm/s forced-flow velocity.
The transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the forced-flow velocity becomes the same order as the diffusive velocity (U/UD = 1) for this geometry.

The flammability map in terms of O2 and stretch rate a (Ref. 5) was shown to consist of a blowoff and new quenching branch where the low power flame (due to the reduced temperature) is too weak to compensate for the surface radiative heat loss. It was pointed out that this is likely only observable in microgravity.

apparatus.text: The BASS hardware from PSI-26 was reused with new samples, igniters and flash cards. The flow duct was the 7.6 x 7.6 x 17 cm black-anodised duct originally built for SPICE gas-jet flames, installed in the MSG in the ISS Destiny Lab. A variable-speed fan drove air through a honeycomb straightener and an inlet screen. Perforated restrictor plates (0, 1 or 2) on the fan inlet set the range: up to about 55 cm/s with none and about 35 cm/s with two. A TSI 8475 omnidirectional air-velocity transducer measured duct flow. It had a response time of about 1 min and displayed whole cm/s only (about +/-0.5 cm/s). So low flows were set by fan potentiometer and converted using fan calibrations made at the end of each operations day. The fan stops at a finite voltage (above 3.8 V), so the lowest flows sit just above shut-off. An uncalibrated thermopile radiometer (CaF2 window, 0.13-11 um) in the downstream top corner gave a relative flame signal. Samples were lit with Kanthal A-1 29-gauge hot-wire igniters (0.8-1 ohm, 3.5-3.8 A). A Nikon D300s still camera (4,320 x 2,968 pixels, 60 mm lens) looked through the top window at about 1 frame/s. A colour video camera looked through the front window via a mirror; its overlay showed N2 flow, fan voltage, air speed and radiometer. New in BASS-II: the MSG GN2 supply (up to 0.5 L/min through a mass-flow controller) diluted the 250 L glovebox work volume. Before and after each burn, hand-held CSA-CP (O2 at 0.1% resolution, CO 0-1,000 ppm, plus HCl and HCN) and CDM (CO2 0-5%) sensors read the well-mixed work-volume gas. The CSA-CP O2 reading was corrected each day by a constant offset to the ISS Major Constituents Analyzer (MCA). Combustion products left the duct into the sealed work volume, whose filters convert CO to CO2 during the post-test purge.

sources.quote: The black anodized 7.6- by 7.6- by 17-cm rectangular flow duct with rounded corners was originally built to perform gas jet diffusion flame studies (Ref. 10).
With no restrictors, the maximum flow velocity was ~55 cm/s, and with two restrictors this was reduced to ~35 cm/s.
The air velocity transducer probe had a response time of approximately 1 min and its digital display only read out to the units place (no decimals) yielding an effective resolution of ±0.5 cm/s.
The fan voltage was calibrated with the airspeed transducer at the end of every operations day.
Note that the fan turns off at a finite voltage (above 3.8 volts), so it is recommended to not use the 3.8 volts zero flow value.
The samples were manually ignited with a Kanthal® A–1 29-gauge hot-wire igniter coil with a nominal hot wire resistance of 0.8 to 1 Ω, powered by 3.5 to 3.8 amps
The top window was used by a Nikon D300s 12.3-megapixel digital color still camera with a 60-mm lens that provided 4,320- by 2,968-pixel images.
The video camera had an overlay that displayed the N2 flow rate (cm3/min), fan voltage (10× V), air velocity transducer reading (cm/s), and the radiometer signal.
The O2 sensor (CSA-CP) is not recalibrated on orbit, so we also used the Major Constituents Analyzer (MCA) (Refs. 6 and 7) data to determine the O2 sensor offset on a daily basis.
The CO sensor in the CSA-CP is zero calibrated every 60 days, with a range of 0 to 1,000 ppm and a resolution of 1 ppm.
BASS-II will utilize the on orbit BASS hardware launched originally for SPICE on STS-126.
The MSG, shown in Figure 1.1, has a set of filter banks that capture particulates and convert the CO to CO2 using an ambient temperature catalyst.
On CSA-CP, verify display indicates readings for OXYGEN, HCN, HCL and CO. On CDM, verify display indicates readings for CO2.
The N2 was regulated with a small (<0.5 liters per minute (LPM)) MKS Instruments 179A mass flowmeter and entered the flow duct through a small nozzle just downstream of the fan.

procedure.text: Each PI had a priority-ordered matrix of about 20 samples, and the ground team directed the crew in real time. For reduced-O2 tests, the crew first flowed GN2 into the closed work volume (MSG air circulation off, BASS fan at maximum) for 25-225 min, as timed by the CSTR dilution model. They recorded CSA-CP and CDM readings before and after each burn. The crew mounted a sample, positioned the igniter within about 1 mm of it, set the flow restrictor and fan, and pulled the igniter lever until a flame appeared; ignition could take up to 60 s in the plan and up to 230 s in practice for rods at low O2. The still camera then ran at about 1 frame/s and the radiometer gain was set. Procedures then differed by sub-investigation. (1) Bhattacharjee: opposed-flow films were ignited at a set flow (mostly 5 cm/s, some 2-10). Flow was then stepped down gradually to radiative extinction, or raised to look for blowoff. Most runs were in air or at about 17% O2, with one at 15%. (2) Miller: thick slabs were burned in opposed flow at 3-20 cm/s for long times, up to about 31 min. Flow was held at plateaus for steady spread and reduced to quenching. O2 was not controlled during a test and drifted down by up to about 3 points as the slab burned. (3) Olson: rods were ignited at the upstream hemispherical tip, typically at 5 cm/s. For quenching limits, the flow was lowered in steps, each held at least about 100 s (the solid response time); tests lasted up to 28 min. For blowoff limits, the flow was raised quickly. Complementary 5.18 s drop-tower blowoff tests were run on the ground. (4) Fernandez-Pello: rods were ignited at the downstream end at high opposed flow. The flow was then reduced in steps, with pauses for steady spread, until extinction. Some tests alternated the fan potentiometer between two settings at 1-2 min intervals to probe the flame's response time. (5) T'ien: fabric was ignited at the leading edge for concurrent spread at 4-11 cm/s, and the flow was often reduced to quenching or raised to blowoff. O2 was fixed by the prior dilution for each test. Partly burned samples were sometimes re-ignited. (6) Ferkul: Nomex was tried in concurrent flow at 8-15 cm/s, and the candle was burned in opposed flow at decreasing flows. After each burn the crew photographed the sample. The work volume was purged for 3 min before access, with further cooling time for touch temperature. The fan was calibrated at the end of each day. Samples were returned to Earth for mass-loss measurements.

psi_data.summary: PSI-25 lists 695 files (274.6 GB). The usable material is small. The 2021 NASA Technical Memorandum (BASS-II Summary Report, TM-20210011385, 141 pages) is the core source: each PI's results, full per-test matrices with crew/PI observations, the dilution model, the anomaly list and a publication list. Also available are the 2010 SRD and hardware manifest, a ReadMe that explains the matrix columns, the per-PI test-matrix workbook, daily fan-calibration data, the crew operations procedure, and the 129-row experimental table with calibrated initial/final O2, CO2 and CO per run. The 125 raw-data 'proof sheets' are downloaded (2,153 text chunks). They hold only per-frame metadata for each still sequence: ISS frame ID, time, shutter, aperture, EV, exposure mode, ISO, and a note on the camera-to-video clock offset. In total about 18,000 frames, mostly 1/3-1/8 s at f/2.0, ISO 1000. The imagery itself is not downloaded: 296 MP4 videos (17.7 GB; downlink, second-view and still-sequence movies) and 264 zips (256.7 GB). The zips are 91 'iss0xxe' crew-camera still archives (135 GB), 58 per-test still zips (96 GB) and 115 'original videos' zips (about 26 GB). No reduced numerical data (spread rates, extinction flows) are in PSI. Numbers exist only in the TM tables and plots, and the TM points to http://flame.sdsu.edu for the Bhattacharjee image data.

findings.claim: Bhattacharjee, thin PMMA films in opposed flow at about 21% O2: flames went out by radiative extinction as the flow was lowered. This happened at about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 um films and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 um (1-2 cm wide, about 1 atm). Within the large uncertainty of flow calibration at such low speeds, the extinction velocity does not depend on thickness, although the spread rate does. A 2-D model gave 1.5 cm/s for all four thicknesses. Approaching extinction, the flame shrank and turned from orange to all blue within about 3 s. With the flow cut off completely, a 100 um flame spreading at 2.2 mm/s went out within 2 s.

sources.quote: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.
Samples were 1- and 2-cm-wide thin films of plastic (PMMA (polymethylmethacrylate)).
However, it must be mentioned that there are significant uncertainties in these values as the calibration at such low velocity has high error bars.
Moreover, the extinction velocity is identical at 1.5 cm/s for all the four thicknesses studied.

After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s, as shown by the radiometer signal drop in Figure 2.2.

findings.claim: Bhattacharjee: lowering O2 raises the radiative extinction velocity of thin PMMA. At about 16% O2 it was about 2.6 cm/s (100 um, 20 mm wide) and about 4 cm/s (200 um, 10 mm wide); the widths differed, and only two tests were made. Summary (mm/s, experiment / 2-D computation / closed-form scaling): 21% O2: 10 +/- 5 / 15 / 7.5; 16% O2: 30 +/- 5 / 35 / 10. The computation showed kinetic effects setting in above about 16 cm/s at 16% O2. The as-run log records high-flow blowoff of 100 and 200 um films at about 17.4% O2 (fan potentiometer 6.0-7.0), whereas two film runs at about 21% O2, with the fan raised to its maximum setting (air display about 10 cm/s), kept spreading without blowing off.

It should be mentioned that the width of the sample was different, 20 mm for the 100-μm sample and 10 mm for the 200-μm sample.

findings.claim: Bhattacharjee: across opposed flows from about 40 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s in microgravity, the highest spread rate over 100 um PMMA (2 cm wide, about 20.7-21% O2) was 2.2 mm/s. This is about the same as the 2.0 mm/s measured for downward spread in 1 g air on the same fuel, and the flame shapes were similar. The authors conclude that downward spread over PMMA at 21% O2 on Earth is thermally controlled with little kinetic effect. Applying the de Ris thin-fuel formula to the 2.2 mm/s maximum spread rate for 100 um film gives F = 4.76. Combined with 1 g thick-fuel data (0.044 mm/s), this gives an effective buoyant opposed velocity of 1.9 cm/s and a thin/thick transition thickness of 5.2 mm for downward spread in air.

sources.quote: The average spread rate over the 100-µm-thick sample in the normal-gravity experiments is found to be 2.0 mm/s (see Figure 2.19(b)).

At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed. The highest spread rate in the microgravity environment, 2.2 mm/s, is about the same as the downward spread rate.
This indicates that at 21 percent O2 level, downward spread over PMMA can be considered thermally controlled with minimal kinetic effect.
With F evaluated, experimental data for flame spread over thick PMMA is used to determine the effective velocity induced by buoyancy as 1.9 cm/s.
For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.

findings.claim: Miller and Wichman, thick PMMA slabs (1-5 mm) in opposed flow at 2-21 cm/s (Table 5.1; the report text says 3-20 cm/s) and 16.8-22.2% O2: steady spread rates were very low, 0.012-0.144 mm/s. Examples are 0.144, 0.131 and 0.106 mm/s for a 1 mm two-sided slab at 5, 3 and 2 cm/s and 19.2-18.7% O2, and 0.012 mm/s for a 5 mm two-sided slab at 10 cm/s and about 18% O2. Spread rate fell with increasing thickness and decreasing flow. Two-sided burns spread faster than one-sided burns (backed by the metal holder), and one-sided flames needed a higher flow to survive. For 1 mm slabs, the 1.2 cm wide samples spread more slowly than the 2.2 cm wide ones. Burns lasted up to 30.7 min. A 2-D FDS direct numerical simulation over-predicted the spread rate.

findings.claim: Miller and Wichman, thick-slab extinction: near air (about 21-22% O2), flames spread over the slab surface and left a long bubbled remnant. Below about 19% O2, two-sided slabs no longer spread over the surface; the flame instead consumed the fuel from the trailing edge, as in 1 g downward burning. Most tests ended in quenching at a finite flow. For one-sided slabs, thicker samples extinguished at lower O2 but higher flow. Two-sided slabs extinguished at much lower flows than one-sided ones, which the authors attribute to heat loss into the backing. The 1.2 cm wide regressing samples went out at about 1 percentage point higher O2 than the 2.2 cm ones. Example logs: a 3 mm one-sided slab self-extinguished at 13-14 cm/s in about 21-22% O2, and a 5 mm one-sided slab at 18 cm/s in about 20% O2.

findings.claim: Olson, PMMA rods (0.318-0.635 cm radius) ignited at the upstream tip in axial stagnation (concurrent) flow: the ISS tests traced a U-shaped flammability boundary in O2 against stretch rate, with a quenching branch at low stretch and a linear blowoff branch at high stretch. Its minimum is about 13.5% O2 at a = 8-12 1/s (about 1.7-2.5 cm/s for the 0.318 cm radius rod). This is well below the 15.4% O2 upward-burning limit measured in 1 g with an extra 4 cm/s forced flow, so the material stays flammable in the weak ventilation that only microgravity provides. The lowest sustained flame (0.476 cm radius rod) quenched at a final reading of 13.6% O2, from a start of 14.8%. Blowoff limits from 5.18 s drop-tower tests agreed with the ISS data. Because the blowoff branch is linear, the authors propose extrapolating 1 g blowoff limits to zero stretch as a conservative estimate of the minimum O2 for flammability in space; ground tests later found the 1 g mixed-convection blowoff boundary also linear.

sources.quote: The minimum in this boundary occurs at a = 8 to 12 s–1 at approximately 13.5 percent O2

The minimum O2 concentration of 13.5 percent O2 at a of 8 to 12 s–1 is significantly lower than the observed upward flame spread limit of 15.4 percent O2 (in normal gravity with an additional 4-cm/s forced flow (Ref. 23)), indicating the material remains flammable under the weak ventilation only obtainable in microgravity.
where the initial O2 setting was 14.8 percent O2 (by volume) and the final O2 reading was 13.6 percent O2.
The drop tower blowoff data, given by the purple dashed line, agrees very well with the flight data.

The fact that the blowoff boundary is linear with flow makes it possible to extrapolate blowoff data down to zero a and use that O2 value as an accurate but conservative estimate of the minimum O2 concentration for material flammability in space.
From these results, the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed.

findings.claim: Olson: the ignition limit lies above the extinction limit. Below about 14.5% initial O2, no sustained flame could be ignited (a 0.476 cm radius rod at 13.6% O2 did not ignite at any flow), yet flames lit at higher O2 survived down to 13.6%. Ignition delay was within about 40 s at higher O2 but rose sharply below 16% O2, to as long as 230 s for the larger rods, because heat is lost into the cold rod. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 uses a fixed igniter time of about 25 s, and BASS-II ignition delays were up to almost 10 times longer. The authors suggest that Test 1 may therefore act as an ignition test rather than a flammability test at near-limit conditions.

sources.quote: Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2, a sustained ignition could not be achieved even though flames were observed when the igniter was on and briefly after the igniter was turned off before extinguishing.
Despite this limiting O2 concentration for ignition, flames ignited at a higher O2 survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2
At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s. Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly.
The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
NASA Test 1 25-s ignition time may be too short for flammability test and so may be an ignition test.

findings.claim: Olson, rod extinction mechanisms and energy balance. Near quenching, the flame shrank to a blue hemisphere (length/width about 0.5). Its open tail leaked fuel, and the radiometer showed oscillations at a steady 1.1 Hz with growing amplitude before extinction, like quiescent candle flames in microgravity. Blowoff began as a hole in the flame at the stagnation point. Once the hole moved more than about one thermal length (about 2 mm) downstream, the flame could not move back upstream even when the flow was reduced; in one of two attempts it did re-close within 7 s. A surface energy balance using a critical Damkohler number shows fuel vaporisation taking about 70% of the flame heat flux on the blowoff branch, falling to 20% on the quenching branch. At the lowest stretch, losses (mostly surface radiation) exceed 60%. Gas radiative feedback rises from 1% to over 13% of the surface heating. The switch from blowoff to quenching occurs where the forced flow equals a diffusive velocity of about 2 cm/s.

sources.quote: Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out. Blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.
The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz as shown in the inset to Figure 6.6

Once the stagnation region is blown far enough downstream of the stagnation region (greater than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ), the flame is unable to propagate back upstream even when the flow is reduced.
It is interesting that across the entire blowoff branch, the vaporization ratio is ~70 percent, whereas it drops precipitously to 20 percent at low a along the quenching branch.
At the lowest a, the total heat loss fraction exceeds 60 percent of the total flame to surface feedback.
The transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the forced-flow velocity becomes the same order as the diffusive velocity (U/UD = 1) for this geometry.

findings.claim: Fernandez-Pello and Link, opposed-flow spread over black PMMA rods (6.35-12.7 mm diameter) at 16.8-20.9% O2 and forced flows of a few mm/s to a few cm/s: spread rate rose with opposed flow and with O2, and thinner rods spread faster. The flames were small, blue, faint and open-tailed at the lowest flows, and luminous, yellow and closed-tipped above about 2 cm/s. No sustained spread was seen below about 4 mm/s for the 6.35 and 9.525 mm rods. In microgravity, spread was sustained down to 17.5% O2, against 19% in 1 g, and was appreciably faster than in 1 g. The related journal paper (flows 0.4-8 cm/s, O2 15-21%) reports that spread rate first rises then falls as opposed flow increases, and gives 17% vs 18% for the lowest O2 sustaining spread in microgravity vs 1 g; these figures differ from the 17.5% vs 19% in the NASA TM.

sources.quote: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 0.00635- and 0.009525-m- diameter rods.
As the flow velocity rises towards 20 mm/s and above, the flames become much more luminous, with bright yellow flames, and a closed downstream tip.
While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
It is also apparent that flame spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1g for cylindrical rods of PMMA.
Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments, as shown in Figure 4.3.
The data show that as the opposed flow velocity is increased, the flame spread rate first increases, and then decreases, different from that on Earth.
Results also show that flame spread in microgravity could be faster and sustained at lower oxygen concentration (17%) than in normal gravity (18%).

findings.claim: Rods at low O2 (Fernandez-Pello and Olson): at 16.3% O2 and 5 cm/s, a black PMMA rod held a cap-shaped flame on its tip. The flame burned the hemispherical tip flat, then went out, and never spread along the rod. Olson notes that opposed-flow spread over rods was not observed below 16.4% O2 at any flow. Post-burn rods show bubble layers of methyl methacrylate vapour that burst as vapour jets. Hot material keeps producing fuel after extinction, and concurrent-rod flame oscillations persisted longer than in 1 g. The authors therefore recommend continuing spacecraft fire suppression until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapour.

sources.quote: The flame survived under the low-O2 conditions until the initially hemispherical rod tip regressed to a flat surface. It never spread along the outer surface of the rod.

This is consistent with tests for opposed-flow flame spread over rods that were also done as part of BASS–II (Ref. 14), where opposed-flow flame spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.
After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools.
This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.

findings.claim: T'ien, SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric in concurrent flow (1.2 and 2.2 cm wide, 16.4-20.8% O2, about 1 atm): 27 BASS-II tests, of which six reached quenching, three did not ignite and one blew off. Quenching flow speeds were 1-5 cm/s, higher at lower O2. This traces the low-speed quenching branch of the concurrent-spread flammability boundary, which the authors call the first such boundary determined cleanly; it agrees qualitatively with earlier theory. Near quenching the flame shrank in length and width to a circular blue flame and went out three-dimensionally. The 2.2 cm fabric did not ignite at 16.4% O2 (5 and 10 cm/s) or 16.8% O2 (5 cm/s). A 1.2 cm sample at 17.2% O2 blew off when the flow was raised from 11 to about 47 cm/s, while a 2.2 cm sample at 16.9% O2 did not blow off at 53 cm/s. The narrow samples had a smaller flammable domain, but their quenching limit was not resolved.

sources.quote: A total of 27 tests were carried out for the fabric samples in BASS–II, including six quenching tests, three nonignited tests, and one blowoff test.
The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower O2 atmosphere.
This is the first time that a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread is determined in a clean and unambiguous manner.
GMT175-T9 2.2 10 16.4 No ignition GMT175-T10 2.2 5 16.4 No ignition
GMT190-T21 1.2 11 to 47 17.2 Blow-off
GMT178-T17 2.2 6 to 53 16.9 No blowoff
In addition, because of the limited number of tests, the quenching limit for the 1.2-cm-wide sample was not resolved.

findings.claim: Ferkul: all three Nomex III fabric samples failed to sustain a flame in concurrent flow at 21.0-22.2% O2 and 8-15 cm/s; they flashed briefly or went out while the igniter was still on. The authors call this an excellent result for ISS, where Nomex is used as a fire barrier. The leftover BASS Japan-wax candle, at 17.4% O2 in opposed flow, had a long ignition and then burned at five decreasing flows from 3 cm/s. The flame went from long and sooty to hemispherical to short and mostly blue before going out at the lowest potentiometer setting (0.305). It ejected a wax droplet upstream, illustrating that low-viscosity melts can carry burning droplets to other materials in microgravity.

sources.quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.
Ignited briefly but did not spread at all and extinguished while the igniter was still on
Long ignition, but blue flame established at 3 cm/s, reduced flow in increments: potentiometers 0.6, 0.4, 0.35, 0.32, 0.31, 0.305 flame extinguished
If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.

sources.note: Ferkul rows F1-F3 of the experimental table CSV: Nomex natural (Nomex III), calibrated initial O2 22.2, 21 and 21.7%, air display 9.5, 15 and 8 cm/s.

findings.claim: Combustion products, all PMMA tests: before-and-after sensor readings showed O2 consumed against CO2 produced following the 6:5 stoichiometric ratio for PMMA over all geometries, flows and initial O2. CO per CO2 depended on geometry. Concurrent rods gave on average about 550 ppm CO per 1% CO2 (about 600 ppm in the rod-only analysis), and opposed thick slabs about 370 ppm. Opposed rods were strongly nonlinear. CO/CO2 ratios were mostly well above the 0.004 typical of efficient combustion, and for concurrent rods rose as O2 fell. O2-consumption calorimetry (13.1 kJ/g O2) puts most flames well below 100 W; the highest were about 100 W for a long thick-slab burn and about 110 W for a concurrent rod. Mass loss of 19 returned samples against O2 consumed gives a global equivalence ratio of about 1.3, so the flames were fuel-rich and released unburnt fuel, soot and CO. Rod flames were near-stoichiometric at high O2 and grew richer near the limit. The authors estimate that a BASS-II-sized fire mixed into the 106 m3 US Lab would raise CO by only about 1.5 ppm, below the 10 ppm long-term spacecraft maximum allowable concentration. The CO sensor saturated (over 1,000 ppm) in several low-O2 rod tests.

sources.quote: As shown, the data agrees very well with stoichiometric ratios for the wide range of test conditions.
Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
The opposed thick slabs fall somewhere in between, producing on average 370 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.

For efficiently burned flue gases (boilers, furnaces, etc.), this ratio is typically less than 0.004. As can be seen, most of our data is well above that, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.

The one long opposed thick slab test that caused the lower downstream corner of the front window damage released close to 100 W. A prior relatively brief concurrent rod test that released almost 110 W did not cause any damage.
we can use the above equations to solve for the effective equivalence ratio for the tests: Φglobal = 1.3, which is fuel rich.
At higher O2 concentrations, the flames are nearly stoichiometric. At lower O2 concentrations, the global equivalence ratio increases.

the CO levels in the lab would only be 1.5 ppm, well below spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) values for even long-term exposure (10 ppm), let alone the 1 hour SMAC of 55 ppm (Ref. 12).

sources.note: 'Final CO (ppm)' column of the experimental table CSV: 'OR', 'over' or '>500' entries for Olson O4, O12, O13b and Miller M5; highest numeric final CO 950 ppm (O13a); highest final CO2 3.22% (M5).

findings.claim: Ground blowoff tests on the BASS-II rod geometry in 1 g (cast PMMA rods of 0.318-1.905 cm radius, 14-18% O2, upward axial stagnation flow in a 7.6 cm tube) gave a linear blowoff boundary that runs parallel to the BASS-II microgravity boundary but at lower forced stretch. Shifting the 1-g boundary by a buoyant stretch of about 78 1/s, equivalent to a forced flow of about 16.5 cm/s for the base rod and consistent with buoyant-velocity estimates, brings the two into agreement. The authors propose measuring the 1-g blowoff boundary, adding the buoyant stretch and extrapolating to zero stretch as a ground estimate of microgravity flammability limits. Whether the buoyant-stretch constant holds for other materials is untested.

sources.quote: The normal gravity blowoff boundary was parallel to the BASS-II boundary, but shifted to lower stretch rates.

In order to account for the additional inherent buoyant stretch, the normal gravity boundary was empirically shifted to the right by a value ab =78 s-1, which for the base rod size corresponds to a forced flow velocity of 16.5 cm/s, in good agreement with buoyant flow velocity estimates.
Further research is needed to determine the applicability of the buoyant stretch constant K for different materials.

relevance.text: Prevention and material screening: BASS-II gives direct evidence that, at about 1 atm, microgravity with weak ventilation can be more hazardous than the 1 g screening configuration. The limit fitted for concurrent PMMA rod flames has its minimum at about 13.5% O2 (lowest reading with a flame: 13.6%), against a 15.4% upward limit in 1 g. Opposed spread over rods persisted to 17.5% O2, against 19% in 1 g, and was faster. Ignition at near-limit O2 took up to about 230 s, against the roughly 25 s igniter time of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, so a material that 'passes' by not igniting may still burn once lit. The dangerous range of flows (about 1-10 cm/s, around the minimum of the U-shaped boundary) is, in the authors' words, typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces. Two practical routes to Earth-based derating come out of the work: extrapolating the linear 1 g blowoff boundary to zero stretch (Olson), and using the de Ris thermal-regime correlation validated in microgravity (Bhattacharjee). For response: in these tests, low-flow flames were extinguished by cutting the ventilation, but hot thermoplastics keep releasing vapour and can eject burning droplets, so suppression should continue until the material has cooled. Nomex III did not sustain a flame in air, which supports its use as a fire barrier. Atmosphere: small (under 100 W), fuel-rich microgravity flames produced CO/CO2 ratios an order of magnitude above efficient combustion. Over 1,000 ppm CO built up in the 250 L glovebox, though dilution into a large module would keep CO low. Limits on transferability: all results are for PMMA, a cotton-fibreglass fabric and Nomex, in a small duct at about 1 atm and 13.6-22.2% O2. They are configuration-specific limits, not certified material ratings.

sources.quote: This “Goldilocks” zone of flow is unfortunately typical of spacecraft ventilation flows near surfaces.
Earthbound flammability tests need a reliable method to account for this extension of flammability in microgravity environments.
While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.

These findings suggest that under certain environmental conditions there could be a higher fire risk and a more difficult fire suppression in microgravity than on Earth, which would have significant implications for spacecraft fire safety.
finally turned fan pot to 0 to extinguish.
since the CO sensor was over-ranged for this test (>1,000 ppm full scale), so we have no quantitative value for CO for this test.

habitat_conditions.text: BASS-II ran at ISS cabin pressure: about 1 atm, with 99.2-99.5 kPa reported for the film tests. O2 ranged from 22.2% down to 13.6% (calibrated readings), close to the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa) and below it. It therefore covers normoxic and hypoxic atmospheres at sea-level pressure only. It does not reach the proposed Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less) or the 100% O2 / 29.6 kPa suit atmosphere. In those, the O2 partial pressure and mole fraction are higher, and the lower density changes residence times and the buoyant and diffusive velocities. The BASS-II limits (e.g. 13.5% O2 minimum for rods, 1-5 cm/s quenching speeds for fabric) are thus lower-bound reference points; they are not limits for exploration atmospheres. The investigators themselves list low pressure and elevated O2 among expected spacecraft conditions, but did not test them. The flow range (below 1 to about 55 cm/s) spans spacecraft ventilation speeds and near-quiescent pockets.

sources.quote: The total pressure is also monitored, which varied from 99.2 to 99.5 kPa in the tests reported.
The ambient O2 concentration in the Microgravity Science Glovebox was varied from 13.6 to 22.2 percent.
These are parameters that in addition to low pressure are expected in spacecraft environments.

Fire safety is a concern in space travel, particularly with the current plans of increasing the length of the manned space missions, and of using spacecraft atmospheres different than in Earth, such as microgravity, low-velocity gas flow, low pressure and elevated oxygen concentration.

earth_benefits.text: Buoyancy-free data with simple flow fields validate combustion models: the 2-D opposed-spread model, the de Ris correlation, the 3-D transient concurrent-spread model and FDS. These models can then be extended to buoyant flames on Earth, such as wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion. The microgravity film data showed that downward spread over PMMA in air on Earth is thermally controlled. They also gave a de Ris coefficient and a thin/thick transition thickness of about 5.2 mm usable in terrestrial fire modelling. The work also feeds normal-gravity surrogate test methods: the narrow-channel apparatus (Miller) and the zero-stretch blowoff extrapolation (Olson).

sources.quote: Detailed combustion models can be validated by data obtained in the simpler flow environment in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity.
For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.
So, the BASS–II results will be used in comparison with ground-based experimental setups aimed at replacing NASA’s current test method for screening materials used onboard spacecraft.

limitations.text: O2 was measured only before and after each burn, as a work-volume average from a hand-held CSA-CP that was out of calibration and corrected by a daily constant offset to the ISS MCA (0.1% resolution). O2 fell during long burns, by up to 3.2 percentage points (Miller M5), so the O2 at a given flow or at extinction is interpolated (Miller assumed a linear decay). Olson's boundary uses the final reading.

sources.quote: We have O2 data available at only the start and end of the test. Assuming a linear profile between these two points; we made O2 concentration graphs for each test
Calibrated initial and final O2: The O2 sensor was out of calibration, so the MCA ISS reading was used to correct the initial ISS ‘air’ reading of the sensor for the day via a constant offset.

sources.note: Largest initial-minus-final calibrated O2 among plausible rows: M5 22.2 -> 19.0 (3.2 points).

limitations.text: Flow is poorly known exactly where the limits lie. The air-velocity transducer responds in about 1 min and reads only whole cm/s. The lowest flows were set by fan potentiometer near the fan's shut-off voltage, and in the logs they are recorded as settings (e.g. pot 0.30-0.36) rather than speeds. Daily calibrations were sometimes incomplete, and flow takes time to reach the flame after a change. Bhattacharjee warns of large error bars, and Olson notes the uncertainty below 1 cm/s on the quenching branch.

sources.quote: However, it must be mentioned that there are significant uncertainties in these values as the calibration at such low velocity has high error bars.
It also emphasizes the uncertainty in the flow at the very low velocities (<1 cm/s) along the quenching branch.
Some days we ran out of time before the fan cal could be complete.

limitations.text: Few tests per condition and repeated use of samples. Each PI had about 20 samples spread over several variables, for example only two film tests at about 16% O2, with different widths. Many samples were re-ignited, cut or had their igniter leads removed, which changes geometry and pre-heating (one rod re-burn quenched at a markedly lower flow than the first burn). Ignition was manual, with variable igniter placement and timing.

sources.quote: Even though there is insufficient data at the lower O2 level, it is clear that the extinction velocity significantly increases as the O2 level is reduced and is independent of the fuel thickness.
Reburn of same rod as previous; decreased flow to extinction at 0.27 pot, much lower than previous; rod heatup effect?
Because the igniter is positioned and activated manually, there is some inherent scatter in the ignition time, but some trends are clear.

limitations.text: Small-duct and holder effects. Heat loss to the sample holders curved the flames and weakened one-sided slab flames. Narrow samples extinguished at higher O2. The duct flow profile was irregular, and wall and fuel boundary layers alter the flow the flame sees. Sample lengths of about 10 cm were too short to fine-tune flow before burnout for concurrent fabric flames, and too short for steady concurrent spread at higher flows.

sources.quote: Heat loss to the metal substrate clearly weakened this flame.
note that the measured flow profile for the BASS–II duct is quite irregular
For this thin fabric fuel in concurrent flow, flame spread rate is relatively large and the sample is not long enough to fine tune the flow speed during the 1 to 2 min of experimental run time.

limitations.text: The bottom (minimum-O2) part of the fabric flammability boundary could not be found by the varying-flow procedure, because ignition becomes sporadic near the limit; a slowly decreasing-O2 procedure would be needed. Likewise, the rod ignition limit (about 14.5% O2) masks part of the extinction boundary.

sources.quote: The bottom part of the flammability boundary that supports combustion in the lowest O2 environment is expected to be flat in this figure and cannot be determined accurately by this velocity-varying procedure. Very near the boundary, ignition of the sample is sporadic. A procedure with gradually decreasing O2 is needed.

limitations.text: Only PMMA, one cotton-fibreglass fabric, Nomex and a candle were tested, at about 1 atm. The Fernandez-Pello comparison with 1 g used non-overlapping O2 and diameter ranges and buoyant flows an order of magnitude larger, and his clear-rod data were too few to report. No suppression tests were run despite the project name.

sources.quote: Thus, in comparing the datasets, some compromises were made. In particular, as can be seen in Figure 4.3, the ranges of O2 concentrations and rod diameters employed do not completely overlap.
A few tests were conducted with clear PMMA for comparison purposes, but the data is too limited to present it here.

limitations.text: Hardware anomalies: on GMT 051 a very long thick-slab burn overheated and bubbled the Lexan door at a duct leak (repaired on GMT 86/91). Video dropped out after GMT 167 (cable repaired on GMT 170). A flat-sample blowoff attempt on GMT 205 left a soot spot. A camera-card limit cut short one Miller run, and loss of signal interrupted others.

Combined with the calibrated final O2, this gives a single extinction-boundary map across all six sub-investigations (films, slabs, two rod configurations, fabric), plotted against stretch or U/U_D.

Rep.: 17% vs 18%), and different flow descriptions (TM: spread rate increases with flow; Sci. Rep.: increases then decreases). Both are reported; the record does not resolve which applies.
