PSI-26.one_line: Astronauts burned small fabric strips, plastic spheres and slabs, and wax candles in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS to see whether solids burn more readily without gravity than in the Earth-based test NASA uses to approve materials, and whether a puff of nitrogen puts the flames out.
PSI-26.summary: BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) burned 41 small solid samples in about 115 burns inside a 76 mm square flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox in 2012-2013, at about 1 atm and 16-23% O2. Fuels were a cotton-fibreglass (SIBAL) fabric, Nomex and Ultem sheets, PMMA spheres and slabs, and wax candles, in fan-driven air flows from below 1 to about 44 cm/s, with an upstream nitrogen jet of up to 500 cc/min. The fabric, which cannot burn downward in 1 g air, spread steadily in 9-10 cm/s opposed flow. Opposed spread peaked at 10-15 cm/s; concurrent spread rose linearly with flow (2.55 versus 1.21 mm/s opposed at about 10 cm/s), and concurrent flames quenched below 1 cm/s. PMMA and candle flames survived for minutes as dim blue flames near 1 cm/s. The nitrogen jet usually removed only the leading edge, and most flames went out only when the airflow stopped. Fire-retarded Nomex HT90-40 and Ultem did not burn at 21-22% O2. Normal-gravity screening therefore does not bound flammability in every configuration.

question.text: BASS tested the hypothesis that a solid with adequate ventilation burns as well as, or better than, the same material in normal gravity at the same pressure, O2 concentration and temperature. If true, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (an upward-burning 1-g test used to screen spacecraft materials) would offer less safety margin than assumed. Testing anything but the thinnest fuels needs minutes of microgravity, which drop towers and parabolic aircraft cannot give. The investigation had two objectives. (1) Begin to bridge the gap between the 1-g Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual flammability in space, using practical, thicker fuels and wake flames (flames sheltered behind an object). (2) Assess how well an inert gaseous agent (nitrogen, similar to the ISS extinguisher agent) puts out flames over different materials, geometries, preheat states and flows. Behind the second objective is the worry that in microgravity the best place to aim a suppressant is unclear, and a jet might even feed the flame by entraining air.

sources.quote: If this hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of safety provided NASA- STD-6001 Test #1.
it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.
As a result, the 1-g test currently used by NASA to rate materials for space may need to be re-evaluated from a margin-of-safety point of view.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a solid heats the unburnt fuel ahead of it until the fuel pyrolyses. The vapour then mixes with oxygen and burns. On Earth, buoyancy drives an induced flow past the flame of order tens of cm/s (the BASS authors give about 20 cm/s at the flame zone for their fabric). In orbit, buoyancy is essentially absent, so the only flow is what the ventilation imposes, and that can be just a few cm/s. Two flow directions matter. In opposed flow the air moves against the direction of spread (downward burning on Earth), and spread is controlled by heat conducted forward from a small region at the flame's leading edge. In concurrent flow the air moves with the spread (upward burning on Earth), and the whole flame and hot plume preheat the fuel, so the flame can grow. A thin fuel's flammability boundary, plotted against flow speed, is U-shaped. At high flow, finite-rate chemistry fails and the flame blows off. At very low flow, the flame's heat release falls until radiative loss is a significant fraction of it, and the flame quenches. The low-flow quenching branch lies below the 1-g buoyant flow limit, so it can only be observed in microgravity. Between the branches there can be conditions, such as moderate opposed flows, where a material that self-extinguishes on Earth burns steadily in orbit. Inert-gas suppression works by diluting the oxygen and adding heat capacity at the flame. In microgravity, however, a jet also adds momentum and can entrain surrounding air, so where and how the agent is delivered matters.

sources.quote: This quenching extinction occurs when the flame power output decreases, and the radiative heat loss rate becomes a significant fraction of the total combustion heat release from the flame.
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.
Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system).
For concurrent-flow flames, the fuel preheating depends on the entire flame and hot plume which means that the flame response time to flow changes is a strong function of the flame size.
For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame.

equations.meaning: Thermal-regime (de Ris) spread rate of an opposed-flow flame over a thermally thin solid. $V_f$ spread rate (m/s); $\lambda_g$ gas thermal conductivity (W/m K); $T_f$ flame temperature, $T_v$ fuel vaporisation (pyrolysis) temperature, $T_\infty$ ambient temperature (K); $\rho_s$ solid density (kg/m3); $c_s$ solid specific heat (J/kg K); $\tau$ fuel half-thickness (m). Valid when gas-phase chemistry is fast compared with the flow residence time (large Damkohler number) and radiative losses are negligible; $V_f$ is then independent of the opposed flow speed. BASS opposed spread over SIBAL fabric instead peaked at 10-15 cm/s and fell on either side, so the BASS flows lie partly outside this regime: kinetic effects at higher flows, radiative losses at low flows.

Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds, in good agreement with previous research [Olson, 1991].

equations.meaning: Damkohler number at the flame leading edge: gas residence time over chemical time. $\alpha_g$ gas thermal diffusivity (m2/s); $U_r$ flow speed relative to the flame (m/s), with $U$ the imposed opposed flow and $V_f$ the spread rate; $\rho_g$ gas density (kg/m3); $Y_{O_2}$ oxygen mass fraction; $A$ pre-exponential factor of a one-step overall reaction (units such that the bracket is a rate in 1/s); $E$ activation energy (J/mol); $R$ gas constant (8.314 J/mol K); $T_f$ flame temperature (K). High-flow branch of the flammability boundary: the flame blows off when Da falls below a critical value, i.e. when $U_r$ is too large or O2 too low. On Earth the buoyant flow at the flame (about 20 cm/s for SIBAL) sets $U_r$, and downward spread over SIBAL blows off; in BASS, 9-10 cm/s opposed flow kept Da above critical, and no blow-off was reached up to about 44 cm/s. Order-of-magnitude scaling, not a fitted relation.

sources.quote: Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system).
The explanation is that in normal gravity, the buoyant flow generated by the flame is too high for the flame to be supported and blowoff occurs.

equations.meaning: Radiative-loss fraction that controls the low-flow (quenching) branch. $\varepsilon$ effective emissivity of flame and hot surface; $\sigma$ Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67e-8 W/m2 K4); $A_f$ radiating area (m2); $\dot m_f$ fuel pyrolysis rate (kg/s); $\Delta h_c$ heat of combustion (J/kg); temperatures in K. As the forced flow falls towards zero in microgravity, oxygen supply and heat feedback weaken, the pyrolysis rate drops faster than the radiative loss, $\Phi_{rad}$ rises towards order one and the flame quenches. Buoyancy keeps $\Phi_{rad}$ small in 1 g, so this branch is observable only in microgravity. In BASS, concurrent SIBAL flames quenched below 1 cm/s, whereas PMMA and wax flames, fed by heat stored in the thick solid, stayed lit near 1 cm/s for minutes. Qualitative scaling, not fitted to BASS data.

equations.meaning: Linear fits reported by the investigators to the steady base spread rate of concurrent-flow flames over SIBAL fabric (ISS cabin air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), one fit per sample width (1 cm and 2 cm). $V_F$ flame-base spread rate (mm/s); $U_\infty$ imposed air speed (cm/s), plotted as negative for concurrent flow, so spread increases linearly with flow magnitude. At $U_\infty = -10$ cm/s the fits give 2.56 and 1.57 mm/s. The source does not label the fits by width; the first matches the 2.55 mm/s measured on a 2-cm sample at about 10 cm/s, and the second the 1.68 mm/s base speed of a 1-cm sample at 11 cm/s, so they are most likely the 2-cm and 1-cm fits respectively. equations.meaning: Investigators' linear fits to flame-base and flame-tip position for a 1-cm-wide SIBAL sample in 11 cm/s concurrent flow on ISS (air, about 1 atm), after the initial growth phase (about 20 s). $x$ position along the sample (mm); $t$ time (s); $L_f$ flame length (mm). For the BASS 1-cm PMMA sphere (617.5 mg, consumed over four burns totalling 325 s at various flows), a NASA analysis gives $\dot m \approx$ 1.9 mg/s and $\dot r \approx$ 0.005 mm/s (0.3 mm/min). apparatus.text: The tests used the SPICE flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross-section), installed in the MSG, which supplied power, imaging and containment. A variable-speed fan with a flow straightener drove air through the duct at nominally 0-40 cm/s (the highest reading logged was about 44 cm/s). A hot-wire anemometer measured air speed, with a minimum measurable speed of 1 cm/s. The BASS control box let the crew turn the fan fully off, both as a safety measure and as a way to extinguish flames. Nitrogen from the MSG gaseous-nitrogen supply passed through a mass-flow controller (0-500 sccm) to a 3.2 mm nozzle upstream of the sample. Samples mounted on magnets in a sample-frame insert. Flat samples had an integral 29-gauge Kanthal wire igniter (about 1 ohm, about 3.7 A, ignition within about 2 s). Spheres, slabs and candles used bendable igniter wires that the crew positioned within about 1 mm of the fuel. Imaging was a Nikon D300s digital still camera looking through the top window at about 1 frame/s, and a colour video camera giving an edge view through the front window at 30 frames/s. A text overlay showed fan setting, air speed, radiometer output, nitrogen flow and time. A wide-angle radiometer measured flame radiation. Overlay parameters were logged at 4 Hz. In 2013 the MSG volume was vitiated with nitrogen, and the crew measured O2 with a CSA-CP (Compound Specific Analyzer - Combustion Products).

procedure.text: For each run the crew installed a sample, closed the duct and the MSG, and set the fan (and nitrogen flow, if used). They started video and still recording, then energised the igniter. For flat samples, flipping the holder 180 degrees put the igniter at the upstream end (opposed flow) or the downstream end (concurrent flow). After ignition the flame was left to burn, nominally for about 60 s in the original plan. For flat samples it usually burned until the fuel was consumed. Many runs changed the flow in steps during the burn. Opposed-flow flames re-reached steady spread within seconds, so one burn could give several flow conditions; concurrent flames respond too slowly for that. In suppression runs, nitrogen was raised in steps up to the maximum (about 495-500 cc/min). Flames that survived were put out by turning the air flow off. Afterwards the duct was cooled and vented: 2 min for thin samples and candles, 9 min for spheres and thick samples. The MSG was purged for 3 min after every 2 burns to dilute hydrogen fluoride (HF), a combustion by-product. Spheres, slabs and candles were re-ignited over several runs, so their shape changed from run to run. The 2012 runs were in ISS cabin air. Before many 2013 runs the MSG volume was diluted with nitrogen to about 16-18% O2, with O2 checked by CSA-CP. The ground team directed the runs in real time over audio and video links, and the crew's verbal observations were logged in the as-run test matrix.

psi_data.summary: PSI-26 holds 212 files (163.6 GB). Almost all of it (195 files, 162.5 GB) is raw imagery that has not been downloaded: 22 zips of 2012 still images (85.1 GB), and for 2013, 114 crew/downlink MP4 videos (22.8 GB) plus 37 zips (55.6 GB) of original images, XMP sidecars and text files. Raw data are organised by date. The data layout document describes 21 image galleries for 2012, and 12 audio/video collections plus 15 image galleries for 2013. No reduced data (spread rates, extinction points, digitised positions) are in PSI. Quantitative results exist only as plots and captions in the presentations and the 2013 US National Combustion Meeting paper. The most useful structured source is the as-run test matrix (xlsx). For each run it logs date and time, sample, igniter, fan and air settings, radiometer, GN2 setting, camera settings, cabin O2, pressure and CO2, and free-text crew/PI observations (outcome, extinction mode, soot). It links each run to its date folder in the raw data. The PSI experimental table CSV is a 6-column extract of it. No raw-data date folder exists before 2012-05-02, so the first 8 as-run tests (2012-03-30 to 2012-04-09) appear to have no imagery in PSI. Both final reports (BASS and SPICE) are listed but were not downloaded.

findings.claim: In opposed flow in microgravity (2-cm-wide SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric, ISS air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), the flame reached steady spread within seconds of each flow change. Spread rate rose with flow to a maximum at about 10-15 cm/s and fell at higher speeds.

findings.claim: The same SIBAL fabric cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) spread in 1 g air: it ignites, then extinguishes, because the buoyant flow exceeds the blow-off limit. In microgravity at about 9-10 cm/s opposed flow it burned steadily over the whole sample. For this fabric and geometry, it is more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g, which supports the BASS hypothesis.

The explanation is that in normal gravity, the buoyant flow generated by the flame is too high for the flame to be supported and blowoff occurs.

findings.claim: In concurrent flow, the base spread rate of SIBAL flames was constant within each run and increased linearly with flow speed, with different slopes for 1-cm and 2-cm widths. The plotted linear fits are V_F = -0.20 U + 0.56 and V_F = -0.15 U + 0.07 (V_F in mm/s, U in cm/s, concurrent flow plotted as negative U). The extracted text does not say which fit belongs to which width, but at 10-11 cm/s the first fit reproduces the 2.55 mm/s measured on a 2-cm sample and the second the 1.68 mm/s base speed of a 1-cm sample, so the steeper fit is most likely the 2-cm width.

findings.claim: Concurrent-flow SIBAL flames reached a steady (limiting) length only below about 10 cm/s for the 2-cm-wide samples within the 8.5 cm sample length. At 10 cm/s and above, the flame tip was still accelerating. 1-cm-wide samples reached steady state, e.g. at 11 cm/s: after about 20 s, base and tip advanced in parallel at about 1.7 mm/s (fits x_base = 1.68 t - 13.81, x_tip = 1.71 t + 2.25, mm and s), with a flame length of about 16 mm.

Extinction occurred at a low but finite flow below 1 cm/s. The authors present this as direct confirmation of the low-flow branch of the U-shaped flammability boundary for a thin fuel.

No blow-off limit was reached either: flames survived opposed and concurrent flows up to about 44 cm/s.

For these fire-retarded materials, microgravity was not more severe at those conditions (the ISS samples were narrower than 1 g test samples). A Nomex III sample did burn at 22% O2 and about 14-15 cm/s concurrent flow, which equals its 1 g ULOI. Its flame narrowed as it spread and went out within 1 cm of the sample end once its width fell below about 1 cm.

findings.claim: Nitrogen from the upstream nozzle at up to about 500 cc/min generally failed to extinguish PMMA sphere flames in air or at 17% O2. It typically blew off the forward-stagnation region (leading edge), and the flame survived as a side- or wake-stabilised flame. The crew log attributes this to the jet entraining air into the flame zone. These flames went out only when the air flow was shut off. The as-run log records clear N2 blow-out only occasionally, e.g. a 2-cm sphere at 5 cm/s, and a weakened minimum flame at max N2 that eventually went out. In their 2013 summary the investigators attribute the failure to heat stored in the thick solid, which kept even small flames alive at the available N2 flow.

findings.claim: The investigators' 2013 summary across all BASS sample types (17% to 21.5% O2, about 1 atm) is that flames were especially sensitive to air speed between 0 and 5 cm/s, and that the gas phase responded to flow changes almost without delay. Below 1 cm/s all flames became dim blue and very stable and, with little convective heat loss, could burn for a long time. Between about 1 and 5 cm/s the flame kept heating the solid, so fuel vaporisation rose and the flame grew stronger and more luminous with time. Only the smallest flames over acrylic slabs were visibly weakened by conductive loss to the solid, and even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing.

sources.quote: Ambient oxygen atmospheres 17% to 21.5% (cabin air).
Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s.

At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time.

At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cm/s) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.
Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing.

findings.claim: NASA's BASS-II summary report gives numbers for two BASS thick-fuel runs. A one-sided, 1-cm-wide PMMA slab burned at slow flow for 7.5 min in total: ignition took over 1 min, the flame reached a steady size after about 3 min, was only 15 mm long, and spread at 0.037 mm/s (2.2 mm/min). A 1-cm PMMA sphere (initial mass 617.5 mg) was fully consumed in four burns at various flow speeds totalling 325 s. That is an average burning rate of 1.9 mg/s, which the report converts to a mean regression rate of about 0.005 mm/s (0.3 mm/min), equivalent to a stretch rate of about 10 1/s.

relevance.text: Prevention and material selection: BASS shows directly that a material which self-extinguishes in the 1 g downward configuration can burn steadily in microgravity at realistic cabin ventilation speeds (about 10 cm/s). Flames over thin and thick fuels can also persist for minutes at flows of 1 cm/s or less. Normal-gravity screening therefore does not bound flammability in all configurations. On the other hand, the fire-retarded Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 behaved as in 1 g at 21-22% O2, and Nomex III burned only near its 1 g limiting O2. So the 1 g upward test was not shown to be non-conservative for the fire-retarded materials actually tested. These are qualitative, few-sample results at about 1 atm, not material flammability limits. Suppression: a nitrogen jet of up to about 500 cc/min from a fixed upstream nozzle generally removed only the leading edge of PMMA flames. Wake- and side-stabilised flames survived, apparently helped by air entrained by the jet, while shutting off the ventilation reliably extinguished small flames. This supports stopping ventilation as an effective response to small flames, and suggests the agent must reach the whole flame zone, including wake regions, not only the leading edge. The nozzle geometry and flow are specific to this hardware, so the agent quantities do not transfer to ISS extinguishers.

sources.quote: Normal gravity results cannot always be used to predict flame behavior and material flammability in spacecraft.
The standard test used by NASA to rate materials relies on burning them in an upward, normal-gravity configuration [NASA, 1998].

habitat_conditions.text: All runs were at ISS cabin pressure: 0.97-1.01 atm (98.3-102.2 kPa). In 2012, O2 was the uncontrolled cabin value, 20.9-22.7% by volume. In 2013 the MSG volume was diluted with nitrogen to 15.9-17.8% O2 for most runs; the rest were at about 20.5-21.2%. The logged O2 is sometimes the reading before vitiation, so a few 2013 runs logged near 21% actually burned at about 17%. BASS therefore covers normoxic and hypoxic (sub-21% O2) atmospheres at about the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa) only. It did not test the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres of exploration: the shared reference for a Moon habitat is 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psi) or less, and a spacesuit is 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi). Its highest O2 (22.7%) is below the Moon-habitat value, and its lowest pressure (98.3 kPa) is well above it. The SRD cites NASA CxP-70024 for such atmospheres but gives no values. BASS results cannot be applied to them without further tests or models. The flow range (below 1 to about 44 cm/s, mostly 0-20 cm/s) does span typical spacecraft ventilation speeds and the near-quiescent pockets behind equipment.

earth_benefits.text: Microgravity's simple, buoyancy-free flow field gives clean validation data for detailed flame-spread and extinction models. Once validated, these models can be extended to buoyant flames and used in designing fire detection and suppression systems on Earth. The team also cites the goal of a new or improved Earth-based flammability test method.

gaps: Final reports (PSI-26_Reports_BASS_FinalReport.pdf and PSI-26_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf) are listed in files.csv but not downloaded, and have no evidence chunks; the BASS final report is reported as unavailable from PSI (HTTP 404; not re-tested here). Both have the identical size of 553,693 bytes, so the 'BASS' report may be a duplicate of the SPICE report. To fill the gap, NTRS was searched: the ASGSR 2013 BASS talk (ntrs.nasa.gov 20140011099) and the BASS-II summary report NASA/TM-20210011385 (Appendix D gives BASS slab and sphere numbers; section 3.1 the leftover BASS candle) were used. The 9th USNCM 2015 fabric paper (ntrs.nasa.gov 20150008962) was read but reports mainly BASS-II runs, so it was not used for BASS findings.

No reduced numerical data (spread-rate tables, extinction flow speeds, sphere regression rates) are in PSI. Quantitative findings are limited to the fabric paper and its plot labels, plus one slab spread rate and one lumped sphere burning rate from NASA/TM-20210011385. For candles, nitrogen suppression and the 2013 low-O2 runs there are only image captions and as-run log notes. Searches of NTRS, Crossref and the web found no published BASS sphere, candle or nitrogen-suppression results: Takahashi et al., 'Burning Characteristics of Paraffin and Japan Wax Candle Flames in a Low-Speed Oxidizing Stream in Microgravity' (ASGSR 2013), Endo et al. PMMA-sphere papers (ASGSR 2014, 2016) and M. Endo's 2016 CWRU dissertation are cited in the TM but no accessible copy was found. The DOIs in the PSI record are mostly BASS-II or ground opposed-flow papers and add nothing on these topics.

The evidence parquet holds only the first rows of each As Run_Test Matrix.xlsx sheet. The full sheets were read directly from the xlsx, and facts from other rows are cited as psi_table sources with the Excel row number, as-run number and exact cell text (or an exact excerpt of it).

The extracted text does not assign the two concurrent-flow linear fits (V_F = -0.20U + 0.56, -0.15U + 0.07) to the 1-cm and 2-cm widths. The assignment given (steeper fit = 2 cm) is inferred from single-run values and should be confirmed from the figure.
Exploration-atmosphere values (O2 and pressure) are not given in any PSI-26 document; the SRD only cites NASA CxP-70024. The habitat comparison uses the shared values in docs/digest/reference.md.

PSI-39.one_line: Fuel droplets about 4 mm across were burned in a sealed chamber on the ISS to study 'cool flames': invisible, low-temperature flames (roughly 700-900 K) that keep a droplet burning after its normal hot flame has gone out.
PSI-39.summary: CFI burned about 4 mm droplets of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane blends (75/25 and 60/40 by mass) and farnesane in the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus on the ISS in 2017, at 0.5-5 atm (51-507 kPa), 17-21% O2 and 0-59% helium. More than two hundred tests were run. Large droplets first burned with a hot flame that went out by radiative heat loss after about 10-14 s in air. A cool flame then kept the droplet burning quasi-steadily, close to the droplet, until it too extinguished at a finite diameter and left a cloud of condensed, partly oxidised vapour. For n-dodecane in air the cool-flame extinction diameter fell from about 1.7-1.9 mm at 0.5 atm to below 0.4 mm at 1.25 atm. Helium dilution increased it, to 2.1-2.6 mm with 59% helium at 1 atm. Iso-dodecane suppressed cool flames. At 2 atm and above, cool flames repeatedly re-ignited hot flames. For spacecraft fire safety, this means a fuel can keep reacting, and producing flammable vapour, after the visible flame has gone out.

question.text: FLEX and FLEX-2 had found, by accident, that large n-alkane droplets keep burning quasi-steadily after their hot flame is extinguished by radiation, supported by low-temperature ('cool flame') chemistry in the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) range. CFI set out to study this regime systematically. It asked how fuel structure (n-dodecane, branched iso-dodecane in blends, and the renewable fuel farnesane), ambient pressure (0.5-5 atm) and helium dilution change the hot-flame and cool-flame burning rates, flame sizes, radiant output and, above all, the droplet diameter at cool-flame extinction. That diameter gives a measure of low-temperature chemical time scales that can be used to test and improve kinetic mechanisms. A secondary aim was to understand soot behaviour during cool-flame burning.

sources.quote: The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.”
the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic characteristic times.
Examine the cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane fuel mixtures, and farnesane fuels over a rage of pressure from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.

The overall goal of the proposed experiments is to improve our understanding of low temperature chemistry by studying the cool flame burning and, most importantly, cool flame extinction of droplet burning with spherical symmetry in a long-duration microgravity environment.

physics.text: Alkane oxidation follows different chemical routes at different temperatures. Below about 900 K, chain branching runs through peroxy radicals (RO2, QOOH, O2QOOH) and ketohydroperoxides. As temperature rises through the NTC region the overall rate falls, because these intermediates dissociate back, before high-temperature branching takes over above about 1100-1200 K. A spherically symmetric droplet diffusion flame normally burns in the high-temperature branch, and its flame radius is many droplet diameters. A large droplet in microgravity has a large flame whose radiative loss scales with flame volume, while heat release scales only with droplet diameter, so it can extinguish radiatively. In FLEX and CFI the gas left near the droplet after this extinction is hot enough for low-temperature chemistry to ignite a 'cool' diffusion flame at roughly 700-900 K. This flame sits close to the droplet (flame standoff ratio about 3) and releases roughly half the heat. It burns quasi-steadily, following a d-squared law, until the residence time in the reaction zone, which shrinks with droplet size, falls below the chemical time at the lower turning point of the NTC branch, and the flame goes out. Pressure shortens chemical times, so it lowers the extinction diameter. Helium raises thermal diffusivity and heat loss, so it raises the extinction diameter. Branched isomers form fewer of the five- and six-membered ring transition states needed for low-temperature branching, so they weaken cool flames. On Earth, buoyant convection on mm-size droplets is far faster than diffusion, so neither the spherical symmetry nor the long residence times these flames need can be achieved. Drop towers are also too short to reach radiative extinction.

sources.quote: FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K.
In microgravity where the buoyancy-induced flow is absent, larger droplets can extinguish as a result of the ex- cessive radiant heat loss from the flame zone (Chao et al., 1991).

The heat release during this second-stage burning is approximately half of what is normally associated with n-heptane combustion and the activation energy associated with the chemical processes is similar to that of low-temperature ignition chemistry Nayagam et al. (2012).

As the droplet size decreases, the residence time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction.

equations.meaning: Quasi-steady d-squared law. D is droplet diameter (mm), D_0 the initial diameter (mm), t time since ignition (s), k the burning-rate constant (mm^2/s). CFI fits k separately for the hot-flame stage (k_hot) and the cool-flame stage (k_cool), over roughly 0.1-0.9 of each stage. Valid for spherically symmetric, quasi-steady burning; it fails during ignition transients, re-ignition and on a disturbed fibre.

equations.meaning: Droplet lifetime (s) from the initial diameter D_0 (mm) and the average burning-rate constant k (mm^2/s). For D_0 = 3-6 mm and k = 0.5 mm^2/s this is 18-72 s, far longer than drop-tower times (up to about 5-10 s). That is why the ISS is needed.

equations.meaning: Ratios of thermal (tau_k) and mass (tau_m) diffusion times to the buoyant residence time tau_b, for droplet diameter D (m), gravity g (m/s^2), gas thermal diffusivity alpha_g and mass diffusivity D_g (m^2/s). Both ratios must be much less than 1 for buoyancy to be negligible and the flame spherical. At 1 g and 1 atm this needs D much smaller than 1 mm, below cool-flame extinction diameters. Diffusivities scale as 1/p, so higher pressure makes buoyancy worse.

equations.meaning: Yang-Gray thermokinetic condition for an NTC region. In the scheme A -> X (initiation), X -> 2X (branching, activation energy E_b), X -> products (low-temperature termination E_t1, high-temperature termination E_t2), the overall rate falls with rising temperature over a range when this ordering holds. It is a conceptual model, not quantitative for real fuels.

equations.meaning: Scaling behind radiative extinction. Radiative loss from the flame grows with flame volume (r_f = flame radius), while heat release grows only linearly with droplet diameter D. Large droplets (and large flames in microgravity) therefore lose a growing fraction of their heat and extinguish radiatively. This sets up the cool-flame stage. Qualitative scaling for optically thin gas radiation.

apparatus.text: The CIR provides a 90 l combustion chamber (rated to about 9 atm; CFI went to 5 atm), gas mixing (FOMA), pressure and temperature sensors, and imaging. It is vibration-isolated by PaRIS (Passive Rack Isolation System), and g-levels were typically below 1e-5 g0. The MDCA deploys a droplet by dispensing fuel between two opposed 250 um outside-diameter needles, stretching it, then retracting the needles quickly. CFI used a thinner 40 um SiC tether fibre than FLEX's 80 um fibre, to keep droplets in view while disturbing them less near cool-flame extinction. Two hot-wire igniters (about 12-13 W, 1-11 s on-time) were positioned near the droplet and withdrawn once it ignited. Diagnostics: a backlit (red laser-diode) HiBMS camera at 30 frames/s for droplet diameter; an intensified camera with hot-flame and cool-flame modes for OH* and cool-flame imaging; a colour camera with live downlink; and a radiometer package with a wideband channel (0.6-10 um, mainly hot flame) and a narrowband channel (5.0-6.5 um water band, sensitive to the cool flame) sampled at 100 Hz. Chamber pressures and four temperatures were logged throughout. The CFI requirements asked for larger fields of view than FLEX (50 mm droplet view, 80 mm flame view) and auto-gain radiometers.

procedure.text: The crew installed fuel syringes and gas bottles. Everything else was run from the Telescience Support Center at NASA GRC. For each test day the chamber was filled with the chosen O2/N2(/He) mixture and pressure and left about 2 minutes to settle. A set amount of fuel was then dispensed between the needles (or onto the fibre), stretched, and deployed. After a dwell of at least 10 s the igniters were powered for a preset time (1-5 s planned; later raised, e.g. to 8 s after a software change), then withdrawn. Cameras and radiometers recorded the hot-flame burn, its extinction, cool-flame burning, cool-flame extinction and vapour-cloud formation. A fan then mixed the chamber for about 15 s. Typically 5-10 droplets of different sizes were burned per atmosphere, about 8 per day, with later tests guided by earlier results. Data were downlinked and reduced to droplet diameter-squared histories (equivalent-area diameter of the backlit droplet), hot- and cool-flame diameters (FWHM and peak-to-peak of the cool-flame intensity profile), burning-rate constants from linear fits, extinction diameters and radiance traces.

psi_data.summary: PSI-39 holds 2,832 files (about 719 GB), 2,125 of them downloaded locally. Nearly all the volume is Raw Data (2,791 files, 718.9 GB): 337 zip image archives (588.9 GB), one per camera stream per test point for 85 test points, with suffixes A, C, D, G and a few S/I; 120 .ts and 126 .mp4 downlink video recordings (109.8 and 18.9 GB); and 1,793 small text files. For each of about 123 CIR test points (CIR ids such as F068A03) there are: test-point settings (igniter power and on-time, needle and igniter positions, dispensed volume), camera settings, filter and CFI-mode logs, chamber readings (pressures in psia and temperatures in deg C, about 1 Hz), radiometer readings, image timing indexes, and a 'Comments' file. The Comments files are data-integrity logs (missing image files, bad frame intervals, re-downlinks), not science notes. For a subset of tests there are reduced text files (FLEX-xxxx_DropletData, RadiometerData, ColorCamData, CoolFlameData, TestSheet), 22 RTF test sheets and 28 Igor .pxp analysis files. The most usable products are the Jan 2021 data-summary spreadsheet, which gives 227 test conditions, and for 146 analysed tests D0, extinction diameters, k_hot, k_cool, re-ignition counts, burn time and peak radiances, with operator comments per test; and 30 Analyzed Data PDFs (FLEX-1206 to 1264 and 1393), each a one-page plot of droplet, flame and radiance histories. The 87-row experimental table is a partial subset of the spreadsheet's Master Sheet.

findings.claim: With pure n-dodecane in air (21% O2, balance N2), droplets of about 3.8-4.7 mm at 0.5-1.25 atm burned first with a hot flame. The flame went out by radiative extinction after about 10-14 s (up to 17 s), with the droplet at about 2.9-4.3 mm. Quasi-steady cool-flame burning usually followed, often ending with a large vapour cloud. Not every test shows this: FLEX-1207 to 1210 have no cool-flame extinction diameter, the FLEX-1207 comment notes no large vapour cloud, and the FLEX-1222 comment says the flame burned to completion. The cool-flame burning-rate constant (0.31-0.43 mm^2/s) was about the same as the hot-flame value (0.30-0.52 mm^2/s).

findings.claim: Above about 2 atm the cool flame often re-ignited a hot flame, sometimes repeatedly. The sequence was hot flame, radiative extinction, cool flame, hot re-ignition, cool flame again, until the fuel was used up. No n-dodecane test at 0.5-1.25 atm re-ignited. In the spreadsheet, re-ignitions are logged for all 4 n-dodecane tests in air at 2 atm (FLEX-1227 twice, 1228-1230 once each) and for up to 7 cycles in one 3 atm test (FLEX-1258, D0 = 5.5 mm). The investigators had not expected this from FLEX. Under fire-safety applications, a CFI presentation notes that in space a persisting cool flame can generate combustible vapour that can re-ignite.

sources.quote: However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed.
This behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments.

findings.claim: Helium dilution at 21% O2 shortened the hot flame and enlarged the cool-flame extinction diameter. At 1 atm, n-dodecane extinction diameters were 0.90-0.97 mm with 29% helium (vs mostly 0.26-0.85 mm without) and 2.10-2.57 mm with 59% helium. Hot-flame burn time fell from about 10-12 s in air to about 7 s at 29% helium and 1.9-3 s at 59% helium. In FLEX-1281 (59% He, 1 atm) the hot flame existed only while the igniters were on.

findings.claim: Adding iso-dodecane suppressed cool flames, most clearly in the 60/40 blend at low pressure. At 0.5-0.75 atm in air, 60/40 droplets had cool-flame burning-rate constants of only 0.10-0.23 mm^2/s, against 0.31-0.37 for pure n-dodecane, and cool-flame 'extinction' diameters of 3.8-5.6 mm, within about 0.1 mm of their hot-flame extinction diameters. In other words, the cool flame barely lasted. The 75/25 blend at 0.75 atm behaved more like pure n-dodecane (extinction diameters 0.48 and 0.90 mm).

sources.quote: The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol.

findings.claim: At 17% O2 and 1 atm the hot flame was weak and short-lived: 4.7-7.2 s for n-dodecane and 3.3-4.7 s for the blends, with hot-flame burning-rate constants often below 0.1 mm^2/s for the blends. relevance.text: CFI is a fundamental combustion-chemistry experiment, not a material-flammability test, but it points to a spacecraft fire hazard. In microgravity, a burning liquid fuel (or, by analogy, a fuel-soaked object) whose visible flame has gone out can keep reacting through an invisible cool flame at about 700-900 K. That flame gasifies the fuel at nearly the hot-flame rate and leaves a cloud of fuel vapour and partly oxidised products. At 2 atm and above it repeatedly re-ignited hot flames, and a FLEX re-ignition burned brighter than the original flame, consistent with a premixed flame through the accumulated vapour. Detection and extinguishment criteria based only on visible flame or hot-flame radiation may therefore declare a fire out too early. The narrowband water-vapour radiometer did detect cool flames. Helium dilution and lower O2 shortened hot flames but increased the cool-flame extinction diameter, so inert agents change how much liquid is left unburned and vaporising.

sources.quote: Since the cool flame mode of droplet combustion can persist after hot-flame extinction (and may even transition back to hot flaming under certain conditions), safety procedures based only on considerations of hot flame properties or sensing may be inadequate for assuring safety under all conditions.

sources.file: PSI-39_Presentations_Cool Flames in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth_CFI.pdf
sources.quote: These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments

This suggests that the reignited hot flame is either a pre-mixed or partially pre-mixed flame propagating through the fuel vapor/air mixture that results from the unconsumed fuel during the cool flame period mixing with ambient air.
The new radiometers, particularly the narrowband radiometer, were sensitive to the cool flame and could detect both the cool flame burning and, most importantly, the cool flame extinction.

habitat_conditions.text: CFI used only 17% and 21% O2, with N2 or N2/He diluent, at 0.5-5 atm (50.7-506.6 kPa). The 21% O2, 1 atm tests match the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa). No test used the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres planned for exploration: the Moon-habitat reference is 30% or more O2 at 70.3 kPa or less, and the spacesuit reference is 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. The 0.5 and 0.75 atm air tests (O2 partial pressure about 10.7 and 16 kPa) are closest in total pressure to a habitat, but have much lower oxygen partial pressure. The low-pressure trend (larger cool-flame extinction diameter and slower cool-flame burning as pressure falls) suggests cool flames would be shorter-lived at habitat pressure, but the effect of 30% O2 was not measured. The SRD planned O2 up to 0.35-0.40 and xenon diluent, but these were not in the flown matrix. The predecessor FLEX tested a 30/70 O2/N2 pre-EVA atmosphere at 0.7 atm.

earth_benefits.text: Data for validating low-temperature (NTC) chemical kinetic mechanisms for n-dodecane, a jet/diesel surrogate component, its branched isomer and the renewable fuel farnesane. These mechanisms underpin autoignition, knock, octane and cetane behaviour and the design of low-temperature engines (HCCI, RCCI). Other suggested applications are cool-flame fuel reforming (for example hydrogen for fuel cells) and new spray-burner concepts.

gaps: Dates conflict. The PSI record gives investigationStartDate 10-01-2020 and investigationEndDate 10-20-2021. The experimental table and data-summary spreadsheet date the tests 9 Mar 2017 to 15 Sep 2017. The Final Report (dated 23 Jul 2020) says operations ran from January 2017 through September 2017. The record uses the dated test span (2017-03-09 to 2017-09-15). The 2020-2021 PSI dates may refer to a data-processing or archiving period; no document explains them.

The spreadsheet Master Sheet dates FLEX-1411 (farnesane) to 2011-09-06, which is clearly a typing error for 2017 (neighbouring tests are August-September 2017). The tests table now corrects it to 2017-09-06 using its CIR code.

The experimental table CSV (87 rows) lists FLEX-1285-1289 and 1295-1297 twice, so it has only 79 unique tests. It omits all farnesane tests and pure-dodecane tests at 0.5, 0.75, 3 and 5 atm and with helium. FLEX-1219 to 1222 list O2 0.21 + N2 0.76 (sum 0.97). Pressure strings carry trailing spaces. The full 227-row list is in the data-summary spreadsheet, which was read directly; facts from rows beyond its preview are cited as psi_table.

The PSI record's approach says the chamber pressure ranged from 0.25 to 0.5 atm, and its objective and the Final Report mention 0.25 atm. No test below 0.5 atm appears in the table or spreadsheet, and the Operational Requirements give 0.5-5.0 atm. The approach also calls nitrogen 'atomic nitrogen' (it is N2).

The Final Report text says 'n-dodecanol' and 'iso-dodecanol' in section 5.1, which are evidently typos for n-dodecane and iso-dodecane (its figure captions and all data use the alkanes). The PSI record hypothesis says 'faresane' for farnesane.
The SRD says the initial chamber temperature will be 'around 250 C'. This is presumably a typo for about 25 C: the FLEX-1206 test sheet logs 299.19 K and the chamber readings about 24-27 C.
The PSI record contact list gives D. Dietrich's email with a misspelled surname; contact emails were not copied into this record.

The Final Report figures (cool-flame extinction diameter vs pressure; helium effect; backlit soot images) have no text layer for the plotted values, and the PDF pages could not be rendered here (no poppler). Values were taken from the data-summary spreadsheet instead. FLEX-1248_Summary.pdf failed text extraction (PdfStreamError).

The main CFI results paper (Dietrich et al. 2024, Microgravity Sci. Technol., doi 10.1007/s12217-024-10115-x) is closed access, and its abstract is not available from Springer, Crossref or Semantic Scholar. Its results are not included. The 2020 ASGSR abstract on NTRS and the Williams and Nayagam 2020 Combustion and Flame abstract were reachable and are cited.

Raw image zips, .ts and .mp4 videos (about 718 GB) were not inspected. The per-test 'Comments.txt' raw files sampled (e.g. F068A03, F160A03, F180D04) contain only image-integrity logs, not science observations. Science observations are in the spreadsheet Comments sheet.

The two presentations (2013, 2015) predate CFI flight and describe FLEX cool-flame results and theory (partial-burning regime, flame standoff ratio about 3.1, extinction correlated with oxygen concentration to the -3/2 power). They give no CFI data.

No 30-day operational accomplishments report exists (the Final Report appendix says 'Not available'). The Final Report gives the PSI data organisation as FLEX-1206 to 1284 (n-dodecane), 1285 to 1387 (blends) and 1388 to 1431 (farnesane).

Publication review (Nov 2026; per-paper notes in data/publications/PSI-39.json): of the 7 listed publications, 1 was read in full (NTRS preprint of Nayagam et al. 2015), 3 by abstract and 3 not at all (Nayagam et al. 2012 Combustion and Flame, the 2024 CFI results paper, and the NASA blog post "Science in Short: Cool Flames", whose URL now redirects and whose archived copy refused automated access). The readable papers analyse FLEX/FLEX-2 n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane data from before CFI; none adds CFI-specific results to this record.

PSI-47.one_line: Before flying a smoke-measuring experiment, NASA checked on the Space Station that a commercial particle counter, which normally relies on gravity to recycle its alcohol, still counted particles correctly in weightlessness, and in doing so made the first measurement of how dusty the Station air is.
PSI-47.summary: DAFT was a quick risk-reduction test for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME depended on a TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter, which uses gravity to return condensed isopropanol to its wick. NASA cut capillary grooves into the condenser and flew it with a gravity-insensitive TSI DustTrak photometer as reference. In February and March 2005 (Increment 10) the crew sampled cabin air at three locations and air dusted by separating Velcro. In August 2006 (Increment 13) three 15 L bags of Arizona Road Dust in nitrogen were sampled. The P-Trak ran with no clogging or errors. It read up to about 45,000 particles/cm3 for Velcro dust and 11,400-36,500 particles/cm3 (DustTrak 33-71 mg/m3) for the bags. Undisturbed ISS air averaged under 15 particles/cm3 and under 0.005 mg/m3, far cleaner than the Shuttle or offices. The orbital mass-per-count ratio was about 3.2 times the ground value (mean diameter 1.65 µm), consistent with large particles not settling. The modified counter was accepted for SAME, supporting spacecraft smoke-detector design.

question.text: Can a modified commercial condensation nuclei counter (the TSI P-Trak) count aerosol particles reliably in long-duration microgravity? It was to be the zeroth-moment (number concentration) instrument of the SAME smoke experiment. The P-Trak grows particles into countable droplets by condensing isopropanol on them, and its sloped condenser relies on gravity to drain excess alcohol back to the wick. Two failure modes were feared. Liquid alcohol might clog or obscure the nozzle, laser and optics. The internal flow in the optics chamber might over-count particles. The hypotheses were that the capillary-modified P-Trak would function normally in microgravity, and that the test aerosol, made and filtered as designed, would be within both instruments' ranges. The objective was to retire this risk to SAME by comparing the P-Trak against a DustTrak (insensitive to gravity) and a reference dust aerosol.

sources.quote: Two potential failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system, containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured and 2) that the internal flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause an over counting of the particulates and give unreliable (high) readings.
was designed to ensure that a modiﬁed P-Trak®—a key component of the forthcoming NASA Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)—will perform properly in the unique enviroment of micro- gravity.

physics.text: Smoke detectors respond to particle size. Ionisation detectors favour small particles; scattering detectors favour particles near and above the wavelength. Spacecraft detectors were designed from 1-g smoke data, but shuttle experiments suggested smoke particles are larger in microgravity, so SAME set out to measure moments of the smoke size distribution in orbit. A condensation particle counter makes particles as small as about 20 nm visible by drawing them through a warm, alcohol-saturated region and then a cooled condenser. The vapour becomes supersaturated and condenses on each particle, growing droplets of a few micrometres that are counted one by one with a laser. On Earth, excess liquid draining down the sloped condenser returns to the wick by gravity. Without gravity it could pool and flood the optics, so the condenser was given fine longitudinal grooves that move liquid by capillary (surface-tension) forces instead. A light-scattering photometer (DustTrak) measures mass concentration and does not depend on gravity. Dividing its mass reading by the number count gives an average particle mass, hence an equivalent diameter, which is a check on the counter. In microgravity, particles in a sample bag do not settle, so a bag aerosol keeps more of its large particles than on Earth.

sources.note: Condensation particle counter principle, capillary flow in grooves and gravitational settling of aerosols are standard aerosol and fluids background.

sources.quote: The P-Trak® is a commercial device that counts ultra- ﬁne particles (it can recognize particles as small as 0.02 micrometer in diameter).

The removal of buoyancy reduces the velocities in the high temperature zones in flames, increasing the residence time of smoke particles and consequently allowing longer growth time for the particles.
This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.

For DAFT-3 bag 1 (voice-down averages 43.15 mg/m3 and 17,314 cm-3) this gives $\bar{m}_p$ = 2.49e-12 g and $\bar{D}$ = 1.68 µm. Valid only as a consistency check. The DustTrak is calibrated for a reference dust, the P-Trak undercounts particles above its range, and the true density of Arizona Road Dust is not 1 g/cm3.

equations.meaning: Kelvin equation: the smallest particle diameter $d^*$ (m) on which vapour condenses and grows at saturation ratio $S$. $\sigma$ is the liquid surface tension (N/m, isopropanol); $v_m$ is the molecular volume of the liquid (m3); $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant (J/K); $T$ is temperature (K). The P-Trak's cooled condenser sets $S$ so that particles down to about 0.02 µm are activated, which fixes its lower size limit. apparatus.text: The P-Trak is a handheld condensation nuclei counter for particles 0.02 to more than 1 µm, with a maximum count of 500,000 particles/cm3. Its pump draws sample through a saturator, where an alcohol-soaked wick supplies isopropanol vapour, then through a cooled condenser tube where droplets grow, and past a laser and photodetector. The flight unit's condenser had about 60 machined longitudinal grooves to return liquid alcohol to the evaporator by capillary action. Its mercury orientation switch was removed, and it was flight-hardened and covered in foil tape for flammability. The DustTrak, a laser (Mie) scattering photometer reading mass concentration in mg/m3 for 0.1-10 µm particles, was the reference; it was fitted with a 2.5 µm inlet impactor for the dust tests. DAFT-1 contained the modified P-Trak, alcohol wick and batteries; DAFT-2 the DustTrak and batteries. DAFT-3 was the aerosol system: a fill assembly that metered ISS gaseous nitrogen through a dust holder (0.25 g Arizona Road Dust) into 15 L Mylar bags, and a DAFT impactor to strip particles above about 2.5 µm (about 50% efficient). DAFT-4 was an unmodified, flight-hardened P-Trak. HEPA filters zeroed both instruments before and after each run.

procedure.text: DAFT-1 and -2 reached the ISS on Progress 16P in December 2004. With no dust source yet on board, cabin air was sampled. Session 1 was on 22 Feb 2005 (GMT 053, Leroy Chiao, Increment 10), test point 1 at EXPRESS Rack 4, about 12 min. Session 2 was on 4 Mar 2005 (GMT 063) with three test points of about 9-13 min each: Velcro separation at the inlet, Lab 1 near Port rack 6, and Node 1 mid-cabin. Each run was: battery in, warm-up (P-Trak about 1 min), HEPA zero check (P-Trak below 10 particles/cm3, DustTrak -0.001 to 0.003 mg/m3), about 6 min of sampling through a shared hose, a second HEPA zero, then shutdown. Both units logged at 1 s, and video was used to synchronise clocks. In Increment 13 (Jeff Williams), the first ARD session (GMT 229, 2006) was aborted. The fill assembly's HEPA filter was found broken off and a laptop COM-port mismatch blocked downloads, so a cabin-air sample was taken instead. After a safety review the opening was covered with grey tape. On 21 Aug 2006 (GMT 233) three bags were filled with 4, 6 and 8 toggles of the dust fill valve and sampled through the DAFT impactor. Readings were called down every 30 s and recorded on the ground, because the electronic data from these runs did not arrive by downlink. DAFT-4 (unmodified P-Trak) was not run. Only 3 of up to 15 planned dust test points were made.

psi_data.summary: PSI-47 is small but nearly complete for its purpose, about 42 MB. It holds the instrument logs for the 2005 runs (six text files: P-Trak and DustTrak test IDs 2-4) and 12 Excel workbooks. Eight of the workbooks are copies of the same 'flight data 063' workbook. Others hold the 22 Feb 2005 data with a note, the voice-down and post-flight logged data for the three 2006 dust bags with mass-per-particle analysis, and a 'Retrieved Data Summary' with all seven logged runs from both instruments. There are also a 30-day post-flight report (PDF, text extracted) and final and 1-year reports (Word .doc, no extracted text, read directly). Presentations include a fact sheet PDF and two .ppt decks. Engineering documents comprise four crew procedures, a condenser-modification drawing (scanned, no text) and an image deck, plus one on-orbit photo. The time series are directly usable. The 2006 dust-bag time series exist only inside the Retrieved Data Summary workbook. The experimental table has only two rows and mislabels them (see gaps).

findings.claim: The modified P-Trak worked in microgravity. In all sessions (2005 and 2006, runs of about 8-39 min) it showed no alcohol flooding, optics obscuration, nozzle clogging or error codes. Readings rose from zero into the middle of the range and returned to zero on HEPA zero checks. This was the main failure mode the condenser modification was meant to prevent.

findings.claim: ISS cabin air was exceptionally clean. Undisturbed US Lab and Node 1 air averaged fewer than 15 particles/cm3 (P-Trak) and under 0.005 mg/m3 (DustTrak) in three 2005 runs. For example, the 4 Mar 2005 Lab 1 / Port 6 run had a median of 1 particle/cm3 and a maximum of 10. The 30-day report calls this almost an order of magnitude below a typical laboratory (about 4,000-6,000 particles/cm3), but its own numbers put it roughly 300-fold or more lower, so the report's wording understates the gap. It is also below the roughly 0.050 mg/m3 measured on the Space Shuttle. It is attributed to HEPA filtration of ISS cabin air and the small crew of two. NASA describes this as the first measurement of ISS background particulate.

When the crew repeatedly separated Velcro at the inlet, it rose to several readings above 30,000 particles/cm3 (logged maximum 45,400) and fell back in a logical way. The DustTrak also responded but stayed below 10% of its range. These readings could not be tied quantitatively to individual Velcro separations.

findings.claim: The P-Trak and DustTrak both read the reference dust in range. For three ARD/N2 bags on 21 Aug 2006, voice-down averages were 17,314 particles/cm3 with 43.2 mg/m3 (bag 1, 4 toggles), 17,256 with 34.1 mg/m3 (bag 2, 6 toggles) and 24,350 with 63.2 mg/m3 (bag 3, 8 toggles). The P-Trak ranged from 11,400 to 36,500 and the DustTrak from 32.8 to 71 mg/m3. Data logged in the instruments and read after their return gave similar averages: 17,236/45.6, 16,589/33.8 and 26,578/62.7.

The orbital count/mass ratio pointed to larger particles, not over-counting. In orbit the DustTrak/P-Trak ratio (mean mass per particle) was about 3.2 times the May 2003 ground value: the spreadsheet's "slope" 0.00249 against 0.00077 mg/m3 per particle/cm3. The 0.00249 is the ratio for bag 1 alone, not a fit across bags; the three bags give 0.00249, 0.00198 and 0.00259, and their mean (about 0.00235) gives a ratio of about 3.1. That implies mean particles about 1.45-1.5 times larger in diameter: average mass 2.5e-12 g (range 2-3e-12) and diameter 1.65 µm (range 1.56-1.70) at unit density. The investigators attribute this to large ARD particles staying suspended without settling, with the impactor removing only about 50% of them. Over-counting, the feared failure mode, would have shifted the ratio the other way.

relevance.text: DAFT burned nothing. Its fire-safety value is in detection. It validated in orbit the condensation particle counter that SAME used to measure the number concentration of smoke from spacecraft materials, data needed to redesign smoke detectors that were sized from 1-g smoke. It also measured the ISS background particle level a detector must discriminate against: under 15 particles/cm3 and 0.005 mg/m3 in undisturbed air, with transient spikes above 30,000 particles/cm3 from ordinary crew activity (Velcro). The low background helps detection sensitivity, but nuisance sources can produce large short-lived signals. The finding that bag aerosols kept more large particles in microgravity illustrates why particle sizes differ from 1 g. Caveats: dust, not smoke, was sampled; only one counter unit; few test points; no comparison with the unmodified instrument.

sources.quote: Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke data, all current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed based upon normal-g conditions.
These background levels are critical to the design of future smoke detectors.

habitat_conditions.text: All sampling was in normal ISS cabin air, essentially the Earth sea-level atmosphere (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa); O2 and pressure were not recorded by DAFT. No measurement was made at reduced pressure or enriched O2 such as the proposed Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less). Condensation-counter performance and particle behaviour at lower pressure were therefore not tested. Ambient pressure affects the instrument's flow and vapour supersaturation, but this was not evaluated.

sources.note: Pressure dependence of condensation particle counter operation is general instrument knowledge, not a DAFT result.

gaps: The experimental table is misleading. Its two rows are labelled as sessions D1 (GMT 54, 2005) and D2 (GMT 63, 2005) but describe hardware sets DAFT-1 (modified P-Trak) and DAFT-2 (DustTrak); both sessions used both instruments. Both rows say Arizona Road Dust was sampled, but the 2005 sessions sampled cabin air and Velcro debris. ARD was used only on 21 Aug 2006 (DAFT-3), which the table omits, as it omits the aborted 17 Aug 2006 session. tests.csv inherits this: 2 'condition_set' rows with fuel 'arizona road dust' and date 2005-02-23.

Date inconsistencies. GMT 54 in the table corresponds to 23 Feb 2005, but the reports, analysed-data file name (GMT053) and instrument logs give 22 Feb 2005. The 30-day report says the first 2006 session was 'August 18, 2006 (GMT 229)', but GMT 229 of 2006 is 17 Aug, matching the instrument log date. The time-history workbook has a garbled GMT entry '7:181:25' for bag 1 at 360 s. Bag 3 times are offset by one row between the 'time hist' and 'urban' workbooks.

The final report (.doc), 1-year report (.doc) and two .ppt decks have no extracted text in evidence.parquet. They were read by extracting text runs directly from the binary files and are cited as psi_table with sheet 'Word document body text' / 'slide text'. This is a workaround: these sources cannot be checked by the quote validator. The 1-year report is an earlier draft of the final report with near-identical content. The condenser-modification drawing (PDF, no text layer) was not read.

The 30-day report PDF text layer is column-scrambled (fragments missing first letters, for example 'avid Urban'). Only clean spans were quoted; figures 1-7 (time traces and ground correlation) exist only as images.

Eight Analyzed Data workbooks ('flight data 063' and its _DTrk/_PTrk/_TIMING variants) contain the same sheets and are redundant. Raw Data has text logs only for 2005 test IDs 2-4. Test ID 1 and the 2006 logs exist only inside the Excel workbooks.

The record's 'removed' list holds 185 legacy files (about 5 GB), 178 of them under 'Legacy/DAFT P-TRAK Experiment Data/DAFT/CVB/...' (bitmap images named stability_*.bmp). These look like misfiled data from another investigation (CVB, possibly the Constrained Vapor Bubble), not DAFT. They were not downloaded.
Source inconsistency: NTRS 20050215648 says the DAFT impactor removes the smallest particles, whereas the DAFT reports say it removes the larger ones (above about 2.5 µm). The reports were followed.
The fact sheet lists the particle size range in '(mm)'; values 0.02 to >1.0 and 0.10 to 10 are micrometres.

Investigator roles differ by source. PSI lists Urban (PI) and Fortenberry (Project Scientist); the fact sheet and final report list Urban and Ruff as PIs; the 30-day report lists Co-Is Mulholland, Yuan, Yang and Cleary. The record gives the acronym 'DAFT / DAFT-2', but DAFT-1 to -4 were hardware packages of one experiment.

Personal data: the fact sheet, NTRS 20050215648 and the 2007 presentation contain phone numbers and e-mail addresses; the time-history workbook names the ground staff who transcribed data. These were not copied beyond the verbatim measurement-provenance quote. No text addressed to an AI was found.

External sources used: NTRS 20050215648 (2004 Research & Technology article), NTRS 20070031686 (2007 ISDC presentation). The two DOI publications (AIAA 2005-341, SAE 2005-01-2930) were not read; their content overlaps the PSI presentation 'SmokeDetectionfromMicrogravityFires.ppt'. The DAFT web page cited in the documents (microgravity.grc.nasa.gov/combustion/daft/) was not tried, as it is a defunct GRC address.

SAE 2005-01-2930 confirms findings[1] (first ISS ambient-aerosol measurement, very low levels); AIAA 2005-341 is a programmatic research plan that does not mention DAFT. Full texts are paywalled. identity.title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
principal_investigators: Mitchell D. Smooke (Yale University) - Principal Investigator
Marshall B. Long (Yale University) - Co-Investigator
Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA Glenn Research Center) - Project Scientist
identity.platform: Ground (computational modelling and image re-analysis) using ISS coflow flame data
identity.hardware: None of its own; analysed DSLR images from the Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE, PSI-107) and Yale laboratory flames; the resulting paper also uses the ACME coflow burner configuration

source.quote: The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI.

PSI-60.one_line: Yale researchers re-analysed Space Station photographs of sooty ethylene flames and ran detailed computer models to find out why flames in weightlessness make so much more soot than on Earth, concluding that the models mainly get the flame temperature wrong.
PSI-60.summary: This PSI-funded ground investigation (2019-2022) combined re-analysis of microgravity flame images with detailed numerical modelling of sooting, laminar, ethylene-air coflow diffusion flames. Over 1600 raw camera images from the Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) were decoded into colour channels and analysed by colour-ratio pyrometry to obtain soot temperature fields; the SPICE absolute light calibration then gave soot volume fractions. A coupled flow-species-soot model, extended with radiation re-absorption and sectional aggregate formation, simulated the Yale and ACME burner flames at 1 g and 0 g. Simulations reproduced the known trends: at 0 g the flame becomes longer, broader and more diffuse, cooler, with more soot and longer residence time, but these effects were much weaker for the smaller ACME flame. Perturbing soot sub-model parameters and radiation treatment did not remove the gap between model and measurement; the authors conclude the model mispredicts the temperature field, and that imposing measured temperatures and accounting for heat loss to the burner lip should improve soot predictions. For fire safety the work bears on soot, smoke and radiation modelling of microgravity fires.

question.text: Why do laminar diffusion flames in microgravity form so much more soot than the same flames in 1 g, and why do detailed models fail to reproduce the difference? The study aimed to extract temperature and soot volume fraction fields from SPICE images in PSI, compare them with detailed soot simulations of normal- and microgravity flames, identify which processes (soot formation and oxidation, radiative re-absorption, aggregate growth) control the discrepancy and the approach to the smoke point, and assess sensitivity to model parameters. The hypothesis was that microgravity flames are longer, more diffuse, cooler and sootier, and that imposing measured temperature fields in the simulations would reduce the mismatch between measured and predicted soot.

sources.quote: In this paper, we consider a combined experimental and computational study of sooting, ethylene-air, laminar, coflow diffusion flames under normal and microgravity conditions.

physics.text: In a coflow diffusion flame, fuel issues from a central tube into a slower annular air stream and burns where the two meet. On Earth, buoyancy accelerates the hot gases, thinning the flame and shortening the time soot particles spend in the hot fuel-rich region. In microgravity there is no buoyant acceleration, so for the same fuel flow the flame is longer and wider, gas residence times are longer, and soot particles have more time to nucleate and grow; the larger soot load radiates more heat, lowering flame temperature, which in turn slows soot oxidation and can lead to smoke release at the flame tip (the smoke point). Soot temperature can be measured without probes by colour-ratio (two-colour) pyrometry: the ratio of soot emission in two camera colour channels depends on temperature through Planck's law and the soot emissivity's wavelength dependence; with absolute intensity calibration the emission intensity then gives soot volume fraction. Accurate soot prediction therefore depends strongly on the predicted temperature field, which in turn depends on radiation losses, re-absorption and heat transfer to the burner.

sources.note: Buoyancy effects on coflow flame residence time, soot-radiation coupling and colour-ratio pyrometry are standard combustion background.

sources.quote: at 0 g, the flame is lengthened, becomes broader and more diffuse, temperatures decrease and soot levels and gas residence times increase.

equations.meaning: Two-colour (colour-ratio) pyrometry in the Wien limit: ratio of spectral intensities I at wavelengths lambda_1, lambda_2 (m) emitted by soot at temperature T (K); epsilon is spectral emissivity (for soot roughly proportional to 1/lambda), C_2 = 1.4388e-2 m K is the second radiation constant. Measuring the ratio in two camera colour channels gives T independent of soot amount; valid for optically thin soot, so self-absorption in heavily sooting flames biases it. In practice the camera's spectral response is integrated over each colour filter rather than at single wavelengths.

With T known from pyrometry and an absolute intensity calibration, the emitted intensity gives kappa_lambda and thus f_v (after tomographic inversion of line-of-sight images for an axisymmetric flame).

PSI-62.one_line: University at Buffalo researchers built and tested fast computer models of flames spreading over solid fuels in weightlessness, checking them against Space Station burning tests, as a step toward predicting which spacecraft materials can burn at which oxygen levels and air speeds.
PSI-62.summary: This PSI-funded ground investigation (2019-2021) developed flamelet generated manifold (FGM) models for flames spreading over solid fuels in microgravity, using the ISS Burning and Suppression of Solids experiments (BASS and BASS-II) as benchmarks. An FGM tabulates detailed flame chemistry from simple one-dimensional flame solutions so that multidimensional simulations need only a few transported variables. The team built a two-dimensional flame-spread model with multi-step chemistry and fully coupled radiation, compared it with BASS spread rates at 20.6% oxygen (over-predicting them by up to 2.7 times), and then built coupled radiative FGMs from one-dimensional flames with a quasi-coupled fuel surface boundary, which proved critical to capturing how mixture fraction varies along the fuel surface. The manifolds reproduced the chemical states in most of the flow but differed near the flame attachment point because of flame-wall interaction and flame curvature. An analytical thin-flame theory captured the low-strain radiative extinction branch of the U-shaped oxygen-versus-strain flammability map and agreed qualitatively with BASS-II PMMA rod data, predicting a minimum of 11.1-12.6% oxygen, 0.9-2.4 points below experiment. The aim is numerical screening of spacecraft material flammability.

question.text: Can a reduced-chemistry approach, the (unsteady, radiative) flamelet generated manifold, reproduce flame spread over solid fuels in microgravity with enough fidelity to predict flammability limits of spacecraft materials? Concurrent and opposed flame spread over solids is hard to model because heat transfer, mass transport and chemistry are tightly coupled near the solid-gas interface, and conventional hybrid turbulence/chemistry models are inconsistent and miss intermediate reaction pathways. The hypothesis was that the unsteady FGM approach, coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport and chemical processes with the far-field flow, could reproduce microgravity flame spread including the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone (burning only within an intermediate range of flow speed) reported by Olson and Ferkul for BASS-II PMMA rods. The long-term aim was a tool to predict flammability limits and to serve as a subgrid model in large-eddy simulations of spacecraft fires.

sources.quote: The U-shape defines the limiting flammability bounds from radiative extinction and flame blow-off. The minimum of the U corresponds to the minimum possible oxidizer concentration where burning can occur, and is an important quantity of interest for fire safety.

physics.text: When a solid burns, heat from the gas-phase flame pyrolyses the surface, and the fuel vapour feeds the flame; flame spread is the advance of this coupled process over unburnt material. In microgravity there is no buoyant flow, so the only flow is what ventilation imposes, often a few cm/s. The flammability of a solid then depends on oxygen and on the flow (expressed as a stretch or strain rate): at high flow the residence time is too short and the flame blows off (a Damkohler-number limit), while at very low flow the flame is weak, radiative losses from the flame and the hot surface dominate, and it quenches. Plotting minimum oxygen versus strain gives a U-shaped boundary whose minimum is the lowest oxygen at which the material can burn; in microgravity this minimum can lie below the 1 g value because buoyancy always imposes a relatively high strain on Earth. Flamelet models assume the local flame structure resembles a simple 1-D flame, so the chemistry can be pre-computed and tabulated against a few variables (mixture fraction, progress variable, and here enthalpy to represent radiative loss).

sources.note: Solid-fuel flame spread, blowoff/quenching limits and flamelet tabulation are standard combustion background.

sources.quote: Quenching was observed when the flow became sufficiently weak that the flame could no longer provide adequate heat flux to compensate for the heat losses (conduction into the rod and radiation).
The flammability boundary is shown to represent a critical Damkohler number, expressed in terms of the reaction rate divided by the stretch rate.

equations.latex: Da = \frac{\tau_{flow}}{\tau_{chem}} \propto \frac{A\,\exp(-E_a/R T_f)}{a}, \qquad Da = Da_{crit} \text{ on the flammability boundary}
equations.meaning: Damkohler number for the stagnation region of a burning solid: ratio of chemical reaction rate (pre-exponential A, activation energy E_a in J/mol, flame temperature T_f in K, gas constant R) to the stretch (strain) rate a (1/s). Olson and Ferkul showed the BASS-II PMMA rod flammability boundary corresponds to a critical Da; on the blowoff branch T_f is nearly constant so the limiting oxygen rises linearly with a, while on the quenching (low-a) branch radiative and conductive losses lower T_f and the exponential makes temperature critical.

sources.quote: For the blowoff branch, the boundary exhibits a linear dependence on oxygen concentration and stretch rate, indicating that the temperature at blowoff must be fairly constant.

equations.latex: Z = \frac{s Y_F - Y_{O_2} + Y_{O_2,\infty}}{s Y_{F,s} + Y_{O_2,\infty}}
equations.meaning: Mixture fraction Z (0 in the far-field oxidiser, 1 in pure fuel vapour) for a one-step reaction with stoichiometric mass ratio s (kg O2 per kg fuel); Y_F, Y_O2 are local fuel and oxygen mass fractions, Y_O2,inf the far-field oxygen and Y_F,s the fuel mass fraction at a reference fuel surface. FGM tables are indexed by Z (plus progress variable and enthalpy); over a pyrolysing solid the surface value of Z varies along the surface, which is why the investigators' quasi-coupled fuel boundary in the 1-D flamelets was needed.

sources.note: Standard Burke-Schumann-type mixture fraction definition.

apparatus.text: No hardware. Computational tools: (1) an existing fully coupled fluid-solid framework for charring and ablating materials, extended to a detailed 2-D flame-spread model with multi-step chemistry and fully coupled radiation heat transfer; (2) unsteady and coupled radiative flamelet generated manifolds (UFGM, CR-FGM) built from 1-D flame solutions with a quasi-coupled fuel boundary; (3) an analytical thin-flame theory with a solid-fuel heat and mass transfer model and a Damkohler-based reaction progress variable, compared with a 1-D detailed-chemistry, radiation-coupled numerical model in planar and spherical geometry. Image analysis: a two-colour pyrometry flamelet manifold (TCFM) diagnostic for DSLR images, with flame-hull reconstruction and 3-D ray tracing for radiative heat flux, intended for BASS/BASS-II imagery.

The TCFM is a function of two variables; the ratio of red to green intensities (flame index) and physical distance to the stoichiometric surface defined using a level-set function.

Publication review (data/publications/PSI-62.json): full texts of the two 2023 papers and the 2021 diagnostic paper were read as accepted manuscripts on OSTI (purls 2576508, 2417649, 1772898). This updates three statements above: (1) findings[0] previously read 'A detailed 2-D flame-spread model with multi-step chemistry and fully coupled radiation, validated against NASA BASS data, predicts reasonable flame spread rates over a range of far-field oxygen levels (spread-rate values and error not available in the abstracts read).' The full text shows the BASS comparison at a single O2 level (20.6%) with 1.5-2.7x over-prediction; the abstract's 'range of far-field oxygen levels' is not shown in the paper's BASS comparison. test_matrix.varied[0] previously read 'range of BASS oxygen levels (values not available)', and the summary said the model was 'validated it against BASS data over a range of oxygen levels'. (2) Spread-rate error and oxygen levels are now available (gap above partly superseded). (3) Both 2023 papers acknowledge NASA grant 80NSSC20K0426, the PSI-62 grant, so their funding by this investigation is confirmed, not assumed. (4) The 'Goldilocks flammability zone' wording appears in the introduction of 10.1016/j.combustflame.2023.112910 ('A particularly interesting aspect of their work is identifying a Goldilocks flammability zone, lying between quenching and blow-off limits').

Flow configuration: the PSI title says 'concurrent flame spread', but the 2-D model and its BASS comparison (10.1016/j.combustflame.2023.112939) are for opposed-flow spread over a thin PMMA slab, and the flammability maps (112910) compare with stagnation-flow PMMA rod data.
