PSI-68.one_line: The follow-on to FLEX burned single drops and pairs of drops of practical-fuel ingredients and fuel mixtures (octanes, heptane, decane, alcohols) on the Space Station to give engine and fire modellers clean benchmark data, and showed that the 'cool flames' found in FLEX occur for many normal-alkane fuels.
PSI-68.summary: FLEX-2 extended the ISS FLEX droplet-combustion experiments in the CIR Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus from two pure fuels to transportation-fuel components and mixtures. The PSI table lists the planned conditions: eight fuels (iso-octane, n-octane, n-heptane, n-decane, ethanol, propanol/glycerol 95/5 and 80/20, heptane/iso-octane 50/50), droplets 1.5-5 mm, oxygen mole fractions 0.17-0.30 in nitrogen or helium, pressures 0.5-3 atm and imposed relative flow 0.1-5 cm/s, plus binary droplet arrays. Published results from the programme show three-stage burning of large n-alkane droplets: hot-flame radiative extinction, a quasi-steady cool-flame stage, then cool-flame extinction and vapour-cloud formation. A scaling based on a critical flame temperature correlates radiative extinction diameters across CO2, He and Xe dilution. At about 2 atm, decane/hexanol droplets switched from cool-flame burning back to a hot flame spontaneously. For fire safety this establishes that invisible cool-flame burning and re-ignition are general features of alkane fuels, not specific to heptane.

question.text: FLEX-2 set out to provide benchmark data on isolated and interacting droplet combustion for fuels and conditions closer to practical combustors than FLEX: bi-component and surrogate mixtures, a range of pure fuels, elevated pressure, sub-buoyant convective flow and droplet-droplet interaction. Itemised goals were the role of liquid-phase mixing in bi-component droplets, steady and unsteady phenomena in pure-fuel burning, flame extinction mechanisms and boundaries, soot formation and soot-shell dynamics, the influence of droplet interactions on flammability limits of arrays, and validation of numerical models whose chemistry, radiation and phase-coupling approximations had not been tested against benchmark data.

sources.quote: FLEX-2 uses fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions.

physics.text: As in FLEX, a quiescent microgravity droplet burns with a spherically symmetric diffusion flame whose squared diameter decreases nearly linearly in time, and the flame can extinguish diffusively (too little residence time when the droplet is small) or radiatively (too much radiant loss when the flame is large). FLEX-2 adds three ingredients. (1) Multicomponent liquids: in a mixture the more volatile component evaporates first from the surface, and slow liquid-phase diffusion relative to surface regression (large liquid Peclet number) traps the less volatile component, changing the burning rate, causing staged burning or micro-explosion (e.g. propanol/glycerol, where glycerol is nearly involatile). (2) Soot: sooting fuels form a soot shell between droplet and flame whose size and position depend on initial diameter, increasing radiative loss for large droplets. (3) Low-temperature chemistry: n-alkanes have a negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) range in which a weak cool diffusion flame at roughly 700-800 K can sustain quasi-steady burning after hot-flame radiative extinction, in Linan's partial-burning regime where fuel and oxygen leak through the reaction zone. Pressure, diluent (He, CO2, Xe), droplet interaction and slow flow each shift the balance between these regimes. Sub-buoyant flows of 0.1-5 cm/s, imposed by translating a tethered droplet, are slower than any buoyant flow on Earth and probe the transition from spherical to convective burning.

sources.note: Multicomponent droplet vaporisation (liquid Peclet number), soot-shell formation and Linan diffusion-flame regimes are standard combustion theory.

sources.quote: Cool flames arise in the Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) region
Since both fuel and oxygen leaks through the flame partial-burning regime is appropriate for cool-flame combustion of droplets

equations.meaning: d-squared law: droplet diameter $D$ (mm) at time $t$ (s) from initial diameter $D_0$ (mm) with burning-rate constant $K$ (mm2/s). In FLEX-2 n-alkane tests it holds separately in the hot-flame stage and the cool-flame stage, each with its own $K$; e.g. an n-decane droplet (4.03 mm, air, 0.5 atm) had $K$ = 0.41 then 0.33 mm2/s. Not valid during ignition, at extinction, or when multicomponent effects make burning staged.

sources.note: Godsave/Spalding d-squared law.

sources.quote: The burning rate constants K (=dD2/dt) corresponding to the ﬁrst and second stage combustion were found to be 0.41 and 0.33 mm2/s respectively.

equations.meaning: Liquid Peclet number for a multicomponent droplet: ratio of surface-regression rate to liquid species diffusion. $K$: burning-rate constant (m2/s); $D_l$: liquid-phase mass diffusivity (m2/s, typically ~1e-9). With $K$ ~ 1e-7 m2/s, $\mathrm{Pe}_l$ ~ 100, so in the absence of internal circulation (as in quiescent microgravity) the volatile component is depleted only in a thin surface layer, the involatile component accumulates there, and staged burning or disruption can follow. A FLEX-team paper used n-propanol/glycerol droplets burned in reduced gravity to estimate liquid species diffusivities (title only read).

sources.note: Diffusion-limit model of multicomponent droplet vaporisation (Landis and Mills; Makino and Law).

sources.quote: Estimates of Liquid Species Diffusivities in N-Propanol/Glycerol Mixture Droplets Burning in Reduced Gravity

equations.latex: \frac{D_{ext}^{rad}}{D_0} = f\!\left(D_0,\; \text{ambient } c_p,\ \lambda,\ \kappa_P,\ x_{O_2}\right) \text{ from } T_f(D_f) = T_{crit},\ \dot Q_{rad} = \chi_r \dot Q_{chem}
equations.meaning: Structure of the FLEX-2 radiative-extinction scaling (Nayagam et al. 2018): extinction is assumed when flame temperature $T_f$ (K) falls to a critical value $T_{crit}$, with radiative loss $\dot Q_{rad}$ a fraction $\chi_r$ of heat release $\dot Q_{chem}$; because radiative loss grows with flame volume, the droplet diameter at radiative extinction $D_{ext}^{rad}$ (mm) is set by initial diameter $D_0$ and gas-mixture properties (heat capacity, conductivity, Planck-mean absorption coefficient $\kappa_P$, oxygen fraction). Only the functional form is given here; the paper's fitted expression was not available to us.

sources.quote: a simple scaling analysis, based on the assumptions that radiative extinction occurs when the flame temperature drops to a critical value and that the radiative heat loss rate is a fraction of the heat-release rate at the flame

equations.meaning: Flame standoff ratio: flame diameter $D_f$ over droplet diameter $D$. For the hot flame, classical quasi-steady theory with transfer number $B$, ambient oxygen mass fraction $Y_{O,\infty}$ and stoichiometric fuel-to-oxygen mass ratio $f$ (about 0.29 for alkanes) gives large values (about 34 for $B \approx 8$ in air) that n-alkane hot flames never reach (they stay in the transient zone). The hot-flame expression is our reconstruction of the textbook quasi-steady form, not taken from the FLEX-2 documents. For the cool flame, partial-burning theory with the NTC turnover temperature in place of the adiabatic flame temperature predicted 3.1, and a frame-averaged image of a cool flame around an n-decane droplet in 1 atm air gave 3.2.

sources.note: Burke-Schumann quasi-steady droplet flame position.

sources.quote: Measured FSR 3.2, predicted 3.1!
Hot flame FSR QS model predicts FSR orders of magnitude greater than experimental or numerical results

apparatus.text: Same CIR chamber and MDCA insert as FLEX (opposed-needle deployment, retractable hot-wire igniters, backlit droplet camera, OH* UV camera, colour camera, radiometers), with an added second High Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and crossed silicon-carbide fibre arrays to pin droplets at several positions for droplet-interaction tests. Droplets could be free or fibre-supported, and a fibre could be translated to impose a slow relative flow.

sources.quote: FLEX-2 uses the MDCA insert in the CIR, using the same diagnostic packages with the addition of a second High Bit Depth/Multispectral Imaging Package (HiBMS) camera.
silicon carbide (SiC) fiber arrays will be flown to allow for pinning droplets at multiple locations for studying the interaction of combusting droplets.

procedure.text: The chamber was filled to 0.5-3.0 atm with 0.1-0.4 O2 and a diluent balance and allowed to settle ~2 min. For tethered tests, a predetermined amount of fuel was dispensed onto the support fibre; after needle retraction a dwell of at least 10 s let deployment-induced liquid motion decay. The igniter was powered for 1-5 s and retracted; for convective tests the droplet translation started as the igniter retracted. The colour-camera video was downlinked in near real time to verify deployment, ignition and progress, and chamber pressure and temperature were recorded. Independently varied parameters: fuel type, ambient gas composition, pressure, initial diameter, translation velocity (and acceleration), and droplet spacing and size in a binary linear array.

Nothing quantitative about outcomes can be computed from PSI; all results below come from publications listed in the record.

findings.claim: Cool-flame (second-stage) burning after hot-flame radiative extinction occurs for several n-alkanes, not only heptane: n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets in O2/N2/CO2 and O2/He/N2 at 0.5, 0.7 and 1 atm (14-25% O2) showed quasi-steady low-temperature burning, cool-flame extinction at a finite diameter and vapour-cloud formation, while smaller droplets burned to completion or disrupted. Cool-flame extinction diameters of the three alkanes followed a trend resembling their ignition delay times.

sources.quote: Large n-alkane droplets exhibited quasi-steady low-temperature burning and extinction following radiative extinction of the visible flame while smaller droplets burned to completion or disruptively extinguished.
Remarkably the “cool ﬂame” extinction diameters for all the three n-alkanes follow a trend reminiscent of the ignition delay times observed in previous studies.

findings.claim: n-Decane at 0.5 atm in O2/N2: a 4.03 mm droplet in air burned with K = 0.41 mm2/s in the hot-flame stage (visible extinction at ~14.6 s) and 0.33 mm2/s in the cool-flame stage, whose end was marked by a drop in the narrowband radiometer signal; at 25% O2 a 3.79 mm droplet avoided radiative extinction and micro-exploded at 26 s (K = 0.52 mm2/s); at 17% and 14% O2 hot/cool K were 0.31/0.27 and 0.29/0.25 mm2/s with earlier extinctions.

sources.quote: The burning rate constants for the ﬁrst and second stage combustion were 0.31 and 0.27 mm2/s, respectively.
In general it can be summarized based on the results presented in Fig. 1 that reducing the ambient oxygen concentration leads to earlier hot and cool ﬂame extinctions.

findings.claim: Helium substitution for nitrogen at 21% O2 and 1 atm (n-octane): hot/cool-flame K rose from 0.48/0.38 mm2/s (no He, 3.6 mm) to 0.54/0.43 (15% He) and 0.63/0.53 mm2/s (50% He), with shorter burning in both stages; at 75% He the hot flame died within a fraction of a second and the cool flame also ended quickly, so quasi-steady burning was not achieved. A later FLEX-team analysis reports that helium drastically increases the cool-flame extinction diameter compared with N2, CO2 or Xe, while xenon gives longer burning and a smaller extinction diameter.

sources.quote: The ﬁrst and second stage burning rates are now 0.54 and 0.43 mm2/s, respectively, which is slightly higher than R298 due to increased thermal conductivity of helium compared to nitrogen.

The results show that the cool-flame extinction diameter is drastically increased with helium dilution compared to N2, CO2 or Xe, and Xe dilution leads to longer burning with a smaller extinction diameter.

findings.claim: Radiative extinction of large n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets with CO2, He and Xe replacing nitrogen at moderately varied pressures is correlated by a simple scaling that assumes extinction at a critical flame temperature with radiative loss a fixed fraction of heat release; the extinction diameter depends on initial diameter and ambient-gas properties.

sources.quote: It is shown that a simple scaling analysis, based on the assumptions that radiative extinction occurs when the flame temperature drops to a critical value and that the radiative heat loss rate is a fraction of the heat-release rate at the flame, is able to correlate the measured droplet diameter at extinction

findings.claim: Pressure changes the cool-flame regime: 50/50 decane/hexanol droplets in air showed sustained cool-flame burning after radiative extinction at >= 0.10 MPa; at 0.20 MPa fibre-supported droplets burned with a cool flame and then the hot flame spontaneously re-ignited; at about 0.30 MPa the droplet burned to completion with a cool flame that appeared fundamentally different from the 1 atm cool flame. Hexanol enlarged the cool-flame extinction diameter relative to pure decane, suggesting it inhibits cool-flame burning.

sources.quote: At 0.20 MPa large fiber-supported droplets radiatively extinguished then burned with a cool flame for a period of time before the hot flame spontaneously re-ignited.

The droplet diameters at cool-flame extinction were larger for the decane/hexanol droplets than for pure decane droplets at atmospheric pressure, suggesting that hexanol inhibits the cool-flame burning.

findings.claim: Initial-diameter effects for sooting n-alkanes (n-heptane, n-octane, n-decane) in 1 atm room-temperature air, combining ISS and drop-tower data over D0 = 0.5-5 mm: burning rate decreases monotonically with D0 as soot and radiative losses grow; for D0 > 3 mm a three-stage process appeared (early radiative extinction, continued evaporation, then a second abrupt limit attributed to cool-flame extinction), with oscillatory flame peel-away before final extinction.

sources.quote: The results show that the burning rate monotonically decreases with increasing Do.
A three-staged burning process was found for Do > 3 mm suggesting several extinction modes.

findings.claim: Cool flames were imaged directly for the first time by removing camera filters and dimming the backlight: around an n-decane droplet in 1 atm air the frame-averaged cool flame was broad, weak and closer to the droplet than a hot flame, with standoff ratio 3.2 against 3.1 predicted by partial-burning theory; the same theory predicts cool-flame K within about 20%. In binary n-decane droplet arrays at 17% O2 and 1 atm, droplets of a size that burned only with a hot flame when isolated showed cool-flame burning when paired.

sources.quote: Similar size droplets: Single droplets only hot flame – Binary droplets cool flame
Predicts K within ± 20%
They are located closer to the droplet surface compared to the hot flames

findings.claim: Simplified cool-flame chemistry (a 6-step reduced mechanism based on the San Diego mechanism with activation-energy asymptotics) gives reasonable agreement with ISS cool-flame extinction diameters for heptane and octane but over-predicts n-dodecane extinction diameters, and deteriorates with increasing pressure; widely used detailed mechanisms also fail to predict second-stage cool-flame extinction accurately.

sources.quote: Agreements for heptane and octane seem reasonable, but dodecane extinction diameters are over predicted appreciably.
indicates deterioration of the simplified chemistry with increasing pressure in predictions of droplet diameters at cool-flame extinction.

findings.claim: Cool-flame extinction scaling: in O2/N2 atmospheres the cool-flame extinction diameter of n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets varies with ambient oxygen molar concentration to the power -3/4. With CO2 or He replacing N2 and at 0.5-1 atm this no longer holds, but the residence time at extinction D_ce^2/K_c (with the measured cool-flame burning-rate constant) correlates with oxygen concentration at the predicted slope of -3/2. The exponent comes from an NTC-crossover argument: activation energies of about 120 kJ/mol (crossover) and 180 kJ/mol (ketohydroperoxide branching).

sources.quote: The cool flame extinction diameters vary as oxygen molar concentration to the power -3/4 for oxygen/nitrogen mixture.

Remarkably the data are reasonably well correlated, considering the number of variables involved in the experiments, and, within the appreciable scatter, the results are in agreement with the theoretical slope of -3/2.

findings.claim: The FLEX-2 surrogate-fuel image set has 278 burns of 11 fuels: n-decane; decane/propylbenzene 25/75, 50/50 and 75/25; n-heptane; heptane/iso-octane 50/50; heptane/toluene 50/50; iso-octane; n-octane; propylbenzene; and toluene. 13 burns were tethered, 11 were fully hidden by soot, and droplets measured 1.17-3.81 mm. An automated circle-fitting algorithm (backlit 1024x1024 camera at 30 fps, field about 30 mm) measured 98% of free-droplet runs, with a precision of +/-0.2 pixel (about 6 um) when soot occlusion was limited, and gives a precision estimate for each diameter. Several of these fuels are not in the PSI experimental table.

sources.quote: The FLEX-2 experiments on surrogate fuels comprised 278 individual experiments (Table 1) for 11 different fuel types.
The actual diameter of the droplet varies from 1.17 mm to 3.81 mm.
In cases of limited occlusion, a measurement precision of ±0.2 pixels for the FLEX-2 dataset was achieved.

findings.claim: Large 50/50 decane/hexanol droplets: as pressure rose from 0.05 to 0.3 MPa, the visible and OH* luminosity of the hot flame fell steadily while its broadband radiance stayed nearly constant. The cool flame that followed hot-flame extinction radiated more at higher pressure, reaching almost half the hot-flame radiance at 0.3 MPa. This prompted the idea that a cool flame and a hot flame coexist around the droplet. A Burke-Schumann analysis finds such a dual-flame structure possible only over a narrow range of conditions.

sources.quote: It was also observed that the cool flames that formed immediately following hot-flame extinction had radiant outputs that increased with pressure, reaching almost one-half of the hot-flame radiance at 0.3MPa.
A Burke-Schumann analysis of this dual-structure seems to indicate such flame structures are possible over a narrow range of initial conditions.

findings.claim: The partial-burning model of cool-flame droplet combustion gives reasonable magnitudes for the measured cool-flame burning-rate constants but does not reproduce their apparent dependence on pressure or initial droplet diameter. The 0.30 MPa decane/hexanol cool flame also appears inconsistent with currently available cool-flame kinetics.

sources.quote: The simplified predictions are found to produce reasonable agreement with the experimentally measured values of burning-rate constants but not with their apparent dependencies on pressure or on the initial droplet diameter.
This result does not appear to be consistent with expectations based on currently available cool-flame chemical kinetics and may suggest the need for a different chemical-kinetic mechanism.

relevance.text: FLEX-2 was framed mainly around fuel and engine science, but its results matter for spacecraft fire safety in two ways. First, it showed that invisible cool-flame burning after hot-flame extinction is a general feature of large n-alkane droplets (heptane, octane, decane, dodecane, alkane/alcohol mixtures) and that at elevated pressure a cool flame can spontaneously re-ignite into a hot flame, so 'flame out' seen on a camera is not proof that reaction has stopped and partially oxidised vapour may accumulate. Second, its diluent comparisons (N2, He, CO2, Xe) quantify how inert-gas properties shift radiative and cool-flame extinction. Transferability is limited: mm-size droplets of hydrocarbon fuels in quiescent or slowly moving gas, not solid materials or large fires.

sources.quote: At 0.20 MPa large fiber-supported droplets radiatively extinguished then burned with a cool flame for a period of time before the hot flame spontaneously re-ignited.
These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments

habitat_conditions.text: The planned envelope (O2 0.17-0.30 at 0.5-3.0 atm, i.e. 50.7-304 kPa) brackets the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa) and includes 30% O2, the oxygen level of the Moon-habitat reference, but the listed pressures (0.5 and 1.0 atm) straddle rather than match its 70.3 kPa; which O2/pressure combinations were actually run is not in PSI. The 100% O2 spacesuit atmosphere (29.6 kPa) is outside the range. Most published FLEX-2 results are for air or diluted air at 0.5-3 atm.

sources.note: PSI-68 table: O2 0.17-0.30, pressures 0.5/1.0/1.5/2.0/3.0 atm for every fuel.

earth_benefits.text: Benchmark data for surrogate transportation fuels and for low-temperature (cool-flame) chemistry used in engine design, aimed at cleaner, more efficient combustors and validated jet-engine models.

limitations.text: PSI contains no per-test data for FLEX-2, so no result can be checked or extended from PSI; the condition table repeats one envelope for all eight fuels and does not say which combinations were run.

sources.note: All 8 rows identical apart from fuel.

limitations.text: Fuels in the PSI table differ from those described in other sources (e.g. propylbenzene, toluene, heptane/hexadecane, decane/propylbenzene, heptane/toluene in the 2012 plan; decane/hexanol and dodecane in publications), and CO2/Xe diluents used in publications are absent from the table, so the table is not a complete description of the campaign.

sources.quote: The FLEX-2 fuels are pure n-decane, ethanol, propylbenzene, and toluene, and mixtures of heptane-hexadecane, propanol-glycerol, decane-propylbenzene, and n-heptane-toluene.

limitations.text: Single droplets and pairs of mm-size liquid fuel in near-quiescent gas; results do not transfer directly to solid-material fires, sprays or ventilated cabins. Cool flames were usually inferred from droplet regression and radiometers rather than imaged.

sources.quote: Both the color camera and the UV-camera are not sensitive enough to register any ﬂame images during this period.

open_questions: Obtain the per-test FLEX-2 table (fuel, pressure, diluent, d0, hot- and cool-flame K, both extinction diameters, translation speed) to build cool-flame extinction maps comparable to the FLEX table.
Compare multicomponent (propanol/glycerol, heptane/iso-octane) burning rates and disruption times with diffusion-limit models to extract liquid diffusivities.
Quantify how droplet spacing in binary arrays shifts hot- and cool-flame extinction and flammability limits.
Map conditions under which cool flames re-ignite into hot flames as a function of pressure, oxygen and fuel, as a fire-safety hazard boundary.

Attribution between FLEX and FLEX-2 is blurred in the literature: papers speak of 'FLEX experiments', the two PSI records share most publications, and test numbers (e.g. R298, R377, R694) are not labelled by investigation. Results assigned here to FLEX-2 are post-2011 tests with fuels or features (octane, decane, mixtures, arrays) outside the FLEX matrix; this is our inference.

Dates: PSI gives 2016-08-12 to 2019-09-30, but the 2012 overview says FLEX-2 operations started in January 2012 (planned to July 2014); the PSI dates may be the grant period (NNX16AR09A). Record totalFileSize (~1.22 TB) does not match the single 1 kB file in PSI.

Table oddities: header ' Ambient Temperature (C)' has a leading space and 'Ambient Gas Mixture ' a trailing space; O2 list '0.17; 0.21;0.25; 0.3' has inconsistent separators; pressure entries have a trailing space; the envelope is identical for all eight fuels; the table lists no CO2 or Xe diluent although publications report them; the record approach states O2 0.1-0.4 versus 0.17-0.30 in the table. Gas names here keep their digits (O2/N2), unlike the FLEX table.

Not read: the Shaw and Vang (2015) propanol/glycerol diffusivity paper (10.1007/s12217-015-9455-8; Springer redirected to login, no abstract in OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar); 'Multistage oscillatory cool flame behavior ... elevated pressure' and several other record publications with no DOI; Elsevier full texts. No FLEX-2 per-test summary report (analogous to NASA/TP-2015-216046 for FLEX) was found on NTRS.
Number of FLEX-2 tests is not stated in PSI; the 2012 plan targeted ~400 test points, and the 2014 preprint says over three hundred droplet tests were completed across the FLEX series to that date.
Shaw's affiliation is blank in the PSI contacts; contact details were not copied.
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions was found in the PSI files.

Publication review (Nov 2026; per-paper notes in data/publications/PSI-68.json): of 48 listed publications, 5 were read in full, 21 by abstract and 22 not at all (closed journals without an open copy or indexed abstract). About 19 are ground-based or modelling studies.

Fuel list conflict: the PSI experimental table lists 8 fuels (iso-octane, n-octane, n-heptane, n-decane, ethanol, propanol/glycerol 95/5 and 80/20, heptane/iso-octane 50/50) and droplets of 1.5-5 mm. Rasul et al. 2022 (IEEE TPAMI; OSTI 1998037) report that the flown surrogate-fuel set had 278 burns of 11 fuels, including toluene, propylbenzene, decane/propylbenzene and heptane/toluene, which are absent from the table, and droplets of 1.17-3.81 mm. The table appears to be a planning envelope, not a test list. The 278 covers only the surrogate-fuel part of FLEX-2 (not the decane/hexanol, CO2/Xe or array tests), so n_tests stays null.
Analysis of the 2014 preprint (NTRS 20140006750) gives the decane test R383 as 14% O2 and 96% N2, which sums to 110% (probably 86%).

PSI-69.one_line: Single drops of methanol and heptane were burned floating freely on the Space Station in air thinned with nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium, to find how little oxygen still lets a fuel burn in weightlessness and how well these gases put flames out; it also discovered that heptane drops keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame dies.
PSI-69.summary: FLEX burned isolated, mostly free-floating methanol and n-heptane droplets (initial diameter about 1.1-4.7 mm) in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack between March 2009 and December 2011, in oxygen/nitrogen atmospheres diluted with carbon dioxide or helium at 0.7-3 atm. Cameras recorded droplet diameter and flame size, giving burning-rate constants (typically 0.4-0.6 mm2/s), extinction diameters and burn times for 274 tests. Small droplets extinguished diffusively, large ones radiatively, and the limiting oxygen index (LOI), where the two limits meet, was about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for heptane in nitrogen at 1 atm. Adding carbon dioxide to air raised the LOI to about 0.14 and 0.17; helium raised it to about 0.14 and 0.15. These limits are lower than in normal gravity, so terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards carry less safety margin in orbit. Large heptane droplets kept burning after visible radiative extinction, supported by low-temperature cool-flame chemistry, which raises the possibility of an unseen fire re-igniting.

question.text: FLEX asked how much inert gas (carbon dioxide, helium, or extra nitrogen) is needed to stop a liquid fuel burning in microgravity, and how this depends on oxygen fraction and pressure, with the limiting oxygen index (LOI, the lowest ambient oxygen fraction supporting quasi-steady burning) as the headline quantity. The underlying hypothesis was that the absence of buoyant convection changes transport, radiative loss and chemistry so much that flammability limits and suppressant efficacy differ from those measured on Earth. The droplet was chosen because its spherical symmetry makes the problem one-dimensional, so measurements can test detailed chemical-kinetic and transport models that can then be used for spacecraft fire-suppression design. Pressures down to 0.5-0.7 atm were included because venting a cabin is itself a suppression strategy.

sources.quote: will assess the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression.
one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the habitat where it exists and vent the cabin to space.
FLEX is motivated by the need to better identify and predict limiting oxygen indices (LOIs) and inert-gas suppressant efficacy.

physics.text: A fuel droplet in still microgravity burns inside a spherical diffusion flame: fuel vapour diffuses outward, oxygen inward, and they meet at a flame several droplet diameters away. Heat conducted back from the flame evaporates the liquid, so the burning rate is set by gas-phase diffusion and the squared diameter falls linearly in time (the classical d-squared law). On Earth, buoyancy elongates the flame and blows fresh oxidizer in; without it the flame is larger, cooler, slower and long-lived, so two extinction mechanisms appear. Diffusive (kinetic) extinction happens late, when the shrinking droplet brings the flame so close that residence time is too short for chemistry (low Damkohler number). Radiative extinction happens early for large droplets, whose big flames lose a large share of their heat release to radiation from CO2, H2O and soot. Lowering oxygen makes diffusive extinction occur at larger diameters and radiative extinction at smaller ones; the oxygen fraction at which the two meet is the LOI, below which only transient burning after ignition is possible. Diluents act through heat capacity (CO2 lowers flame temperature and also radiates), conductivity and diffusivity (He raises burning rate and Lewis-number effects) and radiation. Methanol is special because it absorbs product water, which eventually dilutes the fuel and triggers extinction at a size that grows with initial diameter. Large n-alkane droplets showed a second, previously unknown regime: after radiative extinction of the hot flame, low-temperature (about 700 K) cool-flame chemistry in the negative-temperature-coefficient range sustains quasi-steady evaporation until a second, cool-flame extinction, after which unburned vapour forms a visible cloud.

sources.note: Quasi-steady droplet combustion, d-squared law, Damkohler-number extinction and radiative loss scaling are textbook combustion theory.

The numerical predictions show the peak gas temperature during the second stage to be approximately 700 K, consistent with the presence of low temperature chemistry.

equations.meaning: The d-squared law: for quasi-steady, spherically symmetric burning the square of droplet diameter $D$ (mm) falls linearly with time $t$ (s) from its initial value $D_0$; the slope is the burning-rate constant $K$ (mm2/s). FLEX reports an average $K$ from a linear fit of $D^2(t)$ between about 0.1 and 0.9 of the burn time (from shortly after ignition to extinction). Valid after the ignition/heat-up transient and away from extinction, where the instantaneous slope decreases; methanol water absorption and large radiative losses cause departures.

sources.note: Godsave/Spalding d-squared law.

sources.quote: The average burning rate constant (¯k) comes from a linear fit of the droplet-squared history between approximately t = 0.1τb and 0.9τb
Burning rate—average burning rate constant from a linear fit of the droplet diameter squared versus time from shortly after ignition to extinction

equations.latex: K = \frac{8\lambda_g}{\rho_l c_{p,g}}\ln(1+B), \qquad B = \frac{q_f Y_{O,\infty} f + c_{p,g}(T_\infty - T_b)}{L}
equations.meaning: Classical quasi-steady burning-rate constant used by the FLEX team to compare with measured $K$. $\lambda_g$: gas thermal conductivity (W/(m K)); $c_{p,g}$: gas specific heat (J/(kg K)), both evaluated with the Law-Williams property rule; $\rho_l$: liquid density (kg/m3); $B$: Spalding transfer number (dimensionless); $q_f$: heat of combustion per unit fuel mass (J/kg); $Y_{O,\infty}$: ambient oxygen mass fraction; $f$: stoichiometric fuel-to-oxygen mass ratio, so $q_f Y_{O,\infty} f$ is the heat released per unit mass of ambient gas; $T_\infty$, $T_b$: ambient and fuel boiling temperatures (K); $L$: latent heat of vaporization (J/kg). It explains why helium (high $\lambda_g$) raises $K$ and why $K$ increases with oxygen. It neglects radiation, transient flame growth and water absorption; FLEX found small methanol droplets burned faster than this prediction.

sources.note: Spalding B-number theory of droplet burning.

sources.quote: It is interesting to note that the smaller droplets have a higher burning-rate constant than the classical quasi-steady prediction.

equations.meaning: Burn time implied by the d-squared law: $t_b$ (s) is the time from ignition to visible flame extinction at droplet diameter $D_{ext}$ (mm), for initial diameter $D_0$ (mm) and average burning-rate constant $K$ (mm2/s). Applied to the 188 PSI table rows with all four quantities and a non-zero extinction diameter, the tabulated burn time is a median 1.05 times this estimate (interquartile range 1.03-1.09), the small excess being the ignition transient. This consistency is our check that the PSI column 'Burning rate; mm' is $K$ in mm2/s.

sources.note: Direct integration of the d-squared law.

Computed from PSI-69_Experimental table_FLEX.csv: ratio of 'Burn time; s' to (d0^2 - d_ext^2)/K for rows with d_ext > 0 and all values numeric (n = 188); median 1.053, IQR 1.03-1.09, median 1.05 for both fuels.

equations.meaning: Damkohler-number criterion for diffusive (kinetic) extinction. $t_{res}$: residence time of reactants in the flame zone (s), scaling with flame diameter $D_f$ squared over thermal diffusivity $\alpha$ (m2/s); because $D_f/D$ is roughly constant during quasi-steady burning, $t_{res}$ shrinks with $D^2$. $t_{chem}$: chemical time (s), which grows steeply as flame temperature falls (lower O2). For CO2 dilution this simple picture does not hold: the precursor methanol work at fixed 21% O2 found that more CO2 slightly decreased the extinction diameter. Extinction occurs when Da drops to a critical value $\mathrm{Da}_c$, so lower oxygen gives larger diffusive extinction diameters. The FLEX team's earlier CO2 precursor work correlated methanol extinction diameters with a critical-Damkohler theory; activation-energy asymptotics with water absorption were later used.

sources.note: Damkohler-number extinction theory of diffusion flames.

sources.quote: These results are interpreted using a critical Damk hler number for extinction as predicted by an earlier theory
An activation energy asymptotic theory accounting for time-dependent water dissolution or evaporation from the droplet is shown to predict the measured diffusive extinction conditions well.

equations.latex: \frac{\dot Q_{rad}}{\dot Q_{chem}} \sim \frac{\kappa_P\,\sigma T_f^4\,D_f^3}{q_f\,\rho_l K D} \propto D_f^2 \;\; (D_f \propto D)
equations.meaning: Order-of-magnitude reason why large droplets extinguish radiatively. Radiative loss from an optically thin flame scales with flame volume ($\propto D_f^3$), with Planck-mean absorption coefficient $\kappa_P$ (1/m), Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ and flame temperature $T_f$ (K); chemical heat release scales with fuel mass burning rate, $\propto \rho_l K D$ ($q_f$ heat of combustion). The ratio therefore grows with flame (and droplet) size, so above some size the flame cools below its extinction temperature soon after ignition. CO2 dilution increases $\kappa_P$ and lowers $T_f$, moving radiative extinction to smaller droplets. A later FLEX-team scaling based on a critical flame temperature correlates measured radiative extinction diameters.

sources.note: Optically thin radiative loss scaling for spherical diffusion flames.

sources.quote: a simple scaling analysis, based on the assumptions that radiative extinction occurs when the flame temperature drops to a critical value and that the radiative heat loss rate is a fraction of the heat-release rate at the flame, is able to correlate the measured droplet diameter at extinction
Carbon dioxide is also a radiatively participating gas

equations.meaning: Operational definition of the limiting oxygen index used by FLEX. $x_{O_2}$: ambient oxygen mole fraction. As $x_{O_2}$ decreases, the diffusive extinction diameter $D_{ext}^{diff}$ (mm) increases and the radiative extinction diameter $D_{ext}^{rad}$ (mm) decreases; where they become equal no droplet size can burn quasi-steadily. Below it, ignition can still produce short transient burning sustained by igniter energy. Measured values (1 atm): methanol 0.12 and heptane 0.15 in O2/N2.

sources.quote: the limiting oxygen index (LOI), the oxygen concentration below which quasi-steady combustion cannot be supported. This is also the ambient oxygen mole fraction for which the radiative and diffusive extinction diameters become equal.

apparatus.text: The CIR provides a ~90-95 L combustion chamber rated to about 9 atm (limited to about 3 atm for FLEX by safety analysis), a Fuel and Oxidizer Mixing Apparatus that fills the chamber from gas bottles and ISS nitrogen, and a vent to space. The MDCA insert dispenses fuel from syringe reservoirs (about 2.5 ml methanol and 1.25 ml heptane) through two opposed 250 um needles, stretches the liquid bridge, then retracts the needles to leave a nearly motionless free droplet; some tests used an 80 um SiC fibre that could also translate the droplet slowly. Two hot-wire igniters at 180 degrees ignite the droplet and retract. Diagnostics: backlit High Bit-Depth Multispectral camera (1024x1024, ~30 mm field, 30 fps; droplet size and soot), intensified Low Light Level UV camera with a 310 nm OH* filter (~50 mm field), and the MDCA colour camera (~93 mm field, downlinked live for operations). MDCA radiometers were not sensitive enough for quantitative data in 2009-2011. The rack sits on the Passive Rack Isolation System; measured g-levels were typically below 1e-5 g0.

procedure.text: Tests were run remotely from the Telescience Support Center at NASA Glenn, about 4-10 droplets per session; crew changed fuel reservoirs, gas bottles and fibres. For each test the chamber was filled (or an existing fill reused after ~1 min fan mixing), a droplet of chosen size was dispensed and stretched, the needles retracted, the igniters energised for a preset time and withdrawn, and cameras recorded for typically ~40 s. Because atmospheres were reused, the reported composition was computed from fill records and corrected for oxygen consumed and CO2, H2O and fuel vapour produced. The LOI search started at a high oxygen fraction (0.21 at 1 atm, or 0.25 with CO2 at 0.7 atm) and progressively added diluent (N2, then CO2 at constant pressure, then He) until quasi-steady burning was no longer observed, using droplets mostly of 3-4 mm and both free and tethered droplets; the original plan was to vary droplet size at each oxygen level until radiative extinction and then lower oxygen until no ignition. Early tests (Mar-Jul 2009) were in cabin air and in 0.21 O2/0.70 CO2/0.09 N2 at 2-3 atm; the high-pressure series was cut short because the fuel system responded poorly to pressure cycling.

psi_data.summary: PSI holds a single experimental table (24.8 kB CSV, 274 rows, one per test) with test number, CIR identifier, date and GMT, fuel, pressure (mmHg), initial O2/N2/CO2/He mole fractions, initial droplet diameter, visible-flame extinction diameter, burning-rate constant, burn time and how the test ended. It reproduces Table IX of NASA/TP-2015-216046 (which also gives droplet and flame histories as plots), but drops the fibre/no-fibre flag and the per-test notes, and its own test numbers run 1-274 consecutively whereas the report numbers FLEX-001 to FLEX-280 with gaps. No images, droplet/flame time histories, radiometer data or documents are in PSI for this accession, although the record's totalFileSize (~924 GB) suggests the raw image data exist elsewhere. Outcome statistics, burning-rate constants and extinction diameters can be analysed now; flame sizes and LOI cannot be re-derived (no no-ignition tests are listed).

findings.claim: Limiting oxygen index in O2/N2: about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for n-heptane droplets. NASA describes the LOI found as significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted; the 2012 FLEX overview states microgravity flames burned at as much as 2-3 percent less oxygen (the source does not say whether relative or absolute). Consistent with this, the PSI table lists methanol tests that burned 5-11 s and extinguished at 0.12 O2 (8 tests) and heptane tests at 0.13 O2 that burned only 1.0-1.5 s with extinction diameter about equal to the initial diameter (transient burning below the LOI).

findings.claim: Carbon dioxide as suppressant: dispersing CO2 into 1 atm air raised the LOI to about 0.14 for methanol (0.14 O2/0.56 N2/0.30 CO2) and about 0.17 for heptane (0.17 O2/0.63 N2/0.20 CO2), i.e. roughly 30% and 20% CO2 by volume were needed to prevent quasi-steady burning of these fuels. The authors attribute the higher LOI to CO2's larger heat capacity (lower flame temperature) and its radiative participation. The PSI table shows methanol still burning 3.4-5.9 s at 0.14 O2 with 0.36 CO2, and heptane at 0.17 O2/0.20 CO2 extinguishing after 1.6-1.9 s with d_ext/d0 = 0.97.

findings.claim: Extinction regimes: as ambient oxygen was reduced, the diffusive-extinction droplet diameter increased and the radiative-extinction diameter decreased; quasi-steady burning existed only between the two. Radiative extinction was frequent for heptane and often preceded by flame oscillations at about 1 Hz; diffusive extinction of heptane was hard to observe because droplets disrupted first. Methanol seldom extinguished radiatively in the tested sizes but extinguished diffusively at large diameters because of absorbed water; below about 14% O2 radiative extinction took over. In the PSI table, 24 of 56 heptane extinctions with a measured extinction diameter had d_ext/d0 > 0.9 (extinction soon after ignition, radiative), against 14 of 103 for methanol.

findings.claim: Discovery of droplet cool flames: for large n-heptane droplets, after the visible hot flame extinguished radiatively the droplet kept vaporising at a nearly linear D^2 rate for many seconds, then stopped abruptly at a finite diameter, coincident with a large vapour cloud. The team attributed this to quasi-steady, soot-free, low-temperature (~700 K in simulations) cool-flame chemistry that was invisible to the cameras. It was observed repeatably in air and in N2-, CO2- and He-diluted atmospheres, only after radiative hot-flame extinction, and was unexpected; NASA states it was thought impossible by many in the community.

sources.quote: After the visible hot flame radiatively extinguished around a large heptane droplet, the droplet continued to burn with a cool flame. This phenomena was observed repeatably over a wide range of ambient conditions.
A defining feature is that it only occurs after radiative extinction of the hot flame.
This cool flame supported droplet combustion was not only unexpected, but also thought to be impossible by many in the peer community
the science team has concluded that the event is a unique observation of second-stage vaporization sustained by a low-temperature, soot-free, chemical reaction

findings.claim: Cool flames as a fire-safety hazard: the investigators warned that safety procedures based only on hot flames may be inadequate, because cool-flame burning persists invisibly after hot-flame extinction, produces partially oxidised fuel (a vapour cloud) and might re-ignite into a hot flame. Theory by the FLEX PI predicts a separate LOI for cool-flame-supported heptane combustion of order 0.10 O2 in O2/N2, below the hot-flame LOI.

sources.quote: Under certain conditions, it may be possible that a cool flame could reignite in the hot mode, essentially restarting the fire that the crew had thought to be extinguished.
These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments

for heptane burning in oxygen-nitrogen mixtures at normal room temperature, a corresponding oxygen mole fraction on the order of 0.10 in the ambient atmosphere, below which cool-flame-supported combustion cannot occur.

findings.claim: Burning-rate constants: across 258 tests K ranged 0.05-1.06 mm2/s (median 0.50). For methanol in O2/N2 at 1 atm the median K rose with oxygen from about 0.35 mm2/s at 0.12-0.14 O2 to 0.52 at 0.21 and 0.68 at 0.30. At 0.21 O2/0.49 N2 the remaining 0.30 as N2, CO2 or He gave methanol K of 0.52, 0.45 and 0.70 mm2/s respectively: helium's high conductivity raises K, CO2 lowers it. The classical quasi-steady B-number prediction correlated measured K reasonably well, with small methanol droplets burning faster than predicted.

findings.claim: Methanol diffusive extinction is set by water absorption: product water condenses into the droplet until about 30% of its mass is water, after which water evaporates outward and quenches the flame; hence the extinction diameter grows roughly linearly with initial diameter, nearly independent of diluent type. An a-priori activation-energy-asymptotics model reproduced the trend but under-predicted extinction diameters in air unless an effective (water-diluted) flame temperature near 1700 K was used. The CO2-dilution data also showed a quasi-steady flame standoff ratio of about 5 for methanol.

findings.claim: Outcome statistics in the PSI table: of 274 tests, 186 ended in flame extinction at a finite droplet size, 61 in droplet disruption and 27 in burning to completion. In the oxygen-enriched N2 atmospheres at 0.7 atm (0.30 and 0.34 O2, 17 tests) no droplet extinguished: 15 disrupted and 2 burned to completion, which is why the team moved the matrix to lower oxygen. Burn times reached 39.2 s (methanol, 4.35 mm, 0.20 O2/0.05 CO2, 1 atm), far beyond drop-tower durations.

findings.claim: Heptane is much more sensitive to dilution than methanol near the limit: at 0.7 atm with CO2, heptane burn time fell from about 10 s (0.24 O2/0.20 CO2) to 0.55-0.6 s (0.17 O2/0.45 CO2) with extinction at essentially the initial diameter, whereas methanol at 0.15 O2/0.50 CO2 still burned 1.3-3.4 s. Heptane extinction diameter ratios d_ext/d0 at 0.7 atm CO2 had medians above 0.96 at each O2 level <= 0.21 (one test at 0.18 O2 gave 0.954), i.e. early radiative extinction dominated across this range.

Data quality: needle conformal coating contaminated the fuel in the 2009-2011 tests; the team judged burning rates, flame sizes and radiative extinction diameters minimally affected, but methanol disruptive extinction probably caused by the contaminant, and heptane disruption possibly. Droplets often drifted out of the 30 mm backlit field of view due to residual deployment velocity and g-jitter, truncating diameter histories; some extinction diameters were extrapolated.

findings.claim: Numerical modelling of FLEX conditions (Farouk and Dryer) found distinct diffusive and radiative extinction regimes for methanol, with the transition strongly influenced by CO2 concentration, and helium dilution favouring diffusive extinction with higher burning rate; detailed-chemistry simulations including low-temperature chemistry reproduced the two-stage heptane burning.

findings.claim: Methanol extinction mode versus oxygen at 1 atm (O2/N2/CO2, D0 about 2-4 mm): at 18% O2 or more every droplet extinguished diffusively, at 14% O2 or less every droplet extinguished radiatively, and at 15% and 16% O2 a critical initial diameter separated the two modes, larger droplets switching to radiative extinction (the switch happening at a larger D0 at 16% than at 15%). Tests with more CO2 lay closer to the radiative (no-burn) line, which the authors attribute to CO2's higher infrared emissivity; CO2 affected diffusive extinction about as N2 does.

findings.claim: Interpreting methanol extinction with the Zhang-Card-Williams water-absorption theory, diffusive extinction at 1 atm occurs when the infinite-rate (ideal) flame temperature falls to about 1800 K in 21% O2 (calculated lines for 1800 K and 1750 K bracket the data) and below 1650 K at 18% O2. Radiative extinctions occurred so close to the initial diameter that burning was transient and depended on ignition energy; the authors suggest such atmospheres are effectively outside the LOI and that water absorption can be neglected for them.

findings.claim: Methanol flame-standoff ratio (quasi-steady average of flame/droplet diameter) rises as ambient oxygen falls, at both 0.7 and 1 atm. A simplified quasi-steady model that includes water absorption predicts it reasonably, but measured ratios in O2/N2/He mixtures are consistently above the prediction while O2/N2/CO2 data agree better; the authors leave the cause open.

relevance.text: FLEX is the main ISS measurement of inert-gas suppression of liquid-fuel fires in quiescent microgravity. Its message is that weightless flames are weaker but more persistent: they survive at 2-3 points lower oxygen than on Earth, so suppressant concentrations derived from terrestrial standards give less margin in orbit, and CO2 needed roughly 30% (methanol) or 20% (heptane) dilution of 1 atm air to block quasi-steady burning, with helium less effective for heptane. Radiation, not convection, controls extinction of large quiescent flames. The cool-flame discovery adds a hazard: an alkane fire that appears extinguished can keep reacting invisibly, release partially oxidised vapour and possibly re-ignite. Transferability is limited: these are single, mm-size droplets of two pure fuels with a fixed, well-mixed diluent, not spreading fires on solids, sprays, or suppressant discharged into a ventilated cabin.

sources.quote: The research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.
Terrestrially-based fire suppression protocols are insufficient on their own for application in space; and protocols for spacecraft and space habitat fire safety will need to be much more rigorous.
Safety procedures based only on considerations of hot flames may be inadequate for assuring safety under all conditions.

habitat_conditions.text: Most tests were at 1 atm (100-103 kPa, the ISS/Earth sea-level reference) or about 0.7 atm (70-73 kPa). The 0.7 atm / 0.30 O2 condition was chosen by the team to represent the ISS EVA pre-breathe atmosphere and the maximum proposed exploration-vehicle oxygen; it essentially coincides with the reference Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 at 70.3 kPa), and 0.34 O2 was also tested at 0.7 atm. Under these enriched conditions with nitrogen only, no droplet extinguished at a finite size (15 of 17 disrupted, 2 burned out), and CO2 dilution at 0.7 atm began from 0.25 O2. The 100% O2 spacesuit atmosphere (29.6 kPa) and pressures below 70 kPa were not tested in FLEX.

Technol. (open access), Nayagam et al. 2013 US National Combustion Meeting paper (NTRS 20130014061), the 2012 FLEX overview (NTRS 20120015928), the MDCA-FLEX fact sheet (NTRS 20090014812), a 2021 JASMAC presentation (NTRS 20210022617), NTRS abstracts 20110020695 and 20120016855, and NASA's 2015 combustion researcher's guide.

Column units verified: 'Burning rate; mm' is the burning-rate constant K in mm2/s (Table IX of the NASA report labels it 'Burning rate, mm2/s'; our d-squared consistency check gives burn time / ((d0^2-d_ext^2)/K) = 1.05 median). Subscripts were lost in the PSI headers: 'O', 'N', 'CO' mean O2, N2, CO2.

Table oddities: test C11M201 (PSI row 114) has ambient pressure 0 mmHg (also 0 in the NASA report); its sibling tests were at ~535 mmHg and its GMT 19:14:22 equals that of heptane test C11H201 on the same date, so date/time/pressure look mis-entered. Identifier 193F001 appears twice (rows 70 and 73) with identical date and GMT but different d0 (4.67/4.64), K (0.41/0.56) and burn time, as in the report. Six rows (e.g. 193R002, 203F001) have compositions summing to 0.98. Eight rows give extinction diameter 0 (including one 'Completion'), one row (C13H102) has d_ext > d0, and 192F001 is 'Completion' with an extinction diameter of 1.56 mm. Burn times '~6' and '~9' are non-numeric. Row 24 (196F003) contains byte 0x96 (cp1252 en dash used as 'missing'), and the file is cp1252 encoded. Dates mix 2- and 4-digit years.

PSI test numbers run 1-274 consecutively and do not match the report's FLEX-001 to FLEX-280 numbering after test ~155 (e.g. C03H401 is PSI 156 but FLEX-157); the report also lists 284 tests in its summary versus 274 rows.
Report Table III lists tests 019-024 at 0.400 O2 / 0.600 N2 while Table IX (and PSI) give 0.34/0.66 for the same tests; unresolved.
Dietrich et al. 2014 contain apparent typos: helium-diluted LOIs are given with 'N2/CO2' compositions (e.g. '0.14/0.56/0.35 O2/N2/CO2'). We report only the LOI values.

PSI dates (2007-08-01 to 2016-07-31) look like grant dates; ISS testing in the table runs 2009-03-05 to 2011-12-08 and further FLEX tests with xenon were planned for late 2012. Record totalFileSize (~924 GB) does not match the single 25 kB file in PSI.

Abstracts of the key Elsevier papers (Nayagam et al. 2012 'Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?', Hicks et al. 2011 tethered methanol/CO2, Nayagam 2013 AEA, Farouk and Dryer cool-flame 2014) were not available via OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar; their content is cited only through the NASA summaries. Most other publication DOIs in the record are ground-based precursor or modelling studies and were not read in full.
The xenon tests mentioned in NASA documents and Shaw and Vang (2015) are not in the PSI table (it ends Dec 2011); SF6 named in the PSI objective does not appear in any test.

Investigator affiliations in PSI (Dryer at South Carolina, Choi at Missouri) differ from those in the 2015 NASA report (Princeton, Connecticut). One contact email in the PSI record has a malformed domain; contact details were not copied.
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions was found in the PSI files.

Publication review (Nov 2026; per-paper notes in data/publications/PSI-69.json): of the 51 listed publications, 8 were read in full (NTRS preprints/reports, open-access journals), 18 by abstract only and 25 not at all (closed Elsevier/Springer/Taylor & Francis papers with no open copy or indexed abstract, including Nayagam et al. 2012 "Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?" and Nayagam 2013 AEA). About 20 are ground-based or modelling studies outside the ISS data. The open-access Dietrich et al. 2014 PDF was blocked by a bot check this time; the record's earlier quotes from it were not re-verified.

Run numbers in papers do not always equal PSI row numbers: Nayagam et al. 2013 (NTRS 20130014061) 'Run #204' (methanol, 2.75 mm, air, De 1.10 mm) is PSI row 203 (N01M201), and 'Run #263' (2.67 mm, 21% O2/30% He at 0.7 atm, De 1.42 mm) is PSI row 257 (H12M201); Run #110 equals PSI row 110. That paper also writes air as '20% O2 and 79% N2' where the table has 0.21/0.79.

Hicks et al. 2012 ASGSR slides (NTRS 20130010979) give FLEX-145 as '20% O2 / 75% CO2 / 5% N2', D0 3.38 mm, Dext 1.66 mm, K 0.44 on one slide but 'O2 20% / N2 75% / CO2 5%', D0 3.3 mm on the next; PSI row 145 (C01M201) has 0.20 O2/0.75 N2/0.05 CO2, 3.33 mm, 1.61 mm, 0.45 mm2/s. The first slide appears to swap N2 and CO2.

Nayagam et al. 2011 (NTRS 20120016855) describe a 1 atm methanol extinction test 'at 21% O2 had 70% CO2 and 9% N2' (Fig. 3, captioned 1 atm), but every 0.21/0.09/0.70 row in the PSI table (rows 10-18) is at 1546-2320 mmHg (2.0-3.05 atm); the only methanol one with an extinction diameter is row 16 (256F009, 2072 mmHg). The same paper counts 104 methanol tests by October 2011, against 142 methanol rows dated before then in the table (cut-off not stated).

The conclusions of NASA/TP-2015-216046 give initial diameters 'between 2 and 5 mm' and atmospheres of O2 with N2, CO2 and mixtures, but its Table IX (the PSI table) has d0 down to 1.10 mm (26 tests below 2 mm) and 50 helium-diluted tests; its Appendix A says it covers March 2009 to December 2010 although the table runs to December 2011.

PSI-98.one_line: NASA lit a 94-cm-long sheet of cotton-fibreglass fabric inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS, the first large fire deliberately set in orbit, to see whether a fire in microgravity keeps growing or settles to a steady size.
PSI-98.summary: Saffire-I burned a 40.6 cm x 94 cm sheet of SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric inside the uncrewed Cygnus OA-6 cargo module on 14 June 2016, after it left the ISS. This was about ten times larger in each dimension than any earlier microgravity flame-spread sample. Cabin air (about 21.7% O2, near 1 atm) was drawn through a flow duct at about 20 cm/s, and the sample was ignited at its upstream edge. The concurrent flame settled to a steady length of about 40 mm and spread steadily at 1.8 mm/s over about 84 cm for 420 s, releasing about 1.2 kW. On Earth, upward spread over this fabric accelerates. A contingency opposed-flow burn over the last ~10 cm spread at 1.3 mm/s; this fabric cannot burn downward in 1 g. Spread was slower than in the small BASS duct at half the flow, which the investigators attribute to duct size. The fire used about 0.2 percentage points of O2 and raised cabin pressure about 0.3 kPa. A steady flame size lets designers bound a fire's heat release.

question.text: Saffire-I asked two questions. (1) How rapidly does a large fire grow in low gravity, and does flame spread over a large, realistic piece of fabric reach a steady spread rate and a limiting flame size, or keep accelerating as upward fires do on Earth? (2) How do low-g flammability limits compare with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1)? Saffire-I addressed the first; Saffire-II (PSI-99) addressed the second. The motivation is that all earlier microgravity flame-spread tests used samples no larger than about 10 cm in length and width, in small chambers, while a real spacecraft fire would be much larger. Designers have therefore relied on terrestrial fire data and standards, which carry large uncertainty for missions far from Earth. Full-scale fire tests had never been possible in a crewed vehicle; an expendable cargo vehicle after it leaves the ISS removes the risk to crew.

sources.quote: The specific objective of SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-III tests is to determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low-gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a thin solid heats the fuel ahead of it until the fuel pyrolyses; the vapour mixes with oxygen and burns. On Earth, upward (concurrent) spread over a fabric is driven by a buoyant plume whose induced velocity grows with height, so the heated region, the flame and the spread rate all keep growing: upward fires accelerate. In orbit there is no buoyancy; the only flow is the imposed ventilation, here 20 cm/s, which is in the range of spacecraft cabin air circulation. In concurrent flow the flame and its hot plume extend downstream over unburnt fuel and preheat it, while the fuel behind the flame burns out. For a thin fuel, the burning (pyrolysis) zone has a length L_p set by how long the fuel takes to burn out, and the spread rate V_f is L_p divided by that burnout time. If the flame length is limited by the oxygen supply carried by a fixed forced flow, the flame, the pyrolysis zone and the spread rate can all reach steady values, so the fire stops growing. In opposed flow (the air moving against the spread, like downward burning on Earth), spread is governed by heat conducted forward from the flame's leading edge and is usually slower. A thin fabric that cannot spread downward on Earth because the strong buoyant flow blows it off can spread in a gentle forced opposed flow in microgravity. Two scale effects matter for comparisons with small experiments: a wider sample has less oxygen supply per unit width from the sides, and a small duct accelerates the flow around a flame because the hot gas expands, which increases spread rate.

sources.quote: In contrast, upward (concurrent) flame spread at normal gravity on Earth is usually found to be accelerating so that the flame size grows with time.
The forced airflow was 20–25 cm/s, which is typical of air circulation speeds in a spacecraft.
Compared to a wide sample, a narrow sample has more effective oxygen transport across the width of the sample.
This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.
An upward-spreading (concurrent-flow) flame on Earth is nearly always more hazardous than a downward-spreading (opposed-flow) flame.

equations.meaning: Steady concurrent spread over a thin fuel. $V_f$ spread rate of the pyrolysis front (mm/s); $L_p$ steady pyrolysis length, the burning zone between the burnout front and the pyrolysis front (mm); $t_b$ local burnout time of the fuel (s). A steady state needs $L_p$ to stop growing, which happens when the forced flow limits the flame length; in 1 g buoyant upward spread $L_p$ keeps growing and the flame accelerates. Li et al. use this definition of burnout time to compare the 5 cm and 41 cm Saffire samples.

sources.quote: While steady state pyrolysis lengths were similar, the 5 cm wide sample had a slightly larger spread rate (by ∼13%) and a shorter burnout time (pyrolysis length over spread rate) compared to the 41 cm wide sample.

equations.meaning: Heat release rate of a steadily spreading flame over a sheet. $\dot Q$ (W); $m''_c$ areal density of the combustible part (kg/m2; SIBAL: 0.75 x 18 mg/cm2 = 0.135 kg/m2); $W$ sample width (m); $V_f$ spread rate (m/s); $\Delta h_c$ heat of combustion (J/kg, about 16 MJ/kg for cellulose, textbook value); $\eta$ fraction of the cotton actually burned (combustion efficiency). For Saffire-I ($W$ = 0.406 m, $V_f$ = 1.8 mm/s) complete combustion gives about 1.6 kW, of the same order as the investigators' estimate of 1200 +/- 300 W; smoulder residue and incomplete burnout lower $\eta$. Valid only once the spread is steady.

sources.quote: Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W

equations.meaning: Complete combustion of cellulose consumes one O2 molecule per CO2 produced, so the drop in cabin O2 mole fraction equals the rise in CO2 mole fraction ($x$, mole fraction or %). This is how the investigators derived the O2 decrement from the CO2 sensor (21.7 to 21.5%), and it matches the +0.21 percentage-point CO2 rise in the PSI sensor file. It neglects CO, soot and absorption by the vehicle's CO2 removal (if any) during the burn.

sources.quote: i Derived from measured CO2 production and referenced to initial O2 concentration reported by ISS.

equations.meaning: Thermal-regime (de Ris) opposed-flow spread rate over a thermally thin solid. $\lambda_g$ gas conductivity (W/m K); $T_f$, $T_v$, $T_\infty$ flame, pyrolysis and ambient temperatures (K); $\rho_s c_s \tau$ solid heat capacity per unit area (J/m2 K), here with $\tau$ the half-thickness. Textbooks differ on this convention: de Ris's original form uses $\sqrt{2}$ with the half-thickness, and some texts pair $\pi/4$ with the full thickness, so the coefficient depends on that choice. It predicts a spread rate independent of the opposed flow when chemistry is fast and radiation negligible. It is the reference against which the Saffire-I opposed rate (1.3 mm/s at 20 cm/s) and the BASS opposed rates can be compared.

apparatus.text: The Saffire flight unit (about 53 x 90 x 133 cm) was a flow duct with an adjoining avionics bay, separated by a Lexan panel. It was strapped into the Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module (PCM) and was open to the cabin air at both ends. Fans at the top (outlet) of the duct drew air through a flow straightener at the bottom; the duct cross-section was about 18 x 20 in (about 46 x 51 cm; a later paper gives a 25 cm duct height on each side of the sample and a 45 cm width). Two anemometers, one on each side of the sample, measured the air speed and fed the fan control loop. The single sample card sat in the middle of the duct. Hot-wire igniters were woven into the fabric along the upstream edge (main igniter) and the downstream edge (redundant igniter). Two cameras in the avionics bay viewed one face of the whole sample; a green LED was switched on 1 s in every 3 s to show the pyrolysis front. Four radiometers (two viewing the front and two the back, each pair upstream and downstream) measured broadband radiation. Six thermocouples were sewn into the fabric at the centreline, with beads at several heights above the surface, at two streamwise stations; six more measured plume temperature, and one the inlet temperature. procedure.text: Saffire-I launched in the Cygnus OA-6 PCM on 22 March 2016 and stayed unpowered while the vehicle was berthed to the ISS. Before unberthing, the crew checked that the duct inlet and outlet were not blocked by stowed trash. After Cygnus left the ISS and moved to a separate orbit, the ground (Orbital ATK and NASA flight operations teams) powered the unit, ran a built-in test, recorded pre-test smoke-wire flow visualisation (F1), and sent the RUN command. On 14 June 2016 the fan set the flow to about 20 cm/s and, about 60 s into the recording, the upstream igniter was powered for 8 s (about 182 W measured; the 2017 slides give 165 W, 4.1 W/cm of width). The flame then spread downstream (concurrent flow) until the 420 s allotted burn time ended and the fan was switched off, which extinguished the flame at once. About 90% of the fabric had burned, so the contingency opposed-flow test was run: about 11 minutes later the downstream igniter was powered for 8 s and the flame spread upstream into the flow over the remaining ~10 cm, for about 70 s. Post-test flow visualisation (F2) followed. Images were compressed on board and downlinked over the following days, limited to 20 Gbit in total; selected raw (uncompressed) frames were then requested. The relays were opened on 19 June 2016 and Cygnus re-entered on 21 June.

psi_data.summary: PSI-98 holds 76 files (12.25 GB). Almost all of it (61 zips, 12.18 GB, not downloaded) is imagery: for each run (S1, S2, F1, F2) and camera (C1, C2) there are on-board jpegs, distortion-corrected ('Mapped') jpegs, raw camera frames (DistroMaster, with the 8-byte offset fixed), demosaiced TIFFs, and PNGs annotated with exposure and gain, plus checkerboard distortion grids. The S1 sets are split into parts and are the largest (the annotated PNG sets alone are 1.0-1.5 GB per part). What is usable now are the downloaded sensor workbooks. 'Sample 1/2 Sensor Data Complete TM graphs.xlsx' (25 MB each) hold a 'Calibrated Data' sheet at about 30 Hz for 660 s per run: fan speed, CO2, O2, two anemometers, ambient pressure, four radiometers (raw and baseline-subtracted, labelled upstream/downstream, front/back), humidity, inlet temperature, six plume and six sample thermocouples, radiometer temperatures, igniter current and voltage, avionics housekeeping and control flags; plus a 'Camera Data' sheet of per-frame exposure and gain. 'Telemetry Data Good Process Version.xlsx' holds the low-rate real-time telemetry (radiometers, anemometers, fan tachometer, igniters for all 9 Saffire-II-style channels) and Cygnus vehicle data (PCM air temperature and pressure, smoke detectors, cabin fan pressure rise, body rates, accelerations). Two docx files hold the sensor plots. The MergeResult xlsx lists every image file by timestamp, whether it was received or corrupted, and its zip (about 36,000 images each for S1 and S2). No reduced data (flame position vs time, spread rates) are in PSI; the published results come from NASA technical reports and journal papers.

findings.claim: In concurrent flow at about 20 cm/s and 21.7% O2 (falling to 21.5%) near 1 atm, the flame over the 40.6 cm x 94 cm SIBAL sheet reached a steady state: it spread at a constant average 1.8 mm/s, and the flame length reached a plateau of about 40 mm. It burned about 84 cm of the 94 cm sheet during the 420 s allotted. On Earth the same configuration (upward burning) consumes the whole sample with an accelerating flame. This answers the main Saffire question: a large concurrent fire in microgravity, under forced ventilation, need not keep growing.

sources.quote: For the concurrent flame, the length reaches a plateau value of around 40 mm, while the opposed-flow flame is a bit shorter at 24 mm.

findings.claim: The opposed-flow flame (spreading into the 20 cm/s flow, ~21.5% O2) burned the remaining ~10 cm of fabric in about 70 s at an average 1.3 mm/s, with a flame length of about 24 mm. In 1 g this fabric does not spread downward (burn length ~0). So for this material, opposed-flow spread is possible in microgravity at a cabin-like ventilation speed but not on Earth. findings.claim: Scale and duct size matter. The Saffire-I concurrent flame (1.8 mm/s at 20 cm/s in a ~46 x 51 cm duct) spread more slowly than BASS flames over the same fabric in the 7.6 cm SPICE duct, even though the Saffire sample was much wider and the flow was twice as fast. BASS 2-cm strips spread at 2.55 mm/s at about 10 cm/s, and BASS's linear concurrent fits (printed as V_F = -0.20 U + 0.56 and -0.15 U + 0.07 mm/s on an axis where concurrent flow is negative; written with U as the concurrent speed in cm/s, V_F = 0.20U + 0.56 or 0.15U + 0.07) extrapolate to about 3.1-4.6 mm/s at 20 cm/s (our extrapolation). The investigators attribute this to flow acceleration from hot-gas expansion in the smaller tunnels, and conclude that concurrent spread is more sensitive to duct dimensions than anticipated. Small-duct microgravity data can therefore overestimate concurrent spread in an open cabin.

sources.quote: Compared to previous microgravity work in smaller tunnels, the flame in the larger tunnel spread more slowly, even for a wider sample. This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.
Concurrent flame spread (with the wind) was shown to be more sensitive to the flow duct dimension than previously anticipated.

findings.claim: Sample width effect: a 5-cm-wide SIBAL strip burned on Saffire-II at the same 20 cm/s spread at 2.1 mm/s versus 1.8 mm/s for the 40.6-cm sheet (the model paper says about 13% faster; 2.1/1.8 is 17%), with a similar steady pyrolysis length and shorter burnout time. Part of the difference is the higher starting O2 (22.1% vs 21.7%). A 3-D transient model attributes the narrow sample's shorter burnout time to more effective oxygen transport across its width; neither source splits the spread-rate difference between this and the O2 difference. The large sample also showed an initial overshoot of pyrolysis length before reaching steady state, which the model explains by flow reduction in the growing boundary layer.

relevance.text: Saffire-I is the first measurement of how a realistically large fabric fire behaves in a spacecraft. Its key result is that, with forced ventilation of about 20 cm/s and no buoyancy, a concurrent flame over a thin charring fabric does not keep growing as it would on Earth. It reaches a steady spread rate (1.8 mm/s) and a limiting size (flame length ~40 mm, about 1.2 kW for a 40 cm front). The investigators note that a bounded flame size lets designers set the heat release rate a fire can impose on the vehicle. The opposed-flow burn confirms that a fabric which cannot burn downward in 1 g can burn against a cabin-like flow in orbit, so the 1-g downward configuration is not conservative. The duct-size effect means small-chamber microgravity flammability data (BASS, glovebox tests) are not directly transferable to an open cabin: here the larger enclosure gave slower spread. Vehicle impact was small: about 0.2 percentage points of O2 consumed and a 0.3 kPa pressure rise in the Cygnus PCM. This bounds the effect of one ~1 kW, 7-minute fire in a cargo-module-sized volume, not a worst case. The vehicle telemetry (smoke detectors, pressure, temperature) gives a first data set for detection and habitability modelling. The result applies to one thin cellulosic fabric at about 21% O2 and 1 atm; it is not a flammability limit and does not cover thick fuels or exploration atmospheres.

sources.quote: The existence of a flame size limit has important considerations for spacecraft fire safety as it can be used to establish the heat release rate in the vehicle.
Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low-gravity showed that steady flame spread was possible (unlike normal gravity).

habitat_conditions.text: Saffire-I burned in Cygnus cabin air: 21.7% O2 at the start (ISS reading at hatch closure), falling to 21.5%, at about 14.5-14.8 psi (99.9-102.3 kPa depending on the sensor). This is essentially the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa), and slightly O2-enriched. It is far from the exploration atmospheres in the shared reference: a Moon habitat at 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less, and spacesuits at 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. Higher O2 mole fraction generally raises spread rates and flame temperatures, so these results do not bound fire growth in such atmospheres. The Saffire team listed elevated-O2, reduced-pressure flame behaviour as a follow-on objective, to be compared with Saffire-I to III. The 20 cm/s flow is representative of cabin ventilation.
