PSI-99.one_line: Nine strip-shaped samples of spacecraft materials were set alight inside an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit to see whether they burn more or less readily than in NASA's standard ground flammability test; silicone and Nomex would not burn in weightlessness, while a cotton-fibreglass fabric and thick acrylic burned but with flames that stopped growing.
PSI-99.summary: Saffire-II burned nine 5 cm x 29 cm samples in a fan-driven flow duct aboard the uncrewed Cygnus OA-5 vehicle after it left the ISS in late 2016. Samples were sized and ignited like NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (736 J over 9.2 s) so that microgravity flammability could be compared with this 1-g upward screening test. Air flowed at 20 cm/s (25 cm/s for one sample) with about 22.1% O2 near 100 kPa. None of four silicone sheets (0.27-1.03 mm) spread a flame, although the 0.27 mm sheet is fully consumed in 1-g tests and the 0.37 mm sheet burns downward in 1 g. Nomex HT90-40 did not ignite even after about two minutes of heating by a roughly 460 W PMMA pilot flame. Cotton-fibreglass fabric burned completely at a steady 2.1 mm/s (20 cm/s) and 2.6 mm/s (25 cm/s), instead of accelerating as in 1 g. Flames on 1 cm thick PMMA stayed anchored at a limiting size for 10-15 minutes. At these flows the 1-g test was conservative for these materials, and concurrent flames reached a bounded size.

question.text: Saffire-II asked whether NASA's normal-gravity material screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, an upward-burning test on 5 cm x 30 cm strips in which a material fails if more than 15 cm burns) gives flammability limits that hold in long-duration microgravity with spacecraft-like ventilation. Its two stated objectives were to find how fast a large fire grows in low gravity and to compare low-g flammability limits with those from the 1-g screening test. The hypothesis is that fire behaviour differs enough between 1 g and low gravity that designing spacecraft fire safety from terrestrial tests and standards carries real but unquantified risk. That risk grows for exploration missions far from Earth, and microgravity data for designers are scarce. The approach was to burn materials whose 1-g limits lie near the cabin atmosphere (about 21% O2) in an expendable, uncrewed vehicle, so that whether a flame spreads or self-extinguishes is itself the result.

sources.quote: One main objective of the Saffire-II experiment is to ascertain if the flammability limits determined in 1-g using NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 are the same as those in low-gravity.
This is a “worst case” upward flammability test, and the material is said to fail if more than 15 cm is consumed.
The materials have been selected to be near their normal-gravity or hypothesized low-gravity maximum oxygen concentration in 21% O2.
Saffire 2: Verify oxygen flammability limits in low gravity

physics.text: On Earth a flame climbing a vertical strip is driven by its own buoyant plume. The hot gas accelerates upward, thins the boundary layer and lengthens the flame, so the flame heats more fuel ahead of it and spread accelerates. In orbit there is no buoyancy. The only flow is the forced ventilation, here 20-25 cm/s, which is slower than typical buoyant velocities. In concurrent (flow-assisted) spread the flame then settles to a limiting length, set by the point where the net heat flux at the flame tip falls to zero. A thin fuel then spreads steadily. A thick fuel burns out more slowly than its pyrolysis zone extends, so the flame stays anchored near the upstream edge and its spread is controlled by burnout (regression). A slower flow also means a thicker boundary layer, lower convective heat flux to the solid and relatively larger radiative losses. Materials that only just burn in 1 g can therefore be extinguished. Silicone adds a complication: it produces silica powder that can deposit on fresh fuel as an insulating layer, and buoyant flow may sweep it away in 1 g but not in microgravity. Opposed-flow (downward) spread is governed by the heat conducted forward through the gas against the flow.

sources.note: Buoyant versus forced-flow boundary layers, concurrent and opposed flame spread over thin and thick solids, and limiting flame length are textbook flame-spread background.

sources.quote: the microgravity flames reached a steady size (limiting length) for a fixed forced convective flow in agreement with theory (i.e. there is a zero net heat flux at the flame tip).

The limiting length implies that the spread rate of the flame will be controlled by the regression rate (burnout rate) of the material because the flames remains anchored to the upstream end of the fuel samples.
Silicone produces fine silica powder as it burns, which could be deposited on the fuel and impede pyrolysis.

It is seen that the microgravity flame spread rate is significantly lower than in normal gravity at the same ambient pressure, indicating that the buoyantly induced flow velocity plays an important role in normal gravity concurrent flame spread.

equations.meaning: Mixed-convection velocity used by Thomsen et al. to compare Saffire-II thick-PMMA concurrent spread with 1-g reduced-pressure tests. $U_m$ is the equivalent pure forced-flow velocity (m/s) that gives the same boundary-layer thickness; $U_f$ is the forced-flow velocity (m/s, 0.2 m/s in both the flight and ground tests); $P$ is ambient pressure and $P_0$ the reference sea-level pressure (kPa); $g$ is gravitational acceleration (m/s2); $l_p$ is the characteristic pyrolysis length (m, taken as half the sample length). For $g=0$ it reduces to $U_m = (P/P_0)U_f$. In 1 g, lowering $P$ lowers $U_m$ toward the microgravity value. The authors estimate about 20 kPa would be needed to mimic microgravity, where flame chemistry is no longer pressure-independent.

sources.quote: the following expression is obtained for the mixed flow velocity in terms of pressure, forced flow velocity component of the mixed flow, and gravity.
This is important since it would be necessary to reduce the pressure to values of the order of 20 kPa to simulate microgravity conditions

equations.meaning: Heat-transfer-limited concurrent flame spread rate over a thermally thick solid, as used by Thomsen et al. $V_f$ is the spread rate (m/s); $l_h$ is the heated length of solid downstream of the pyrolysis front (m); $h$ is the convective heat-transfer coefficient from flame to surface (W/m2 K), scaling as $U_m^{1/2}$ for a forced laminar boundary layer; $T_f$, $T_p$ and $T_o$ are the flame, pyrolysis and initial solid temperatures (K); $k_s$, $\rho_s$ and $c_s$ are the solid conductivity (W/m K), density (kg/m3) and specific heat (J/kg K). It assumes flame radiation to the surface roughly balances surface re-radiation and that gas-phase chemistry is fast. The authors note this breaks down at low velocity, low pressure or in microgravity, which is why the model somewhat under-predicts the Saffire-II rate.

sources.quote: From Eq. (2) it is seen that the flame spread rate is proportional to the heating length and the square of the convective heat transfer coefficient at the solid surface

sources.note: Thermally thick spread-rate formula (de Ris / Fernandez-Pello type).

equations.meaning: Order-of-magnitude heat release rate of a steadily spreading flame over a thin sheet. $\dot{Q}$ is flame power (W); $\rho_A$ is fuel areal density (kg/m2, 0.18 kg/m2 for the cotton-fibreglass SIBAL fabric, of which only the cotton burns); $W$ is sample width (m); $V_f$ is spread rate (m/s); $\Delta H_c$ is the effective heat of combustion of the burnable fraction (J/kg). It shows why the 5 cm wide Saffire-II fabric strip (reported 200 +/- 50 W) released far less power than the 40.6 cm wide Saffire-I sheet (1200 +/- 300 W) at similar spread rates. It applies only when the burning region has reached a steady length.

apparatus.text: The Saffire flight unit sat in the Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module. It was a rectangular flow duct, about 460 mm x 510 mm in cross section. Fans at the top drew cabin air through it, and flow straighteners sat at the bottom. For Saffire-II the large single sample used in Saffire-I and -III was replaced by a card holding nine samples, each about 5 cm x 29 cm, mounted mid-duct so air passed on both faces. Each sample was ignited by a resistively heated hot wire (29-gauge Kanthal) at its leading edge. Instruments were two cameras (camera images were the primary diagnostic), thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperature, radiometers, solid-state O2, CO2 and pressure sensors, and two anemometers. The PSI record says two radiometers; Thomsen et al. say four. Data were compressed and downlinked before the vehicle re-entered.

procedure.text: Saffire-II was integrated into the OA-5 Cygnus on 12 May 2016, launched on an Antares from Wallops on 17 Oct 2016 and operated on 21 Nov 2016. It stayed dormant while Cygnus was docked; once the vehicle had unberthed it was run from the ground and the data downlinked before re-entry. Flow-visualisation runs were recorded before samples 2-1 and 2-2. The samples were burned one at a time in cabin air: about 22.1% O2 initially (an ISS reading), falling to 21.9% by the last PMMA test, near 100 kPa. Air speed was 20 cm/s for all samples except 2-6 (25 cm/s). Samples 2-1 to 2-7 were ignited at 80 W for 9.2 s (736 J), mimicking the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 igniter. The thick PMMA samples 2-8 and 2-9 used 97 W for 30 s. All burns were concurrent (upward relative to the flow) except 2-4, which was ignited at the downstream end to spread against the flow. Burn length and spread rate were compared with 1-g tests on matching samples (upward, Test-1-like; downward for the 0.37 mm silicone).

psi_data.summary: PSI holds only a one-page summary table and an ISA-Tab metadata zip. The table lists the nine samples with material, thickness, size, flow, O2, igniter settings, burn time, flow direction, microgravity burn length and spread rate, 1-g burn length and spread rate, and camera file IDs. The metadata zip repeats the record text. The table reproduces Table I of the investigators' papers, with transcription errors (see gaps). Flight video, sensor time series and the 'Experimental Details' file named in the approach text are not in PSI. The record's totalFileSize (16.9 GB) suggests those data exist on the server but were not part of what was downloaded or listed. The findings can be checked against the table but not re-derived.

findings.claim: No flame spread on silicone in microgravity. None of the four silicone sheets (0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm concurrent; 0.37 mm opposed; 20 cm/s air, about 22.1% O2; the PSI table lists sample 2-1 at about 21.5% while the published Table I (NTRS 20170008805) gives about 22.1%) propagated. After the 9.2 s, 80 W igniter switched off, a tiny gas-phase flame remained briefly, did not spread and went out. Burn time was 'insignificant' and microgravity burn length about 0 for all four.

sources.quote: Results were convincing although rather anticlimactic as none of the silicone samples burned.
When the igniter was powered off, a tiny gas phase flame remained but did not spread and quickly extinguished.

findings.claim: Silicone was less flammable in microgravity than in the 1-g test. In 1-g tests on matching samples, the 0.27 mm silicone burned completely with accelerating upward spread, the 0.61 mm burned on average 7.6 cm of 30 cm (1.2 mm/s) and the 1.03 mm did not burn. The 0.37 mm sheet burned completely downward at 0.6 mm/s. Published 1-g Test 1 minimum oxygen concentrations (MOC; the term used by the cited source) for silicone are 18% (0.25 mm), 20% (0.61 mm) and 22% (1.00 mm), so the roughly 22.1% O2 flight atmosphere was at or above the 1-g MOC for every thickness. The investigators conclude silicone flammability in microgravity is reduced compared with 1 g, at least at 20 cm/s. This was unexpected: cellulose and PMMA experience suggested that a material that burns upward in 1 g would also burn in microgravity at moderate flow.

sources.quote: The 0.61-mm thickness burned on average 7.6 cm of the available 30 cm before extinguishing
In downward burning, normal gravity tests, this thickness was completely consumed.

findings.claim: Cotton-fibreglass fabric burned completely at a steady rate. The 5 cm wide SIBAL strips burned their full 29 cm in microgravity at steady concurrent spread rates of 2.1 mm/s (20 cm/s air, 145 s burn) and 2.6 mm/s (115 s). For the second strip (2-6) the published paper (NTRS 20170008805) gives 25 cm/s flow, but the PSI table lists 20 cm/s. In 1 g the same strips burned completely with accelerating spread. Microgravity experiments were conducted during NASA's Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire II), on board the Cygnus spacecraft at 100 kPa with an air flow velocity of 200 mm/s.

relevance.text: Saffire-II gave the first direct test, in long-duration microgravity, of whether the upward 1-g screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is conservative. At about 22% O2 and 20-25 cm/s ventilation it was for every material flown. Silicone that burns completely in 1 g, and Nomex at the edge of its 1-g limit, would not sustain spread. Fabric and thick PMMA that burn in 1 g also burned in microgravity, but at steady or bounded size rather than accelerating. Bounded flames make flashover unlikely and let designers bound heat release. However, long-burning anchored flames can build up fuel vapour in a closed vehicle, and the investigators flag a possible backdraft hazard. Flames out quickly once flow stopped, supporting ventilation shutdown on alarm. Transferability limits: one sample per condition, only about 22% O2 at about 100 kPa, and only 20-25 cm/s flow. The silicone result may reverse at higher flows (60-80 cm/s was suggested). Opposed spread was tested on one sample only. Small (5 cm) strips do not represent large fires.

makes the probability of flashover in a spacecraft unlikely as the flame size will be small for low convective ventilation flow environments typical in spacecraft.

habitat_conditions.text: All burns were in Cygnus cabin air at about 22.1-21.9% O2 and about 100 kPa. That is essentially the Earth sea-level / ISS atmosphere (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa), slightly O2-enriched. Nothing was tested at the proposed Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less) or at spacesuit conditions (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa). The material limits seen here (silicone and Nomex non-flammable, fabric and PMMA flammable) therefore cannot be carried over to enriched exploration atmospheres. For example, the 1-g Nomex threshold of about 24-25% O2 would be exceeded there. The follow-on Saffire-IV to -VI were defined to characterise fire growth in high-O2, low-pressure atmospheres. Ventilation speeds of 20-25 cm/s are typical of spacecraft air circulation.

PSI-100.one_line: A repeat of the first large spacecraft fire experiment, with the air blowing a little faster, to see how ventilation speed changes how fast a large sheet of fabric burns in an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit.
PSI-100.summary: Saffire-III repeated Saffire-I in the uncrewed Cygnus OA-7 cargo module on 4 June 2017. A 40.6 cm x 94 cm sheet of SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric was burned in cabin air (21.2% O2 falling to 21.0%, near 1 atm) in a flow duct. The flow was planned at 30 cm/s but was about 25 cm/s. An opposed-flow burn was run first from the downstream edge and spread into the flow at 0.98 mm/s over about 10 cm in 60 s. The concurrent burn from the upstream edge then spread steadily at 2.3 mm/s over about 84 cm in about 300-320 s. Compared with Saffire-I at 20 cm/s (1.8 and 1.3 mm/s), the faster flow sped up concurrent spread in proportion to the flow and slowed opposed spread. Spread rates were below those of the small-duct BASS strips and the narrow Saffire-II strips. The fire again used about 0.2 percentage points of O2 and raised cabin pressure about 0.4 kPa. Fire growth depends on ventilation speed and on enclosure size, so small-sample tests do not set the hazard.

question.text: Saffire-III had the same objectives as Saffire-I: (1) determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate, and (2) investigate low-g flammability compared with NASA's normal-gravity screening test. Its particular role was to repeat the large-sample burn at a higher forced flow (planned 30 cm/s vs 20 cm/s), to show how the steady spread rate and flame size depend on ventilation speed. The motivation is the same: earlier microgravity tests used samples no larger than about 10 cm in small chambers, and terrestrial fire data carry large uncertainty for spacecraft fire-safety design.

physics.text: The physics is that of Saffire-I (PSI-98): flame spread over a thin charring fabric in a purely forced flow, with no buoyancy. In concurrent flow, the flame and hot plume extend downstream and preheat the fuel. A faster forced flow brings more oxygen and stretches the flame and pyrolysis zone downstream, so concurrent spread speeds up roughly in proportion to the flow, while the steady state (fixed flame and pyrolysis length) is kept. In opposed flow, spread is driven by heat conducted forward from the flame's leading edge. Above a moderate flow speed, faster opposed flow shortens the gas residence time at the leading edge and cools it, so spread slows towards blow-off. BASS (PSI-26) found opposed spread over the same fabric peaks at 10-15 cm/s. Increasing the flow from 20 to 25 cm/s is therefore expected to make concurrent spread faster and opposed spread slower, widening the gap between them. Enclosure size also matters: in a small duct, hot-gas expansion accelerates the flow around the flame, which speeds concurrent spread.

sources.quote: The flame speed is proportional to the air flow velocity

Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds, in good agreement with previous research [Olson, 1991].
This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.

apparatus.text: Same flight design as Saffire-I; the three Saffire units differed only in the sample card. The flow unit (about 53 x 90 x 133 cm) had a flow duct (about 18 x 20 in; 25 cm height on each side of the sample and 45 cm width according to a later paper) and an adjoining avionics bay behind a Lexan window, strapped into the Cygnus PCM and open to the cabin. Fans at the outlet drew air through a flow straightener. Two anemometers, one on each side of the sample, controlled the fan. Igniters were woven into the upstream and downstream edges of the single 40.6 x 94 cm sample. Diagnostics: two cameras (one face), four radiometers (two front, two back), six sample thermocouples sewn into the fabric at two stations with beads at several heights, six plume thermocouples, inlet temperature, O2, CO2, pressure and humidity sensors in the avionics bay, and a smoke wire for flow visualisation. procedure.text: Saffire-III launched in the Cygnus OA-7 PCM (PSI start date 18 April 2017) and stayed unpowered while berthed. After unberthing, the Cygnus team moved the vehicle to a separate orbit, powered the experiment, ran a check, put the vehicle in free drift and started the run. This took about half a day from undocking. The burns took place on 4 June 2017 (sensor timestamps, UTC). Pre-test smoke-wire flow visualisation (F1) started at 21:09. The sensor files show that the opposed-flow sample (S2) was run first: the downstream igniter was powered at about 21:11:16 UTC and the fan was switched off about 60-70 s later. The concurrent sample (S1) followed: igniter on at about 21:14:31 UTC, and the flame spread upstream-to-downstream over about 84 cm. Post-test flow visualisation (F2) began at 21:26. Both burns used the same ~25 cm/s flow; the planned 30 cm/s was not reached. Only a subset of the data was downlinked (20 Gbit limit); about 3,400 raw frames were requested for S1 and S2.

psi_data.summary: PSI-100 holds 87 files (35.2 GB). Imagery dominates: 67 zips (35.1 GB, not downloaded) for the BIT, F1/F2 flow-visualisation and S1/S2 runs per camera, as jpeg, mapped jpeg, Raw2TIFF (demosaiced raw frames), mapped and exposure/gain-annotated sets. Downloaded and usable: 'Saffire III Sample 1 Sensors.xlsx' (690 s, 20,909 rows at 0.033 s) and 'Sample 2 Sensors.xlsx' (160 s, 4,848 rows). Their 'Calibrated Data' sheet has the same columns as Saffire-I without the radiometer position labels: fan speed, CO2, O2, anemometers, ambient pressure, 4 radiometers, humidity, inlet, plume and sample temperatures, igniter current/voltage and housekeeping. 'Saffire-III Telemetry Data.xlsx' has real-time Saffire and Cygnus telemetry (three PCM pressure sensors, air temperature, smoke detectors, cabin fans, attitude rates, accelerations) for 4 June 2017. findings.claim: Concurrent burn (S1) at about 25 cm/s and 21.2-21.0% O2, near 1 atm: the flame spread over about 84 cm of the 40.6-cm-wide sheet at an average 2.3 mm/s, burning for about 300 s (investigators' table; 320 s in the ASGSR slides). In 1 g the same configuration burns completely with an accelerating flame. Together with Saffire-I, the investigators conclude that concurrent spread over this thin fabric in microgravity reaches a steady rate and a limiting flame length.

findings.claim: Opposed burn (S2) at about 25 cm/s: the flame spread into the flow at 0.98 mm/s over about 10 cm in 60 s. This fabric does not spread downward in 1 g (burn length ~0). At 25 cm/s the concurrent flame spread 2.3 times faster than the opposed flame, against 1.4 times at 20 cm/s in Saffire-I.

Raising the flow from 20 cm/s (Saffire-I) to 25 cm/s (Saffire-III) increased the concurrent spread rate from 1.8 to 2.3 mm/s, a ratio of 1.28 against a flow ratio of 1.25. The burn durations (400 vs 320 s in the ASGSR slides) are in the inverse ratio. The investigators state that the concurrent flame speed is proportional to the air flow velocity. By the same scaling, the Saffire-III fire's heat release would be about 1.5 kW (our estimate; no published value).

findings.claim: Run order and termination (our reading of the sensor files). Unlike Saffire-I, the opposed burn came first. S2 recording started at 21:10:16 UTC on 4 June 2017, with ignition at t = 60 s. Its two responding radiometers rose by at most 12-14 mW/cm2 (a small flame) and dropped back at t = 131 s, the same time the fan was switched off (anemometers ~0.15 cm/s by t = 145 s). The opposed flame was therefore ended by stopping the flow, not by running out of fuel. The concurrent burn followed at 21:13:31 UTC (ignition at t = 60 s) with the fan running throughout.

relevance.text: Saffire-III shows how ventilation speed sets the growth of a large fabric fire in a spacecraft. A 25% increase in forced flow (20 to 25 cm/s) gave about 28% faster concurrent spread, and so roughly proportionally faster fuel consumption and heat release, while the flame still reached a steady state. Higher cabin flow therefore worsens a downstream-spreading fire. Upstream (opposed) spread slowed at the higher flow, and the gap between the two modes widened from 1.4x to 2.3x. As in Saffire-I, a fabric that will not burn downward on Earth spread against the flow in orbit, so the 1-g downward test is not conservative for opposed spread. The opposed flame went out when the fan was stopped, which supports ventilation shut-down as a first response. The relation 'flame speed proportional to air speed' and the flame-size limit let designers bound a fabric fire's heat release for a given ventilation speed. The duct-size and width effects mean that small-sample glovebox tests overestimate concurrent spread for this fabric, and that quantitative fire models must include the enclosure. The O2 use (~0.2 percentage points) and pressure rise (~0.4 kPa) give an anchor for habitability models. Results are for one thin cotton fabric at ~21% O2 and ~1 atm, not a flammability limit.

The existence of a flame size limit has important considerations for spacecraft fire safety as it can be used to establish the heat release rate in the vehicle.

habitat_conditions.text: Saffire-III burned in Cygnus cabin air at 21.2% O2 falling to 21.0%. The pressure was about 13.97-13.99 psi (96.3-96.5 kPa) on the Cygnus sensors, or 14.42 psia (99.4 kPa) on the Saffire sensor. This is close to the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa) and far from exploration atmospheres such as a Moon habitat at 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less, or a spacesuit at 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. In those atmospheres higher O2 would be expected to raise spread rates, so these results do not bound fire growth there. Elevated-O2, reduced-pressure tests were planned for the follow-on Saffire flights. The 25 cm/s flow is within the range of cabin ventilation speeds.

gaps: The three PSI-100 presentations (45th, 46th and 47th ICES) were not downloadable from PSI. Equivalent versions were found on NASA NTRS: 20150022123 (2015, silicone buoyancy study, not used here), 20170002628 (2016 status, pre-Saffire-III) and 20170008805 (2017 results; its results table covers Saffire-I and II only). Saffire-III numbers come from the ASGSR 2017 presentation (NTRS 20180005168). File sizes differ slightly from the PSI listings, so the NTRS versions may not be byte-identical.

No Saffire-III flame length, pyrolysis length, flame power or flame-position plot data were found in text form. The Combustion and Flame (2019) paper covering Saffire-III is paywalled; only its abstract was read.

The PSI record gives no end date; relay opening and Cygnus OA-7 re-entry dates were not found. The ASGSR slide lists the launch as 'Mar 27, 2017' while the PSI start date is 18 April 2017; the identity uses the PSI date.

Data quality: the PSI record approach, the readme and the experimental table give 30 cm/s, but the anemometers and the investigators' results give ~25 cm/s. The table thickness '.33 cm' should be about 0.33-0.37 mm. The PSI 'researchImpacts' field text names Saffire-I rather than Saffire-III.

Data quality: the 'Date / GMT' column in the MergeResult-raw workbook gives 2017-06-03, but the epoch times (e.g. 1496610866187) correspond to 2017-06-04 21:14 UTC, which agrees with the sensor workbooks ('6-4-2017 5:13 PM', EDT).

Data quality: in the Saffire-III sensor workbooks the igniter current and voltage peak at only ~0.94 A and ~4.4 V (about 4 W), against 182 W in the investigators' table; the igniter channels appear to use a different calibration from Saffire-I's (4.1 A, 45.8 V). The radiometer columns lack the upstream/downstream labels given for Saffire-I.
The '1 Hz Telemetry Data.xlsx' and 'Saffire_Data_Table2017.161...-EU.csv' cover 5 June 2017 (19:35-21:30 UTC), the day after the burns, so they do not contain the fires.
Sensor-derived values in findings (pressure, CO2, radiometer and thermocouple peaks, run order) are our computations from the PSI workbooks, not published numbers.
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions were found in the PSI-100 documents.

The held pre-flight paper ('SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status', NTRS 20170001636) planned Saffire-III for launch on OA-7 on 30 Dec 2016 with operations on 3 Mar 2017 (its Table 4, as of 30 Apr 2016); the burns took place on 4 June 2017. It is now cited in findings[4] for the planned 30 cm/s. Per-paper review: data/publications/PSI-100.json.

The support of the SAME experiment team and the crews of ISS increments 10, 13, 15, and 24 are gratefully acknowledged.

PSI-101.one_line: On the ISS, small pieces of five common spacecraft materials were overheated (without burning) to make smoke, and instruments measured how big the smoke particles were and whether the Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors would have noticed them.
PSI-101.summary: SAME-R, the 2010 reflight of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment, heated small cylindrical samples of Kapton, Teflon, silicone rubber, cotton lampwick and Pyrell foam below ignition in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox. Air flow past the sample was varied from 8.1 cm/s down to zero, sample temperature was set per material, and smoke was aged in a 6 L chamber for up to about 1900 s. Three instruments measured the zeroth, first and third moments of the particle size distribution; a two-angle prototype sensor, Shuttle (ionization) and ISS (light-scattering) detectors and electron-microscope grids recorded the same smoke. Unaged baseline smoke had geometric mean diameters of 0.05-0.18 um and diameters of average mass of 0.11-0.47 um; aging and low flow enlarged the particles, and zero flow gave much larger particles. Kapton and Teflon smoke was smallest and often fell below the ISS detector's alarm level, while silicone, lampwick and Pyrell saturated it. At 8.1 cm/s, flight sizes matched ground tests. The authors conclude that a single-moment detector cannot cover all smokes without nuisance alarms, and that multi-moment detection is promising.

question.text: Spacecraft smoke detectors were designed from terrestrial smoke data, but smoke in orbit may differ. Without buoyancy, smoke stays longer near its source at high concentration, so pyrolysis droplets could grow larger by condensation and coagulation. Spacecraft materials also differ from standard test fuels. The SAME hypothesis was that microgravity liquid smoke would have substantially larger droplets, with fewer particles for the same mass, and that this could stop some detectors from alarming. SAME-R reflew the 2007 SAME experiment to (1) quantify the sizes smoke particles reach in low gravity and relate them to generation temperature, air flow and aging (transport) time; (2) obtain usable electron-microscope (TEM) samples, since all SAME-1 grids came back contaminated; (3) evaluate the existing Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors against these smokes; and (4) demonstrate a prototype two-moment smoke sensor (MPASS). The goal was a database for designing future spacecraft fire detectors and alarm set points.

sources.quote: Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs.
The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.

physics.text: The target is the earliest stage of a spacecraft fire: an overheated material pyrolysing before it ignites, not flaming soot. Heated polymer releases vapour; as the vapour cools, it becomes supersaturated and nucleates particles, which grow by condensation within about a millisecond. Over much longer times (up to about $10^3$ s) particles collide by Brownian motion and coagulate. Liquid particles (lampwick, Kapton, silicone) merge into larger droplets; solid ones (Teflon, Pyrell) stick into fractal-like agglomerates. Coagulation preferentially removes the smallest, most mobile particles, so the count mean diameter grows faster than the diameter of average mass and the size distribution narrows towards a self-preserving geometric standard deviation of about 1.32. In 1 g, a hot plume rises and dilutes the smoke. In microgravity with no forced flow, transport is only by diffusion and thermal expansion (about 4 cm in 60 s), so the smoke stays concentrated, ages faster and forms larger particles. The experiment's 'moment method' measures moments $M_i=\int D^i f_N(D)\,dD$ of the number distribution: $M_0$ (number concentration, condensation particle counter), $M_1$ (roughly the ionization chamber signal) and $M_3$ (roughly the light-scattering mass signal for 0.2-2 um particles). Then $\bar D = M_1/M_0$ and $D_{avm} = (M_3/M_0)^{1/3}$ need no distribution assumption. For a lognormal distribution, $D_p = D_g \exp(p\ln^2\sigma_g)$ with $p=0.5$ and $1.5$ for these two diameters, so $D_g$ and $\sigma_g$ follow from their ratio. Detector physics matters: an ionization detector responds roughly to $M_1$ and favours numerous small particles, while a forward-scattering detector responds strongly to particles near or above its near-IR wavelength (about 1 um) and weakly to particles of about 0.1 um.

equations.meaning: Investigators' estimate for zero flow in microgravity. Pyrolysis gases spread only by diffusion (effective diffusivity $\mathcal{D}$, cm$^2$/s) over a length $\ell$ in time $t$. In 60 s they fill about 64 cm$^3$ instead of being diluted into the 6000 cm$^3$ aging chamber, so the initial smoke concentration is of order 50 times higher (their figure), and coagulation is correspondingly faster. This is an order-of-magnitude scaling. The 2018 paper instead estimates the vapour concentration as about 8 times higher, from a thermal-expansion flow of 0.5-1.5 cm/s.

apparatus.text: The SAME hardware was installed in the MSG. A sample carousel (six positions) indexed each sample into the smoke generation duct. A stainless-steel wire coiled around the sample both heated it and sensed its temperature through its resistance. A feedback loop held the wire at a set resistance ratio Rt/R0 for about 60 s. A rising piston in a 6 L (6000 cm3) aging chamber drew air past the sample, setting the duct velocity, and captured the smoke. Some smoke was pushed almost immediately into a low-volume diagnostics duct ('unaged'); the rest was held for a set time (secondary aging) and then measured. The diagnostics duct held: the ISS smoke detector (2-pass near-IR laser-diode forward scattering at 30 degrees, minimum reported sensitivity 0.3 um, planned alarm level 2 V); the Space Shuttle (STS) detector (dual-chamber ionization with a pump and inertial separator that rejects particles larger than 1-2 um); a modified TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter for $M_0$, fed through a dynamic nitrogen diluter; a First Alert residential ionization chamber (americium-241) calibrated for $M_1$; and a TSI DustTrak 90-degree photometer for $M_3$ (calibrated per material against a tapered-element oscillating microbalance). For SAME-R, one of the two DustTrak enclosures was replaced by the GRC-built MPASS, which detects scattered light at two angles to estimate the 2nd and 3rd moments. Thermal precipitators (a heated wire above a TEM grid, so particles deposit by thermophoresis) sampled smoke before and after aging for post-flight TEM. The six rebuilt precipitators held 12 grids each.

procedure.text: Six carousels were preloaded (one Pyrell sample in carousel 5 was found unusable, probably shaken loose at launch). Thirty loose samples (6 Pyrell, 6 silicone, 9 Kapton, 5 lampwick, 4 Teflon) were later loaded into carousel 4 in groups, logged as carousels 7(4)-11(4). For each run, the operator set the wire resistance ratio Rt/R0 (material-specific: about 1.22-1.23 for Pyrell, 1.245-1.28 for lampwick, 1.30-1.36 for silicone, 1.38-1.48 for Kapton, 1.445-1.452 for Teflon). The sample was heated for 60 s (one Kapton run 120 s) while the piston drew air through the duct at 8.1 cm/s (baseline), 2 or 1 cm/s, or zero. Zero flow was not in the original design; it was obtained by changing the valve sequence. The baseline temperature was chosen to give 1-2 mg of mass loss in 60 s. Smoke was usually given 11 s of primary aging and 8 s of mixing, then half was measured unaged (net aging about 21-62 s). The rest was aged in the chamber and measured at about 218-1923 s ('a' runs in the table). Five 'aged STS det' runs held all the smoke for 720 s before measurement. The STS detector was used only in selected runs because its pump drew too much flow to allow aging. Flights ran from 16 July to 9 September 2010 in seven periods, with the science team at GRC's Telescience Center. Samples were weighed before and after flight for mass loss. Afterwards, three ground campaigns ran: (a) flow tests to correct the instruments' dilution ratios; (b) 1 g TEM tests under flight conditions; and (c) 'smoke-in-drums' tests in which smoke from the identical ground SAME unit was diluted into 55-gallon drums and measured with a TSI 3936 scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS) to test the lognormal assumption. Actual wire (sample) temperatures were later derived from the logged resistances with a two-section wire heat-balance model.

psi_data.summary: PSI-101 holds 343 files (about 6.3 GB). The most useful file is the analysed workbook 'SAME, SAME-R_Results.xlsx' (about 45 sheets). It holds per-run reduced data for SAME-1, SAME-R and ground tests: test conditions, ISS and STS detector voltages, P-Trak, DustTrak and MPASS outputs, moment diameters, Hatch-Choate sigma_g and D_g, sample temperature and mass loss. It also has sheets for detector-alarm analysis, flight vs ground and SMPS drum comparisons. Another 70 or so per-run .xls files hold the reduced time series for runs 48-114, and per-run TEM size-analysis workbooks cover runs 54, 55, 60, 62, 63, 64 and 94. The 89-page final report (2014) includes the test matrix (Appendix A), mass loss (Appendix C), the TEM grid map (Appendix D/E) and the 2012 ICES paper (Appendix F). Raw data (223 files, 5.7 GB) are mostly not downloaded: 78 zips (1.7 GB), 8 MP4 downlink videos (3.7 GB), 44 housekeeping CSVs and 74 TEM image decks (pptx). The engineering documents are SAME-era (EIRD, verification plan, wire tests). The two legacy .ppt presentations could not be read. The experimental table CSV is a 10-column extract of Appendix A.

findings.claim: Unaged baseline smoke at 8 cm/s was sub-micrometre for every material. Kapton had geometric mean diameter Dg = 0.047 um, count mean 0.062 um and diameter of average mass 0.106 um. Teflon had Dg 0.093 um and D_avm 0.173 um, lampwick 0.103 and 0.271 um, silicone 0.152 and 0.468 um, and Pyrell 0.177 and 0.377 um. The geometric standard deviation was 2.03-2.38. Typical runs had a few million particles per cm3 and 2-15 mg/m3. (These are the final-report values; the appended 2012 paper gives slightly different numbers, e.g. Kapton Dg 0.042 um.)

findings.claim: Aging the smoke for 720 s in the chamber made the particles larger and the distribution narrower. D_avm rose from 0.106 to 0.169 um (Kapton), 0.271 to 0.401 um (lampwick), 0.468 to 0.628 um (silicone) and 0.377 to 0.529 um (Pyrell), and sigma_g fell to 1.67-1.96. Teflon was the exception: Dg did not grow (0.093 to 0.080 um) and sigma_g widened to 2.34. Number counts fell by a factor of 1.7-2.7 over about 800 s. This agreed with coagulation theory within about 20% for number and 4% for D_avm, but sigma_g fell more than twice as much as predicted.

relevance.text: SAME-R is the main PSI dataset on what early (pre-flaming) spacecraft smoke looks like to a detector. Overheated Kapton and Teflon, the insulation materials most likely to overheat first in electrical faults, give very small particles (D_avm about 0.1-0.2 um unaged). The ISS forward-scattering detector would often not alarm on these. Silicone, cellulose and Pyrell give large particles that saturate it. The older Shuttle ionization design handles small particles better but rejects particles above 1-2 um, and long aging or stagnant (avionics-box) conditions push smoke towards those sizes. The authors conclude that a single-moment detector cannot be sensitive across this size range and also reject large background dust. They recommend size-selective detection, either by classifying particles or by measuring two or more moments, as the MPASS demonstrated, possibly with gas-species sensing. Because 1 g and microgravity smoke matched at 8.1 cm/s, ground tests with controlled aging can screen detectors for ventilated conditions. Low-flow and stagnant microgravity cases still need special attention, because they produce larger, differently shaped particles.

PSI-102.one_line: On the Space Station, small pieces of common spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lamp wick) were overheated without burning, and the size of the smoke particles was measured to find out what kind of smoke detector would reliably catch an early spacecraft fire.
PSI-102.summary: SAME characterised pre-fire smoke in microgravity to guide spacecraft smoke-detector design. In the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox during Expedition 15 (2007), wire-wrapped samples of Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose lamp wick and a reference liquid (dibutyl phthalate on a wick) were heated below ignition in a 2-8 cm/s air flow; the smoke was held in an aging chamber for 10-1800 s, then measured by three compact instruments giving the zeroth, first and third moments of the size distribution, from which a lognormal geometric mean diameter and spread were derived. Fresh smoke had geometric mean diameters of 80-189 nm and mass-mean diameters of 179-472 nm (geometric standard deviation 1.84-2.18); 720 s of aging, by coagulation, raised these to 155-352 nm and 267-606 nm. Silicone and lamp-wick smoke carried roughly half their mass above 1 um; Teflon and Kapton very little. At matched 8 cm/s flow, sizes matched 1-g tests. The Shuttle ionization detector responded to every test, the ISS light-scattering detector poorly to Teflon. The investigators concluded single-moment detectors are risky and recommended multi-moment or size-classifying detection.

question.text: Spacecraft smoke detectors (ionization on the Space Shuttle, near-infrared forward light scattering on the US ISS modules) were designed from 1-g data, and the two designs respond to non-overlapping particle sizes. Without buoyancy, smoke from an overheated material stays longer in the hot, vapour-rich zone near the source and takes longer to reach a detector, so particles might grow by nucleation, condensation and coagulation. The earlier Shuttle-glovebox Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment had found larger solid smoke particles in low gravity and a Shuttle detector that was blind to visible silicone-rubber and paper smoke, but could not size the liquid droplets. SAME set out to quantify the particle size distribution of smoke from overheated (not flaming) spacecraft materials in microgravity, including the effect of sample temperature, air flow and aging time, to compare it with 1 g, to test the hypothesis that liquid smokes form substantially larger droplets in microgravity, and to evaluate how the two existing US spacecraft detectors respond.

physics.text: Smoke from a heated but unignited polymer is an aerosol of recondensed pyrolysis products: solid recondensed polymer (Teflon, Kapton) or liquid droplets (silicone rubber, paper/cellulose). Its size distribution is set near the source by homogeneous nucleation of supersaturated vapour, condensational growth and coagulation, and is then modified during transport by coagulation (number falls, mean size rises, mass is conserved) and by wall losses. On Earth the buoyant plume dilutes and carries away the vapour within a fraction of a second; in microgravity the only flow is the imposed or ventilation flow, so residence time at high concentration near the source and transit time to a detector both increase, which favours larger particles. Detectors respond to different moments of the distribution: an ionization chamber signal scales roughly with the first moment (total diameter per unit volume), a light-scattering detector with roughly the third moment (mass) for particles of about 0.2-2 um, so the same smoke can look strong to one and weak to the other. SAME exploited this by measuring three moments and assuming a lognormal distribution, which is fully defined by number concentration, geometric mean diameter and geometric standard deviation. The investigators' CFD model of the ISS Destiny lab showed that, without buoyancy, ventilation mixes smoke through the module instead of collecting it at a ceiling, so detection times are longer and depend on source location.

apparatus.text: An MSG payload assembled by the crew from modular units (about 5 h of crew time) and then run largely from the GRC Telescience Center. Each sample was a roughly 3 mm diameter cylinder of material wrapped in a stainless-steel wire coil that both heated it and, through its resistance, measured and controlled its temperature (setpoints expressed as a resistance ratio Rt/R0: Kapton 1.380, lamp wick 1.245, silicone 1.327, Teflon 1.440). Six pre-weighed samples were mounted per carousel; five carousels were flown. A piston in a 5.65 L aging chamber drew air over the heated sample through the smoke generation tube (design range 2-8 cm/s; software maximum 9.8 cm/s), held the smoke for a set time with a mixing fan, then pushed it into a low-volume diagnostics duct. There the smoke was measured by: a TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter (isopropanol condensation, 20 nm to about 1 um, 0-1e5 cm^-3, after a software-controlled dynamic diluter; condenser grooved for microgravity), a First Alert residential ionization chamber (Am-241), two TSI DustTraks (90-degree red-laser scattering, 0.001-100 mg/m^3) with 1 um and 10 um inlet impactors, plus an ISS laser forward-scattering detector and a Space Shuttle ionization detector with inertial separator. Thermal precipitators sampled smoke onto TEM grids before and after aging. Signals were digitized at 1 Hz (8-bit).

procedure.text: For each test point the ground team uplinked parameters (sample, heater setpoint, flow, aging time, diagnostics and dilution); the carousel rotated a new sample into the flow duct; the sample was heated for about 60 s (75 s in one run) below its ignition point while the retreating piston drew the smoke-laden air into the aging chamber. After the chosen aging time (10 s to 1800 s) the piston pushed the smoke through the diagnostics duct, where the moment instruments and the two spacecraft detectors sampled it; for aging runs the smoke was measured before and after aging. TEM grids were exposed in the thermal precipitators, and samples were weighed before launch and after return. DustTrak response was calibrated on the ground for each smoke source against a tapered element oscillating microbalance; P-Trak and ionization chamber were calibrated with monodisperse dioctyl phthalate (DOP) droplets against reference instruments. D_0.5 and D_1.5 were computed per run and converted to D_g and sigma_g assuming a lognormal distribution. Ground (1 g) comparison runs were made afterwards with the same type of hardware. Dibutyl phthalate samples were reheated repeatedly to obtain extra test points.

psi_data.summary: PSI holds the documents needed to understand SAME: a 68-page final science report (2010) that appends the four SAE/AIAA papers of 2008-2009 and the flight test log, the requirements document (EIRD) with the CSD background and design calculations, a concept description, operations manual, software and crew-interface documents, and two readable 2012-2013 presentations that actually belong to the SAME reflight era (SAME-2). The 59 readable analyzed-data spreadsheets are per-run 1 Hz housekeeping and diagnostic time series (P-Trak, two DustTraks, two ionization channels, ISS and STS detector voltages, heater resistance, flows) for most of the 47 test points, some with averaging windows marked, plus command logs. They contain no computed particle diameters and no calibration curves, so re-deriving the size table requires the ground calibrations, which are not in PSI. The 8-row experimental table reproduces the pre-flight planning matrix, not the as-flown conditions. Three legacy .ppt files and one .doc are unreadable, and 18 engineering drawings have no text layer.

At 8 cm/s, ground tests gave particle dimensions very close to the flight results, and particle size grew substantially as air flow was reduced. The investigators' 2018 Fire Safety Journal paper, which covers both flights (2007 and 2010), settles it in favour of the weaker conclusion: low-gravity smoke was not significantly different from smoke made under equivalent 1-g conditions, and flight and ground diameters of average mass at matched flow, temperature and aging fall on a slope-1 line at 8.1 cm/s. findings.claim: Implication for detector design: any detector that measures a single moment either needs a very large number concentration to alarm on small particles or alarms on very few large particles, such as dust. The investigators showed this with a hypothetical single-point alarm requirement of 2 mg/m^3 for a lognormal aerosol with GMD 500 nm and sigma_g 1.3. They recommended alarm requirements at several sizes across roughly 200-1200 nm and detectors that measure two or more moments or classify particles by size, which would also help reject false alarms.

An alternative is to develop alarm requirements that include criteria at particle sizes spanning the expected range of fire particulate (e.g. 200 to 1200 nm).

Two possible effective means of achieving this size discrimination are to employ a detector that measures more than one mo ment of the size distribution or to use a detector that can classify the particles into size ranges.

relevance.text: SAME is the main microgravity data set behind requirements for next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors. Its central message is that early (pre-flaming) smoke from common spacecraft materials spans roughly 100 nm to beyond 1 um and shifts with material, flow and aging. Teflon and Kapton smoke stays mostly below 300 nm and is hard for light-scattering detectors such as the ISS unit to see. Silicone and cellulose smoke puts much of its mass above 1 um, where ionization detectors with particle separators, such as the Shuttle unit, may lose it (as in CSD). Smoke trapped in enclosures or carried slowly by cabin ventilation coarsens by coagulation. Background dust is mostly large, so a detector that measures two moments, or classifies by size, can both catch small-particle smoke and reject dust. Transferability: these are small, controlled, non-flaming overheat events of four materials at 2-8 cm/s and up to 30 min aging. They are not flaming fires (soot), not full-scale cabin fires, and the gravity effect itself is uncertain because ground tests at matched flow gave similar sizes.

habitat_conditions.text: No PSI document states the oxygen fraction or pressure of the air drawn over the samples. The smoke was generated in air inside the MSG on ISS, nominally cabin air, but this is not documented. Against the common references: Earth sea level is 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa; a Moon habitat would likely have 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less; a spacesuit has 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. SAME gives no data on how oxygen enrichment or reduced pressure would change pyrolysis rate, nucleation or particle size, or on how lower pressure (longer mean free path, faster coagulation and diffusion) would affect detector response. Its results apply to near-sea-level air only by assumption. There is also no partial-gravity smoke data.

earth_benefits.text: The investigators expect the smoke-detector technology to be useful in other confined, extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines and underwater laboratories. The multi-moment detection concept also addresses the familiar trade-off between ionization and photoelectric residential detectors.

Bimodal distributions (suspected for silicone) cannot be represented, and the third-moment instrument depends strongly on particle size and refractive index. The 2012 SAME-1&2 table gives much smaller unaged values, for example Kapton GMD 47 nm. Absolute sizes therefore carry a calibration uncertainty of tens of percent.

PSI-106.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station photographed small gas flames burning from a tube into a gentle stream of air, to see how flames lift off, hold on and make soot without gravity and to provide test cases for computer models of flames.
PSI-106.summary: SLICE ran laminar coflow jet diffusion flames in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox on 12 test days between 9 February and 23 March 2012. Fuel issued from interchangeable nozzles (0.41-3.23 mm inner diameter) into fan-driven air in a 76 mm square duct. Fuels were methane (100, 70 and 40% in N2), ethylene (100 and 20%) and ethane, at about 21% O2 and 100 kPa. The crew set fuel flow and coflow by hand. A colour DSLR recorded more than 4,000 images, used for flame shape, lift-off height, soot temperature (colour-ratio pyrometry), soot volume fraction and CH* chemiluminescence. A matching flight-hardware replica gave 1-g counterparts. For a 100% methane flame (3.23 mm nozzle, 46 cm/s fuel, 18 cm/s coflow), microgravity raised the peak soot volume fraction four- to eightfold and lowered the peak soot temperature by about 200 K. For nitrogen-diluted methane, flame length scaled with methane mass flow, and microgravity flames were on average 28% longer. The results benchmark combustion models; relevance to spacecraft fire safety is indirect (sooting and radiation of non-buoyant flames).

question.text: SLICE aimed to understand the structure and stability of laminar non-premixed (diffusion) flames without buoyancy. Specific aims were: what stabilises the flame base, particularly when it lifts off the nozzle; the lift-off velocity limits for different fuels and nozzle diameters; how nitrogen dilution of the fuel affects soot and stability; and how microgravity changes flame length and radiative loss compared with 1 g. It also aimed to provide a microgravity data set for validating numerical models of flame structure, soot and radiation. The hypothesis was that burner diameter, coflow velocity and fuel composition strongly influence flame structure and stability in microgravity, and that these flames differ fundamentally from 1-g flames. Before SLICE, no direct experiment-computation comparison existed for such microgravity flames. SLICE was also a precursor to refine the test matrix of ACME's CLD Flame experiment.

sources.quote: Therefore, no direct comparison between experiment and computation was available for microgravity flames, making it hard to directly assess the effectiveness of the computational models.
The SLICE experiment was conducted as a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, in order to maximize its science, e.g., through refinement of the test matrix.

physics.text: A coflow jet diffusion flame burns at the interface between a central fuel jet and a surrounding air stream. Fuel and oxygen meet by diffusion, and the flame sits roughly where they are in stoichiometric proportion. On Earth the hot products are strongly buoyant. They accelerate (computed peak axial velocity about 200 cm/s in the 1-g SLICE methane case), which narrows the flame by drawing gas radially inward and shortens residence times. Without gravity, velocities stay near the inlet values (about 90 cm/s peak in the same case). The flame becomes longer and wider and more diffusion-controlled, and fuel spends longer in hot, fuel-rich regions. Soot therefore has more time to grow, and more soot means more radiative loss and a cooler flame. The flame base can be attached to the nozzle rim or, at higher jet or coflow speeds or with diluted fuel, lifted downstream. A lifted base is a partially premixed edge (triple) flame whose position is set by a balance between local flow speed and flame propagation speed. Too much flow blows the flame out. Lifted, non-sooting flames are especially good model test cases because heat loss to the burner is removed.

sources.note: Burke-Schumann / Roper laminar jet flame theory, edge-flame stabilisation of lifted flames and buoyancy-residence-time effects on soot are textbook combustion background.

sources.quote: Due to the buoyancy effect, the hot flow under 1 g is accelerated and the maximum velocity is up to ~ 200 cm/s at the far downstream location, while the μ g maximum velocity is only ~ 90 cm/s at the upstream location around the tip of the burner given the parabolic fuel velocity profile.
The reduction in axial velocity results in longer residence times, and allows more time for soot particles to grow and results in an enhanced soot volume fraction.
In particular, excellent agreement can be achieved when the flow conditions are such that the flame detaches and lifts above (i.e., moves downstream of) the nozzle.

equations.meaning: Laminar jet diffusion flame length scaling (Roper). The luminous or stoichiometric flame length $L_f$ (m) is proportional to the fuel-stream mass flow rate $\dot{m}_F$ (kg/s) and independent of nozzle diameter and jet velocity at fixed flow rate. The full Roper form is $L_f \propto \dot{m}_F/(\rho D\,\ln(1+1/S))$, with $\rho D$ the density-diffusivity product (kg/m s) and $S$ the stoichiometric air-to-fuel-stream mass ratio. This mass-flow form approximates Roper's original, which uses volumetric flow and a molar stoichiometric ratio; the proportionality is the same. It applies to buoyant and non-buoyant laminar flames with modest coflow. The prefactor differs with gravity: SLICE microgravity flames were longer. In SLICE the measured log-log slope of modified flame length (lift-off height subtracted) against fuel-mixture mass flow rate was 1.07 in microgravity and 1.03 in 1 g.

sources.note: Roper (1977) laminar jet flame length correlation.

sources.quote: In 1g, the average slopes of the computed and measured ˜Lf values with respect to ˙mFM on a log-log scale are 1.02 and 1.03; while in μg, the corresponding values are 1.12 and 1.07.

equations.meaning: Colour-ratio (two-colour) pyrometry used to get soot temperature from the DSLR images. $S_1$ and $S_2$ are signals in two colour channels (for example red and green); $\eta_i(\lambda)$ is the measured spectral response of each channel including the BG-7 filter; $\varepsilon(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{-\alpha}$ is the soot spectral emissivity (dispersion exponent $\alpha$; literature values run 0.5-2.2 and SLICE assumed $\alpha = 1.38$ for all flames); $I_b$ is Planck's blackbody intensity at wavelength $\lambda$ and temperature $T$ (K). The measured ratio is inverted for $T$ through a lookup table. Soot volume fraction then follows from the absolute intensity, calibrated against a flame-heated S-type thermocouple. Valid for optically thin soot after Abel inversion of the line-of-sight images.

sources.note: Standard two-colour soot pyrometry relation; the SLICE paper's Eq. (1) is not quoted because it is garbled in the extracted text.

sources.quote: A color-ratio pyrometry approach based on a color DSLR camera, which was developed and discussed in [13, 14], was used in this study.

apparatus.text: The hardware, shared with SPICE and later used for BASS, was based on the ELF experiment flown on STS-87. A DC fan at the upstream end drew cabin air through a ceramic honeycomb and wire mesh into a 76 mm x 76 mm (rounded-corner) square duct, 174 mm tall. Coflow speed was set by fan voltage and referenced by an omnidirectional hot-sphere anemometer. A central fuel tube took five threaded nozzles of 0.41, 0.77, 1.59, 2.14 and 3.23 mm inner diameter. A mass flow controller, manually adjustable over 0-500 sccm (N2-equivalent), metered the fuel. Instruments were a Nikon D300s DSLR with a 2 mm BG-7 filter, an analog colour video camera with fuel flow, fan setting, anemometer reading and timer overlaid, and a thermopile radiometer with manual gain. A replica (engineering/training unit) at Yale provided 1-g tests and hot-wire coflow profiles. The coflow near the nozzle was not perfectly symmetric.

sources.quote: The duct has a 76 mm × 76 mm square cross-section with rounded corners and is 174 mm tall.
The central fuel jet tube has a threaded base that allows five nozzles with 0.41, 0.77, 1.59, 2.14 and 3.23 mm inner diameter to be interchanged.
The fuel flow rate was controlled by a mass flow controller and could be adjusted manually in the range of 0-500 sccm N2 equivalent flow.

The SPICE and SLICE experiments were both c onducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using common hardware which has since been  used for the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment.
The flame instrumentation was limited to a high-resolution digital still camera, an analog video camera, and a thermopile radiometer with a manually-adjustable gain.
Due to hardware imperfections, the coflow near the fuel nozzle is not perfectly symmetric.

procedure.text: The crew (Don Pettit) installed a nozzle, ignited the flame manually, and set fuel flow (mass flow controller) and coflow (fan voltage) by hand. They then took still images in bracketed exposures so that at least one was unsaturated. The flow conditions for each still were recovered by matching the image EXIF time to the video, whose data overlay was read automatically by optical character recognition. Calibration runs included coflow/fan calibrations and pyrometry calibrations; an S-type thermocouple heated in the flame served as an absolute light source for soot volume fraction. Testing ran on 12 days from 9 Feb to 23 Mar 2012, one fuel bottle per day; on most days the bottle was emptied. Over the campaign more than 4,000 high-resolution images were taken. The same conditions were repeated in 1 g at Yale on the replica hardware, and flames were simulated with a vorticity-velocity (MC-Smooth) code with sectional soot model.

findings.claim: Microgravity made a sooting methane flame larger, sootier and cooler. For a 100% CH4 flame on the 3.23 mm nozzle (mean fuel velocity 46 cm/s, nominal coflow 18 cm/s), the microgravity flame was taller and wider than its 1-g counterpart. Its peak soot volume fraction was about 4 to 8 times higher (about 8 at nominal values), and its peak soot temperature about 200 K lower because of the larger radiative loss.

sources.quote: In μ g, a taller and wider flame was produced and the peak soot volume fraction increased by a factor of ~ 8.
The peak soot temperature in μ g is shown to be ~ 200 K lower than its 1 g counterpart.
A 100% CH 4 flame using 3.23 mm ID nozzle with average fuel velocity of 46 cm/s and nominal air coflow of 18 cm/s was measured at 1 g and μ g.
the microgravity flames were found to be sootier than normal gravity flames by a factor of approximately 4 to 8 in terms of the peak soot volume fraction

findings.claim: Soot moved from the centreline in 1 g to the flame wings in microgravity, which the investigators interpret as a change from inception-dominated to surface-growth-dominated soot formation. Computed peak axial velocity fell from about 200 cm/s (1 g, far downstream) to about 90 cm/s (microgravity, near the nozzle), giving longer residence times.

sources.quote: From 1 g to μ g, the peak of soot volume fraction was also redistributed from the flame centerline to the wings.
The soot growth mode is believed to change from an inception-dominated mode to a surface-growth-dominated mode [28].

Due to the buoyancy effect, the hot flow under 1 g is accelerated and the maximum velocity is up to ~ 200 cm/s at the far downstream location, while the μ g maximum velocity is only ~ 90 cm/s at the upstream location around the tip of the burner given the parabolic fuel velocity profile.

findings.claim: The model predicted flame shape and soot location but not the microgravity soot increase. The sectional soot model reproduced the 1-g to microgravity change in flame shape and the shift of soot to the wings. It gave the right order of magnitude for 1-g soot but did not capture the eightfold rise in microgravity. The investigators suspect the optically thin radiation assumption (no reabsorption).

sources.quote: However, the computation does not capture the dramatic increase in soot volume fraction from 1 g to μ g.
It should be noted that the current computational model uses an optically thin radiation assumption that does not account for radiation reabsorption.

findings.claim: Flame length scaled with fuel flow and was longer in microgravity. For N2-diluted methane flames (CH4 fraction 0.4-1.0, mean fuel velocity 23-90 cm/s), the modified flame length (luminous length minus lift-off height) was proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow. Measured log-log slopes were 1.07 in microgravity and 1.03 in 1 g. Microgravity flames were on average 28% longer (22% computed), and the gap widened with flow rate. Computed and measured lengths agreed within 15%.

sources.quote: In 1g, the average slopes of the computed and measured ˜Lf values with respect to ˙mFM on a log-log scale are 1.02 and 1.03; while in μg, the corresponding values are 1.12 and 1.07.
with computed and measured nonbuoyant ﬂames 22% and 28% longer, on average, and the diﬀerence in ˜Lf increases as ˙mFM increases.
where the diﬀerence between computed and mea- sured ˜Lf is always less than 15%.

findings.claim: Methane flow controlled flame shape; dilution and velocity mattered less. Flame shape (length and radius) was set mainly by the methane mass flow rate. With shape normalised by methane flow, the effect of N2 dilution was negligible and fuel-velocity effects were secondary. Buoyancy narrows the 1-g flame by drawing gas radially inward near the flame front.

sources.quote: the effect of fuel dilution on flame shape (i.e., flame length and flame radius) is negligible when the flame shape is normalized by the methane flow rate.
(2) Buoyancy-induced reduction of the flame radius through radially inward convection near the flame front is demonstrated.
(3) Buoyant and nonbuoyant flame structure is mainly controlled by the fuel mass flow rate, and the effects from fuel dilution and inlet velocity are secondary.

findings.claim: Lift-off depended on gravity and dilution. At the low coflow of the published methane subset, only the 40% CH4 flame in 1 g was lifted; the corresponding microgravity flames and all other flames stayed attached. The full data set spans lifted, non-sooting flames to attached, heavily sooting flames, from weak near-extinction flames to strong ones. It supports study of lift-off and blowout, but quantitative lift-off velocity limits were not found in the sources reached.

sources.quote: Since the coﬂow velocity is relatively small in this study, only the 40% CH4 ﬂame in 1g is lifted and all other ﬂames are attached.

This data covers a range of conditions from weak flames near extinction to strong, highly sooting flames, and enabled the study of gravitational effects on phenomena such as liftoff, blowout and soot formation.

findings.claim: CH* rose with coflow in microgravity and tracked total heat release. In soot-free, N2-diluted methane flames in microgravity, peak CH* concentration rose with coflow velocity but depended only weakly on fuel velocity; attached 1-g flames followed the same trend at different peak values. Integrated CH* emission scaled with the computed total heat release rate, but the 2-D CH* distribution was not a good marker of local heat release.

sources.quote: Results show that, in microgravity, the maximum flame CH* concentration increases with the coflow velocity, but it is weakly dependent on the fuel velocity; normal gravity flames, if not lifted, tend to follow the same trend, albeit with different peak concentrations.

it is shown that the integrated CH* emission scales proportionally to the computed total heat release rate; the two-dimensional CH* spatial distribution, however, does not appear to be a good marker for the local heat release rate.

findings.claim: The camera-based diagnostics worked with minimal instrumentation. With only a consumer DSLR, soot temperature and volume fraction were obtained in orbit by colour-ratio pyrometry with a flame-heated thermocouple calibration. Test conditions were recovered automatically from the video overlay by optical character recognition. This approach fed into the design of the ACME CLD Flame experiment.

sources.quote: Despite the limited instrumentation, py rometric measurements were made in 2012 of the soot temperature and volume fraction using the innovative techniques discussed in [23-24].
The SLICE experiment was conducted as a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, in order to maximize its science, e.g., through refinement of the test matrix.

relevance.text: SLICE is a fundamental combustion experiment with a fixed gas-jet burner, not a material flammability test, so it gives no material limits or spread rates. Its fire-safety value is indirect. It shows that, at the same fuel supply, non-buoyant flames are larger, longer-lived in residence time, much sootier (about 8x) and cooler than in 1 g. This bears on how much radiation and smoke a spacecraft fire may produce, and on detector design (larger soot loads and particles). It also gives validated test cases for the soot and radiation models used to predict microgravity fire behaviour. The record's research impacts mention fire safety only in general terms.

sources.quote: The enhanced soot production resulted in increased thermal radiation losses and hence reduced flame temperatures.

sources.note: Link from sootier non-buoyant flames to smoke-detector and radiation considerations is general fire-science reasoning, not a SLICE conclusion.

habitat_conditions.text: Flames burned in cabin air at about 21% O2 and about 100 kPa, essentially the Earth sea-level atmosphere (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa). No oxygen-enriched or reduced-pressure atmosphere was used, so the results do not cover the proposed Moon-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less). The successor ACME experiments in the Combustion Integrated Rack can vary these conditions; for example CFI-G used up to 85% O2. Coflow speeds of about 15-70 cm/s bracket typical cabin ventilation speeds.

sources.quote: In all cases, the atmosphere consisted of ~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.

earth_benefits.text: The record expects improved numerical models of flame behaviour and soot formation to help design cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners with lower soot emissions. The SLICE data serve as a microgravity test case for model development.

sources.quote: The unique set of data serves as an excellent test case for developing more accurate computational models.

limitations.text: Gas-jet burner flames with prescribed fuel flow; they do not represent pyrolysing solids, flame spread or material flammability limits.

sources.note: Difference between a fed gas burner and a burning material.

limitations.text: Manually operated, exploratory hardware with limited instrumentation (one still camera, video, one radiometer). Flow conditions were set by hand and recovered after the fact from video overlay.

sources.quote: The manually-operated hardware, e.g., where the ISS crew controlled the flow with a potentiometer, was base d on the preceding ELF experiment and was designed for exploratory studie s.

limitations.text: Coflow near the nozzle was not perfectly symmetric, and flight and replica hardware may differ in velocity-profile details. This adds uncertainty to the 1-g versus microgravity and the experiment versus model comparisons.

sources.quote: Although the flight and engineering units are very similar and steps were taken to match conditions as closely as possible between the two, differences in the details of the velocity profiles between the two pieces of hardware are possible.

limitations.text: Only one atmosphere (cabin air at about 100 kPa) was tested.

sources.quote: In all cases, the atmosphere consisted of ~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.

limitations.text: PSI holds no images or per-flame conditions, so none of the results can be checked or extended from PSI. Published analyses cover mainly methane subsets; results for ethylene and ethane flames and the lift-off and blowout limits were not found.

PSI-107.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station burned tiny gas jets in a gentle, adjustable air stream and turned the fuel up until each flame just started to give off smoke, to learn how air flow and burner size control soot release when there is no gravity.
PSI-107.summary: SPICE measured laminar smoke points, the largest flame that releases no soot, of round gas-jet diffusion flames burning in co-flowing air inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS between February and June 2009. The crew set the air speed with a fan, ignited the flame on a 0.41, 0.76 or 1.6 mm burner and raised the fuel flow until soot escaped the tip; luminous lengths were measured from the downlinked video. About 526 flame conditions were logged and 52-55 smoke points found for ethylene, propane, propylene and 75%/50% propylene in nitrogen, at co-flow speeds of 5.4-65 cm/s. Methane flames reached the end of the duct without smoking. Smoke-point length grew with co-flow speed and with smaller burners, scaling as d^-0.91 u^0.41, and was roughly proportional to fuel mass flow over stoichiometric mixture fraction; a simple residence-time model did not collapse the data. Propane was unusually sooty in microgravity. For spacecraft fire safety the results show that ventilation speed and fuel-jet size, not only fuel type, decide whether a small non-buoyant flame emits smoke.

question.text: Laminar smoke points are a standard measure of how readily a fuel forms soot, and on Earth they are shaped by buoyancy. In a 1988 paper Glassman predicted that non-buoyant flames would not have smoke points at all, but aircraft and Space Shuttle tests (Laminar Soot Processes, LSP, in still air) found them. SPICE asked how smoke points of non-buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames depend on the surrounding air flow (co-flow velocity) and burner diameter, which together control the residence time of soot in the flame. Specific aims: (1) measure non-buoyant smoke points of several gaseous fuels; (2) find the effects of co-flow velocity and burner diameter on smoke points and luminous flame lengths; (3) rank the sooting propensity of the fuels; (4) test flame-shape and residence-time models against the data. The stated hypothesis (30-day report) was that smoke points would be observed in co-flowing flames and would depend on nozzle diameter and co-flow velocity.

physics.text: A gas-jet diffusion flame burns where fuel from the nozzle meets air diffusing in. Soot forms on the fuel-rich side and is normally burnt out as it crosses the flame sheet near the tip. As the fuel flow (and flame length) is raised, the tip cools, largely by soot radiation, until soot oxidation stops and soot escapes: that luminous length is the laminar smoke point. Shorter smoke points mean sootier fuels. In 1 g, buoyancy accelerates the hot gas, so residence time grows only weakly with flow, and soot forms near the flame sheet and moves inward. Without buoyancy, the flow decelerates, residence times are long, and soot forms near the cool core and is carried straight toward the flame sheet. Radiative losses then dominate and the tip can extinguish, giving an 'open-tipped' flame that sheds soot in an annular shell. An imposed co-flow restores some control over residence time: faster air shortens the time soot spends in the formation region and may speed oxygen transport for soot burnout. A smaller nozzle raises the jet exit velocity at the same mass flow. Both are expected to push the smoke point to longer flames. Flame length itself depends mainly on fuel mass flow divided by the stoichiometric mixture fraction, not on nozzle size. Criteria proposed for the smoke point include a tip (soot) temperature of about 1300 K in 1 g and about 1000 K in microgravity, a radiative loss fraction of 0.2-0.4 (1 g) or 0.4-0.6 (0 g), or a luminous length about twice the stoichiometric length.

The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted.
Open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded 4 and are associated with flame extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell.

apparatus.text: The SPICE module was the reworked Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) apparatus flown in the Shuttle middeck glovebox on STS-87 (1997). It was launched to ISS on ULF-2 in 2008 and run in the MSG at ISS cabin pressure (the MSG runs about 1.3 mbar below cabin). A DC fan drew glovebox air through a ceramic honeycomb and screen into a duct described as about 76 x 76 mm with rounded corners and about 170 mm long. The final report instead gives interior dimensions of 172 x 43 x 43 mm. Air and products left through a perforated copper plate and screen (soot trap) 120 mm downstream of the burner exit. For safety the fan always ran at a minimum of 5.5 V (overlay FAN number 55-139). An onboard TSI 8475 hot-wire anemometer (rated 5-254 cm/s, +/-3% of reading +/-1% of range) near the inlet gave the AIR overlay reading, calibrated on the ground against a probe 13 mm above the burner tip. Three burner tubes (0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm ID) were swapped by the crew. Fuel came from 150 ml bottles through a regulator and a 0-500 sccm (N2-equivalent) mass flow controller set by a potentiometer on the crew control box. A hot-wire (Kanthal) igniter and a retractable 105 mm ruler for length calibration could be swung to the nozzle. An Oriel thermopile radiometer (90 deg view) gave a qualitative radiation signal; it failed its accuracy verification because of EMI susceptibility. Imaging was a Nikon D100 12-bit still camera (3008 x 2000 pixels, 60 mm lens) through the top window and a Panasonic colour video camera viewing the front window via a 45 deg mirror. A titler stamped fuel flow, fan setting, air reading and radiometer gain on the video, logged at 4 Hz.

procedure.text: The safety package planned, per fuel, nine test points (two co-flow levels, 50% and 100% of maximum, times three burners, at 100% and 50% of the smoke-point fuel flow) plus about five repeats: 54 planned flames plus about 30 repeats. In practice the crew set the fan, ignited the flame with the hot wire, then adjusted fuel flow (and in later sessions swept the air speed) to bracket the smoke point. The crew used a cue card: look for the change from a distinct flame tip to dull red/orange breaking through it. Ground staff at the GRC TeleScience Center watched the real-time downlink at the same time. Flames were steady within about 5 s of any change. Typical burns lasted about 60 s, and after every two burns the MSG was flushed with cabin air for 3 minutes. For each condition the crew took a bracketed trio of Nikon stills, and a ruler reference image was taken for scale. Post-flight, smoke-point conditions were picked from the video. L_SP was measured on axis from the burner tip to the point of steepest grayscale change between yellow and black, which spans 2-5 mm. Flow rates were read from the overlay, and pixel-to-mm calibrations were made per day and per video source. Twelve sessions ran from 14 February (GMT 045) to 23 June 2009 (GMT 174). On 15 June (GMT 166) the crew vacuumed soot from the clogged outlet screen. A normal-gravity campaign with the prototype SPICE module and a 13.7 mm unconfined co-flow burner was run at the University of Maryland (Dotson thesis).
