psi_data.summary: PSI-107 holds 188 files (6.95 GB); 59 are downloaded locally. Text-bearing documents are readable: the 2011 final report (a draft with editing notes, appendices B-F empty), the 30-day post-flight report with the 2009 Eastern States paper, the 2009 Dotson M.S. thesis, the 2010 AIAA presentation, two crew-training decks, the safety data package, the science verification report, a duct-velocity memo and an image organization guide. The SRD (.doc) and two .ppt decks could not be extracted. The most valuable structured file is 'Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls' (526 rows, 43 columns). For every logged condition it gives GMT times, test number, fuel, nozzle, overlay fuel/air/fan/radiometer readings, converted fuel and air rates, video and Nikon flame lengths and widths, a smoke Y/N flag, and Nikon file IDs. 'SmokePointReview-0g-3.xlsx' lists the 55 microgravity smoke points with derived u_a, u_f, Re, \dot m_f/Z_st and residence-time estimates, plus normal-gravity and shuttle comparison points. The PSI experimental table is a 9-column extract of the master sheet. It drops the measurement columns (flame length, Nikon dimensions, smoke flag, data timestamp) and the GMT 062 methane session, so it holds flow settings only. Raw imagery (NEF zips, jpeg/contact-sheet zips, 83 downlink frame-grab zips, picture-book .ppt, 20 videos; about 6.9 GB) is not downloaded. 22 duct-calibration and 8 fuel-flow-calibration files are present (one of each not downloaded).

relevance.text: SPICE is fundamental soot science, not a material flammability test. Its main fire-safety value: in microgravity, whether a small flame releases smoke depends strongly on the local ventilation speed and on the size of the fuel source, not just on the fuel. Faster co-flow (5-65 cm/s, spanning typical cabin ventilation) and smaller fuel jets let flames grow longer before smoking. Non-buoyant flames well past their smoke point open at the tip and shed quenched soot, which is also the main carrier of CO and the signal smoke detectors respond to. Propane was relatively sootier in microgravity than its 1 g ranking suggests, so 1 g sooting indices may not transfer directly. The data and correlations (L_SP vs \dot m_f/Z_st, d^-0.91 u^0.41) are benchmarks for soot models used to predict radiation and smoke yield of spacecraft fires. The SPICE duct itself became the platform for BASS solid-fuel flammability and suppression tests and SLICE lifted-flame tests. These are gas-jet results at about 1 atm and 21% O2; they do not give material ignition or spread limits.

sources.quote: Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.

Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities.
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS.

habitat_conditions.text: All SPICE flames burned in ISS cabin air: O2 19-24% (assumed 21 +/- 1%), about 101 kPa, which is close to the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa). Neither O2 nor pressure was varied. The proposed lunar habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less) and suits (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa) are outside the tested range. Higher O2 raises flame temperature and soot formation and lower pressure reduces soot, so SPICE smoke points cannot be applied to those atmospheres without new tests. The co-flow range (5-65 cm/s) does cover realistic ventilation speeds. There is no partial-gravity SPICE data.

Soot is also a pollutant linked to premature deaths and climate warming.

gaps: DATA ODDITY - 34 duplicate rows in the PSI experimental table: they are not repeated tests. The table is a 9-column extract of 'Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls'. In that sheet each condition usually has a video-measurement row and a Nikon still-image row with identical flow settings, differing only in columns the CSV drops (GMT data timestamp, video vs Nikon flame length, smoke flag, ISS image IDs). Matching the CSV row-for-row to the master (minus GMT 062): the 34 extra rows fall in 31 identical-row groups. 27 groups have distinct data timestamps; the other 4 share a timestamp and pair a video length with a Nikon image record. Two are 'Ku LOS' rows with no data. De-duplicating the CSV would therefore delete real measurement records; they should be tagged video/still instead.

DATA ODDITY - air rate -5.92 cm/s (3 rows, GMT 167, 50% propylene, 0.41 mm burner, ignition time 'LOS'): an artefact, not a reverse flow. The master sheet converts the overlay AIR reading with u_a = 0.9402*AIR - 5.918 (Reference sheet). For these three rows the AIR and FAN cells are blank because the downlink was lost (LOS), so the formula returned its intercept. Treat them as missing. Likewise -0.28 and 0.66 cm/s (6 rows, GMT 136) correspond to AIR readings of 6-7 at the minimum fan setting with a soot-clogged outlet screen, below the anemometer's 5 cm/s rated minimum. They mean 'near-zero, unreliable', not negative flow.

DATA ODDITY - the PSI experimental table omits the whole GMT 062 session (3 March 2009; 57 methane rows in the master sheet: 0.41/0.76/1.6 mm, up to 357 sccm, flames to 110 mm). That is why it has 469 rows against the master's 526 ('526 flames' in the PSI approach is the master row count, not 526 separate ignitions). The table also lacks every measured quantity (flame length, smoke flag) and has no smoke-point column, so it cannot be used alone to reproduce SPICE results.

Other table issues: 25 rows have blank air rate ('Ku LOS', 'no data', or Nikon rows where the formula was not filled); 10 rows have zero hydrocarbon fuel rate (LOS rows and a 'ran out of fuel' row); the 75% propylene label is spelled two ways ('75 % Propylene' 119 rows, '75% Propylene' 16); GMT ignition times use mixed formats (14:37:08, 14.43.58, 1744, 'no ku', 'Ku LOS'); in tests.csv the date column is empty because GMT day-of-year was not converted (all 2009); and fuel_fraction is null for pure fuels and methane.

Michael C. Hicks (Technical Point of Contact; NASA GRC)

location.label: Computation · geometry and flow of the ISS SAME experiments

source.quote: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective.
The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments.

PSI-115.one_line: A computer simulation of smoke forming from a hot, vapour-releasing sample in a slow air stream shows that, without gravity, smoke particles can grow larger than on Earth, which matters for how spacecraft smoke detectors are designed.
PSI-115.summary: This NASA-funded ground study (grant NNX17AF08A, 2017-2019) used two-dimensional direct numerical simulation to compare smoke formed in Earth gravity and in microgravity. The configuration mimicked the ISS Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) vapour, a well-characterised surrogate for pyrolysis products, leaves a 473 K block in a channel with 300 K air flowing at 8 or 10 cm/s. A 45-node sectional aerosol model tracked nucleation, coagulation, condensation, evaporation, thermophoresis and Stokes settling. In Earth gravity, buoyancy makes the flow asymmetric and drives vapour to the cool upper wall. There nucleation is about 100 times faster (about 1e14 vs 1e12 per m3 per s). Settling also removes all particles larger than about 40 um, leaving a single size mode near 5 um. In microgravity the wake recirculation traps hot, vapour-rich gas. This gives a second mode near 30-35 um and particles approaching 100 um, or, without that recirculation, a single mode near 10 um. For fire safety, detectors calibrated on terrestrial smoke may meet larger particles in orbit, and the result depends on geometry.

question.text: How does gravity, through buoyant convection and particle settling, change the size distribution of smoke formed from pyrolysis vapour, and which fluid-dynamic mechanisms cause the difference between microgravity and Earth-gravity smoke? The motivation is that smoke detectors developed and calibrated on Earth may respond poorly in spacecraft if microgravity smoke has different particle sizes. Earlier measurements suggested microgravity smoke particles are 2-8 times larger than terrestrial ones. The study set out to explain this with simulations that resolve fluid, thermal and particle interactions which cannot be measured on orbit.

sources.quote: Measurements suggest microgravity smoke particles to be 2 - 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005).
systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al., 2005).
The simulations provide detailed information about fluid/thermal/particle interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit.

physics.text: Smoke from overheated or smouldering material starts as hot pyrolysis vapour. As it cools and mixes, the vapour becomes supersaturated and nucleates into tiny droplets. These then grow by condensation and by coagulation (collisions between particles). How large they get depends on how long they stay in hot, vapour-rich gas. Gravity acts on this in two ways. Buoyancy lifts hot, vapour-laden gas, changing its time-temperature history and carrying it toward cool walls, where supersaturation and nucleation rise. Gravity also makes large particles settle out: the Stokes settling speed is $u_s=(\rho_p-\rho)g d^2/(18\mu)$. For a DBP droplet ($\rho_p\approx1040$ kg/m3) in air ($\mu\approx1.8\times10^{-5}$ Pa s), this is about 0.8 mm/s at 5 um but about 5 cm/s at 40 um, comparable to the 8 cm/s flow. In microgravity neither effect exists. The particles that remain can be recirculated in a wake behind the source, where they keep growing. Thermophoresis, the drift of particles down a temperature gradient (Talbot correlation), pushes particles away from hot surfaces. The study characterises the flow by the Reynolds number $Re=U_0L_0/\nu$ (22.3 and 27.7) and the Froude number $Fr=U_0/\sqrt{gL_0}$ (0.385 and 0.481 in 1 g; infinite in microgravity), with $L_0=4.4$ mm. A Froude number below 1 means buoyancy matters at these low SAME-like flow speeds.

sources.quote: Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling.
These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems (Urban et al., 1998, 2005).

apparatus.text: Numerical model, no hardware. The solver is an in-house compressible Navier-Stokes code, previously validated for aerosol studies. It solves dimensionless mass, momentum (with a gravity term scaled by 1/Fr^2), total energy and DBP-vapour transport equations. It uses a second-order MacCormack scheme on a non-uniform 960 x 240 grid. A scaled dynamic reference pressure reduces the effective sound speed to 8 m/s, avoiding a Boussinesq approximation. The aerosol is represented by a nodal (sectional) approximation to the general dynamic equation (Prakash et al. 2003). There are 45 size nodes, each 2.25 times the volume of the previous one, starting from a single DBP molecule (4.44e-28 m3). Each node is transported with the gas velocity plus thermophoretic (Talbot) and Stokes settling velocities. Size changes come from Girshick-Chiu self-consistent classical nucleation (enhancement factor 3.2e-4 for DBP), Fuchs-Dahneke coagulation, and condensation/evaporation including the Kelvin effect. Flight data from SAME (Mulholland et al. 2015) entered only through the set-up. The geometry was similar to SAME, the reference length L0 = 4.4 mm was representative of SAME, U0 = 8 cm/s was the SAME flow velocity, and the vapour mass flux (8.4e-5 kg/m2/s) was chosen to represent SAME mass-loss data. Simulated size distributions were not compared quantitatively with SAME measurements in the report.

sources.quote: The domain is non-uniformly discretized by 960 grid points in the x direction and 240 grid point in the y direction. The governing equations are solved on this computational mesh with a second-order MacCormack scheme.
The particle size space is discretized by 45 particle nodes, with the volume of each successive node increased by a factor of 2.25, i.e. vk = 2.25 ×vk−1.

This work utilizes a nodal approximation to the general dynamic equation (Prakash et al., 2003), where the particle size distribution is discretized by a set of nodes k, each associated with a particle diameter dk.
We consider the classical nucleation expression modified by a self-consistent correction proposed by Girshick and Chiu (1990).
The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is defined for DBP as cnuc = 3.2 × 10−4
We instead use a scaled dynamic pressure as the reference pressure Po = ρo (c1Uo)2, such that P⋆ = ραRαT Po , where c1 is specified to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s.

The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale, Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015).
The mass flux has been selected to be representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015).
The computational tool used for this work has been well-validated and used for prior studies of aerosols

procedure.text: Air at 300 K enters a channel 40 L0 long and 6.82 L0 high (L0 = 4.4 mm). The channel has isothermal (300 K), no-slip, impermeable upper and lower walls. The air flows past the heated DBP source block, and zero-derivative conditions apply to species and particles at the inlet and outlet. The flow is laminar, and a two-dimensional representation is taken as largely representative of SAME. Each case runs until the hydrodynamic and thermal fields are steady, which takes a few seconds. All fields are reported at t = 7 s, treated as an effective steady state, although particles keep growing slowly in the recirculating wake. Particle size distributions are 'collected' numerically. The particle flux through a vertical plane x' = 26 (in L0 units) downstream of the source is integrated, giving a collected number density per size node (particles per m3, flux-weighted). Mechanisms are isolated by switching off settling (1EG-NS) or thermophoresis (1MG-NT), or by rotating the source block 90 degrees (1MG-R, 1EG-R). Assumptions: spherical particles, particles at the gas temperature and velocity (plus drift velocities), 100% sticking on walls, particle diffusivity floored at node 5, and gas viscosity and conductivity taken as those of air.

psi_data.summary: PSI-115 holds 47 files (264.4 MB), all downloaded and readable: the final report (Aug 2020), a 1-page data organisation document, a metadata zip, and 44 analysed-data .dat files. The .dat files are the simulation fields behind the report figures, at t = 7 s. Field files are plain-text Fortran output. Each has a header line '960 240 1 1' (ni, nj, nk, nvar), followed by 230,400 values, one per line, in PLOT3D-style i-fastest order. The two grid files ('*_sGrid_grid3d.dat', header '960 240 1') hold x, y and z for the same 960 x 240 mesh. x runs 0-40 and y -3.41 to +3.41, in units of L0 = 4.4 mm. Units inferred by opening the files: U/V/uR/vR are velocities divided by U0 (range about -2.5 to 3.6). Temperature is T/T0 (1.00-1.58, i.e. 300-474 K). SpeciesMF/VaporMF is DBP vapour mass fraction (0-0.072). NumDen and NucRate are log10 of number density (m-3) and nucleation rate (m-3 s-1). Values of -20, and -inf for NucRate, mark zero. DAM is the diameter of average mass in metres (up to 6e-5 m), and Vort is dimensionless vorticity. 'Smoke' is the Fig. 16 smoke field, with values 0-14 and unstated scaling. The PSD files are two-column text (node index, collected number density, presumably m-3 as in Figs. 8-15). nodeDiameters.dat gives the 44 particle diameters (1.24 nm to 138.5 um) for nodes 2-45. Coverage is uneven. The 8 cm/s cases (1EG, 1MG) have all fields. The 10 cm/s cases have only NumDen, PSD, Smoke, U and V. 1EG-NS and 1MG-NT have only PSD (and, for NT, NumDen/u/v). The rotated cases have NumDen, u and v but no PSD files. No README defines file units; they were inferred. There are no raw data, because no experiment was run, and no SAME measurements are included.

findings.claim: At the SAME flow speed (8 cm/s), the Earth-gravity size distribution sampled 26 L0 downstream (Case 1EG) has a single maximum near 5 um and no particles larger than about 40 um. The microgravity distribution (Case 1MG) is bimodal, with maxima near 5 um and 30 um, and a small fraction of particles approaching 100 um.

sources.quote: The Case 1MG distribution contains two local maximums: one at 5 µm and another at 30 µm. The Case 1EG distribution contains only one local maximum at 5 µm.
Case 1EG contains a larger number density than Case 1MG for all particle sizes < 20 µm, and Case 1EG contains no particles > 40 µm – these large particle settle out of the system.

findings.claim: In Earth gravity, buoyancy deflects hot DBP vapour toward the cool (300 K) upper wall. The resulting peak nucleation rate is about 1e14 m-3 s-1, against about 1e12 m-3 s-1 in microgravity, where nucleation occurs only around the edge of the wake. Number densities near the upper wall approach 1e12 m-3, so terrestrial smoke has far more particles below 5 um.

sources.quote: Nucleation occurs at a higher rate, ∼ 1014 [ m3 · s ]−1 , in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.
In Case 1EG, a high particle concentration of nearly ∼ 1012 m−3 appears over a large area near the upper surface due to the high nucleation rate in the region.
Case 1EG contains orders of magnitude more particles < 5 µm than Case 1MG.

findings.claim: In microgravity, the flow, temperature and vapour fields stay symmetric about the channel centreline. A symmetric pair of counter-rotating wake vortices forms behind the source and holds particles at about 1e10 m-3, larger than 30 um. Dividing streamlines keep these particles in the hot wake, where they grow by condensation and coagulation until the vapour is used up. In Earth gravity the wake is asymmetric, most of the flow passes below the source, and the wake holds fewer particles.

sources.quote: The microgravity case in panel (a) remains symmetric near the heated vapor source, whereas the Earth gravity case in panel (b) develops an asymmetry with the majority of fluid passing below the heated vapor source
Large particles (> 30 µm) are present in the wake region downstream of the heated vapor source, and large particle number densities (∼ 1010 m−3) occur inside the wake vortices.
The Case 1EG wake contains fewer particles than the Case 1MG wake.

findings.claim: Gravitational settling is what removes the large mode in 1 g. With settling switched off (Case 1EG-NS), the Earth-gravity distribution widens from nanometres to about 100 um and becomes bimodal, with a new maximum near 35 um, like the microgravity case. With settling on, all particles larger than about 35-40 um are removed downstream of the wake.

sources.quote: Eliminating the settling mechanism has expanded the size distribution to include both smaller and larger particles, and has also introduced a new local maximum in the size distribution near 35 µm.
Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling elimi- nates all particles with diameter > 35 µm.

findings.claim: Thermophoresis keeps particles off the hot (473 K) source surface. With it switched off (Case 1MG-NT), particles reach the hot surface and evaporate. The peak collected number density rises by about a factor of five, the mode stays near 5 um, and the 30 um mode weakens. This supports the conclusion that the recirculating wake makes the largest particles.

sources.quote: the peak number density in Case 1MG-NT is greater than Case 1MG by approximately a factor of five – the most frequent particle size is ∼ 5 µm for both cases.

With re- spect to the particle size distribution, this has the effect of decreasing the number of large particles and increasing the number of small particles – this supports an assertion that the wake is responsible for producing the largest particles in the system.

findings.claim: Geometry matters as much as gravity. Rotating the source 90 degrees shrinks the wake, and no particles are trapped in it. The microgravity distribution then becomes unimodal (no 30 um mode) with a mode near 10 um, about twice the 5 um mode of the Earth-gravity cases. The rotated Earth-gravity case (1EG-R) still peaks at 5 um and has no particles above 40 um.

sources.quote: The most frequent particle diameter for Case 1MG-R is dp = 10 µm – approximately two times larger than Cases 1MG, 1EG, and 1EG-R.
Consistent with Case 1EG, Case 1EG-R contains fewer particles larger than approximately dp = 10 µm, and no particles larger than dp = 40 µm.

findings.claim: Raising the inlet speed from 8 to 10 cm/s (Fr 0.385 to 0.481 in 1 g) weakens buoyancy, so particles reach the upper wall only much farther downstream. The most common size stays about 5 um in both gravity levels, and Case 2EG keeps nanometre-scale particles at the sampling plane. The report's summary judges the PSD difference between flow speeds not meaningful, while the same summary also says the faster flow widens the distribution and adds a second maximum near 30 um. The two statements are not fully reconciled.

sources.quote: Although the particle field remains asymmetric, the increased flow velocity has decreased the influence of buoyancy, reducing interaction with the upper surface.
The most common particle size is ∼ 5 µm for both cases. Case 2EG, unlike Case 1EG, contains particles on the nanometer scale
The faster flow conditions present a slightly larger wake but this does not manifest as a meaningful difference in particle size distribution.
widens the particle size distribution to include particles on the nanometer scale, and introduces a second local maximum to the PSD near dp = 30 µm.

findings.claim: Across the two base cases, the diameter of average mass is typically 10-20 um. It is smaller where nucleation is intense, for example near the upper wall in 1 g. No particles smaller than 400 nm reach the far field in microgravity, because nucleation happens only for a short distance behind the source.

sources.quote: The diameter of average mass is typically 10 − 20 µm in both cases.
No particles are present far downstream with diameter < 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated va- por source.

findings.claim: The report identifies three mechanisms that make microgravity smoke larger. First, recirculation geometry changes the time-temperature-concentration history. Second, settling removes large particles in 1 g. Third, buoyancy carries vapour to cool surfaces and raises nucleation. Each is material- and geometry-dependent. The authors hypothesise that microgravity and 1 g smoke are more alike in open spaces without stable recirculation, and most different in a quiescent enclosure (not simulated).

sources.quote: Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. How- ever, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent
contrast, a quiescent, enclosed system is a relevant case where Earth gravity and microgravity smoke are hypothesized to differ significantly, and is a consideration of future work.

findings.claim: A check of the deposited PSD files against nodeDiameters.dat finds the main peak at nodes 33-34 (5.4-7.1 um) in every case, consistent with the report's ~5 um mode. A secondary maximum appears near 27 um (1MG, 1MG-NT), 36 um (1EG-NS) and 21 um (2EG, 2MG). Ratios between files are smaller than the report states. The 1MG-NT/1MG peak ratio is about 2.4, not about 5. The ratio of total number below 5 um, 1EG/1MG, is about 6 rather than 'orders of magnitude'. This may reflect binning or plotting differences.

relevance.text: Detection: spacecraft smoke detectors are sized and calibrated on terrestrial smoke. This study gives a mechanistic reason why smoke from a smouldering or pre-ignition source in microgravity can contain more large particles. With a bimodal distribution, the large mode is above 30 um, a size range almost absent from simulated 1 g smoke. Without recirculation, the mode is about twice the terrestrial size. Detector designs (light-scattering or ionisation sensitivity versus size), sampling inlets and filter or transport losses should therefore be checked against larger particles and broader distributions. The study also shows the answer depends on local geometry (wakes behind objects) and on whether cool surfaces are nearby. A single 'microgravity correction factor' is therefore unlikely to be valid. Transferability is limited. The fuel is a single surrogate (DBP) that forms large droplets, not the SAME materials. The flow is 2-D and laminar at 8-10 cm/s, and no combustion or soot is modelled. This is pre-fire (pyrolysis) smoke only.

sources.quote: Results show that future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments
(2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles)

habitat_conditions.text: All cases use air at atmospheric pressure and 300 K, close to the Earth sea-level reference of 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa. Oxygen plays no role because the model has no combustion. Exploration atmospheres such as a lunar habitat (30% or more O2 at 70.3 kPa or less) were not simulated. Lower pressure would raise the gas mean free path (eq. 15 of the report scales it as 1/P) and the Knudsen numbers of small particles. It would also lower gas density, and so the Reynolds number at a given ventilation speed. All of these feed the nucleation, coagulation and drift terms, so the size-distribution results cannot be transferred quantitatively without new runs.

earth_benefits.text: The PSI record cites better smoke-detection devices and prevention of fires causing loss of material and life. More generally, the same sectional CFD-aerosol approach applies to particle formation in industrial aerosol reactors and building fires.

limitations.text: The simulation is two-dimensional, laminar and short (7 s). The aerosol has not reached true steady state in the recirculating wake. Particles are spherical and in velocity and thermal equilibrium with the gas, Stokes settling is applied even to very large particles, and particle diffusivity is floored at node 5 for numerical reasons.

source.quote: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)

PSI-117.one_line: Detailed computer models of single burning fuel droplets, checked against droplet fires on the Space Station, explain when a droplet flame drops into a dim, low-temperature 'cool flame', how long it survives, and why the gas xenon is a poor fire suppressant.
PSI-117.summary: This NASA ground study (grant NNX17AF97A, 2017-2022) modelled isolated fuel droplets burning in microgravity and compared the predictions with Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) data from the ISS. A transient, spherically symmetric one-dimensional code with detailed low-temperature chemistry, spectral radiation and fibre heat loss was used. For n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane droplets of about 4 mm in air, a hot flame radiatively extinguishes once the flame temperature falls to about 1200 K, and the droplet continues to burn as a cool flame at 720-775 K. Longer alkanes give hotter cool flames and smaller cool-flame extinction diameters (model about 0.95, 0.43 and 0.25 mm at 1 atm). For n-dodecane, the cool-flame extinction diameter falls from about 1.9 mm at 0.5 atm to zero at 3 atm, where a 'warm' flame burns the droplet out. Methanol simulations validated on FLEX-563 gave a limiting oxygen index of about 5% with xenon, against 8-21% for other diluents. The planned three-dimensional study of convective perturbations is not in the deposited files.

question.text: The record states the aim as using FLEX flight data to quantify how imposed thermal and convective perturbations (deliberate heating, drift-induced convection) control established droplet cool flames. These are ignition, oscillation, transition to hot or warm flames, and extinction. It also aimed to explain run-to-run variability and to map stability windows for small and large droplets. The deposited documents address a narrower set of questions with spherically symmetric (unperturbed) models. Why do large n-alkane droplets in microgravity drop from a hot flame to a long-lived cool flame, and what sets cool-flame extinction? How do fuel chain length, pressure and diluent (He, CO2, Xe) change this? Can a cool flame be started directly on sub-millimetre droplets (with ozone seeding) for ground tests? Is xenon a good fire suppressant in microgravity?

physics.text: A fuel droplet in microgravity burns with a spherical diffusion flame surrounding it. Fuel vapour diffuses out, oxygen diffuses in, and heat conducted back to the surface sustains evaporation. The squared diameter falls roughly linearly in time (the d^2 law), at a burning rate K of order 0.3-0.5 mm2/s. Large droplets (do > ~3 mm) build large, strongly radiating flames. As radiation (from CO2 and H2O) and diffusive losses grow relative to heat release, the hot flame cools. Near about 1200 K the hot flame goes out ('radiative extinction'), but the droplet keeps evaporating. Alkane fuels then show 'cool flame' chemistry. This is low-temperature oxidation (about 600-800 K) through alkylperoxy (RO2), hydroperoxyalkyl (QOOH) and ketohydroperoxide intermediates, with degenerate chain branching. Over the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) range, reactivity falls as temperature rises, which allows a stable, nearly invisible flame much closer to the droplet. Such cool flames were first seen in ISS FLEX experiments in 2011, because on Earth buoyant convection shortens residence times and the flame does not survive. They matter for fire safety because a droplet can keep vaporising and partly reacting after visible flame-out. This releases unburnt fuel, aldehydes, CO and hydroperoxides, and the cool flame may later re-ignite as a hot flame. Pressure, diluent thermal diffusivity (He high, Xe very low) and chain length shift the balance between heat release and loss, and so whether hot, 'warm' (NTC, about 950 K) or cool burning persists.

sources.quote: Radiative heat loss pushes the system to transition to the second stage, cool flame burn. • A dynamic balance between heat generation and heat loss maintains the long-duration cool flame burn.

apparatus.text: Numerical models, no hardware. The main tool is the Princeton/USC transient, spherically symmetric, one-dimensional isolated-droplet combustion code. It solves gas- and liquid-phase mass, species and energy conservation, with the far field at 200 droplet radii. Its sub-models are multicomponent molecular diffusion (TRANLIB), detailed chemical kinetics and a fitted statistical narrow-band correlated-k (SNB-CK) radiation model for CO, CO2 and H2O. It also includes surface regression on an adaptive grid, evaporation and product condensation/dissolution (UNIFAC activity coefficients), a one-dimensional energy model of the tether fibre, and an optional sectional soot model. Integration is node-centred finite volume, second order on a staggered grid, with variable-order (up to fifth) backward differentiation in time. Kinetic models used were: Sarathy et al. C7-C20 (583 species, 2609 reactions) for extinction studies; Sun et al. (128/565) and Mehl et al. (652/2827) for n-heptane, with an 11-species, 26-reaction ozone subset (Reuter et al.); and Li et al. methanol (21/93). A two-dimensional axisymmetric counterflow model with and without buoyancy (DME cool diffusion flames) appears only in the 2026 seminar. The PSI record describes a three-dimensional OpenFOAM model with imposed convection and heating. No such model or result appears in any deposited file. Flight data used: FLEX (ISS Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus) droplet diameter, flame diameter and radiometer histories for n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane, plus methanol test FLEX-563 for xenon.

procedure.text: For each case the code is started from a cold droplet in a quiescent, uniform ambient (298 K at the far field). A thermal ignition source is deposited symmetrically around the droplet, and its energy is varied parametrically. For FLEX-563 the ignition-to-combustion energy ratio was 0.01, 0.07 or 0.25, and quasi-steady burning needed more than about 0.4 J. The run continues until extinction or burn-out. Outputs are compared with FLEX histories of droplet diameter (d/d0)^2, flame diameter, flame stand-off ratio and radiant power. The comparisons use the experimental records as published, with no extra processing by the investigators, and model inputs were not tuned to fit. Extracted observables are the average burning rate per stage, hot- and cool-flame extinction diameters, peak gas temperature, FSR and radiative and diffusive losses. Kinetic sensitivity coefficients are computed for burning rate and extinction diameter. The ozone studies seed O3 into the ambient and lower O2 below the limiting oxygen index, to test direct cool-flame initiation and oscillation in sub-millimetre droplets.

psi_data.summary: PSI-117 holds 16 files (70.8 MB), all downloaded. There are 4 conference/seminar presentations (62.5 MB, text extracted), the 2018 PhD dissertation of M. F. E. Alam (USC, 227 pp.; used as the report), a metadata zip, and 10 analysed-data files. The analysed data are figure data behind five papers. A ReadMe workbook maps each file to fuel, do, pressure, composition, DOI and figure number. All are small comma-separated tables with several side-by-side column blocks separated by empty columns, rather than tidy tables. Units are in the headers (time s, diameters mm, K mm2/s, T K, radiance W, P atm). (1) PROCI_2019_Stable_Cool (243 rows) and PROCI_2019_Oscillatory_Cool_Flame (640 rows) are model time series for a 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet with 5% O3 at 21% and 10% O2. Columns: Time, Diameter, K, T_max, D_Tmax/D_drop, D_OHm/D_drop, (D/Do)^2. (2) PROCI_C12_2019_Three_Stage (570 rows) holds FLEX n-dodecane data at 2.75 atm with He. Experimental columns: (D/Do)^2, Dflame/Do and Dflame against t/do^2 (s/mm2), two radiometer traces (W), and cool-flame diameter (HWFM and peak-to-peak). Model columns follow. (3) PROCI_2023_Alkane_Extinction_Diameter_1atm gives experimental and simulated Do, Dext_HF and Dext_CF (mm) for C7, C10 and C12 in air. (4) PROCI_2023_C12_Extinction_Diameter_vs_pressure gives Dext_HF and Dext_CF (experiment, model, error bars) at 0.5-3 atm. (5) MST_2024_Kavg (19 experimental, 6 model points) holds the cool-flame average burning rate against pressure (0.5-5 atm). MST_2024_Dext holds cool and hot extinction diameters against pressure. MST_2024_Burning_history and Radiance_Flame_Diameter (683 rows each) hold n-dodecane d^2, flame diameter, radiance and T_max histories at 0.5, 1 and 5 atm, experiment and model. Experimental points are not tied to FLEX test numbers, and the data look digitised from figures. No model input decks, source code or 3-D results are deposited.

findings.claim: In 1 atm air with do of about 4 mm, n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane all show two-stage burning: a hot flame, radiative extinction, then quasi-steady cool-flame burning. The hot-to-cool transition happens at a nearly universal peak flame temperature of about 1200 K, and at transition the FSR and Tmax of the three fuels are almost identical.

sources.quote: Two-stage hot-cool flame burning mode transitions are demonstrated to exist for the three fuels, and the maximum flame temperature at which transition to the second stage occurred was universally found to be ~ 1200K.
During transition to second stage burn, the FSR and the Tmax for all three fuels are almost identical.

findings.claim: Longer alkanes give more robust cool flames. Predicted cool-flame peak temperature is about 775 K for n-dodecane, 737 K for n-decane and 720 K for n-heptane, and the cool-flame burning rate rises in the same order. The cool-flame extinction diameter falls with chain length. At do = 4 mm in 1 atm air the model gives 0.95 mm (C7), 0.43 mm (C10) and about 0.25 mm (C12). FLEX measurements give 1.10-1.30 mm for C7 (do 3.3-3.9 mm), 0.66-1.32 mm for C10 and 0-0.50 mm for C12 (do 4.0-4.4 mm).

sources.quote: Tmax,CF C12 ~ 775 K > Tmax,CF C10 ~ 737 K > Tmax,CF C7 ~ 720 K • de,CF C7 > de,CF C10 > de,CF C12

findings.claim: Hot-flame extinction is governed by small-species chemistry, so all three alkanes have nearly the same hot-flame extinction diameter for a given do (model: about 3.4-3.8 mm at do of about 4 mm, rising almost one-to-one with do). The cool-flame extinction diameter also varies linearly with do, but the lines do not collapse across fuels, because low-temperature chemistry depends on carbon number.

sources.quote: High temperature combustion is strongly governed by the small species kinetics – all three fuels share nearly identical values of HF extinction diameter for the same do
Universally, de,CF for each fuel varies linearly with initial droplet diameter, but unlike de,HF these relationships do not collapse to a single function.

findings.claim: For n-dodecane (do = 4 mm, 21% O2 in N2), pressure changes the burning mode. At 1 atm or below, burning is two-stage (hot then cool), at 1.25 atm hot-cool cycling repeats, and at 3 atm a stable 'warm' (NTC) flame burns the droplet to completion. The measured cool-flame extinction diameter falls from 1.89 mm at 0.5 atm (50.7 kPa) to 0.49 mm at 0.75 atm and 0.39-0.48 mm at 1 atm, and is zero at 3 atm. The model gives 1.19, 0.41, 0.25 and 0.03 mm. The hot-flame extinction diameter stays near 3.5-3.6 mm (experiment) and 3.4-3.9 mm (model).

sources.quote: • For pressure ≤ 1.0 atm, two stage combustion – hot and cool flame extinction. • At 1.25 atm, multi-cycling of hot-cool-hot-cool flame transition. • At 3.0 atm, the system transitions to a stable “Warm” flame.

findings.claim: The n-dodecane cool-flame average burning rate rises with pressure. FLEX values are 0.315-0.333 mm2/s at 0.5 atm, 0.365-0.408 at 1 atm, 0.445-0.493 at 3 atm and 0.502-0.527 mm2/s at 5 atm. The model reproduces the trend (0.374 at 0.5 atm to 0.501 mm2/s at 5 atm) but over-predicts at 0.5 atm.

At 1.25 atm, a large (do = 7 mm) n-dodecane droplet in air is predicted to undergo four successive hot-cool flame transitions. At each transition the cool-flame temperature drops markedly and the burn time lengthens, while the hot-flame behaviour is unchanged.

sources.quote: Four “Hot-Cool” flame transition. • At every transition, the cool flame temperature decreases significantly, the burn time increases. • The hot flame behavior remains unaltered.

findings.claim: Replacing N2 with helium at 3 atm (n-heptane, do = 4 mm, 21% O2) raises the burning rate. At high He fractions (about 40%) it produces a third stage: a hot flame, then a 'warm' flame at about 950 K, then a cool flame at about 770 K. Diffusive losses dominate in the third stage. Despite the temperature drop, the flame contracts, so droplet regression barely changes. This a priori prediction was qualitatively confirmed by FLEX test 1268 (n-dodecane, 2.75 atm, 21.6% O2, 50.2% N2, 28.2% He).

sources.quote: Introduction of helium increases the burning rate, at higher helium concentration a third stage quasi-steady burn is observed 1st Stage High Temperature burn 2nd Stage Moderate Temperature burn Tflame ~ 950 K 3rd Stage Low Temperature burn Tflame ~ 770 K
The diffusive losses become prominent in the third stage “Cool flame” burn.
Experimental observation with n-dodecane at higher pressure and helium exchange validates the “a priori” numerical predictions of a three stage behaviour inferred from n-heptane simulations.

findings.claim: Xenon is a poor microgravity fire suppressant. In methanol-droplet simulations validated against FLEX-563 (do = 2.771 mm, 8% O2, 63% Xe, 1 atm), xenon gives a longer burn and a higher peak gas temperature than other diluents. Its limiting oxygen index is also far lower: about 5% for Xe, against 8% for Ar and 21% for He and CO2 (do = 1.5 mm). For Xe the LOI is about 4%, 5% and 6% for do = 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm. The cause is xenon's very low thermal diffusivity. The dissertation states that NASA postponed xenon testing as a result.

Oscillation starts when local O2 near the flame falls below a critical value (about 13.5% in the presentation, 12% in the dissertation). It grows because unburnt fuel leaks through the flame: about 34-46% of the fuel vapour in the flame volume appears unreacted at 1.5 x FSR. O3 at 6% or more switches the system to hot-flame burning.

findings.claim: Kinetic sensitivity analysis shows that cool-flame burning rate and extinction diameter are controlled by the competition between O2 addition to QOOH and QOOH-O2 decomposition. Speeding up the reverse reaction O2QOOH -> QOOH + O2 lowers the burning rate and raises the extinction diameter, while O2QOOH -> ketohydroperoxide + OH does the opposite. A revised kinetic model was proposed on this basis.

sources.quote: In general increase in QOOHO2 → QOOH + O2 rate decreased the burning rate and increased the extinction diameter. Vice versa QOOHO2→ Ketohydroperoxide + OH (Q = CnH2n)
The de,CF is most sensitive to: •O2QnOOH → •OQn`OOH + OH •O2QnOOH → QnOOH + O2

findings.claim: In 2-D counterflow simulations of a DME cool diffusion flame at low strain (about 90 /s, 1 atm), buoyancy lifts the flame upward. Without buoyancy, both 1-D and 2-D models place the flame at the stagnation plane, but 1-D gives steeper temperature gradients (more diffusive loss) and a slightly lower peak temperature. The conventional 1-D (OPPDIF) approach is therefore questionable for low-strain cool flames in 1 g.

sources.quote: Without buoyancy, 1D and 2D models predict the flame at or near the stagnation plane due to momentum- balanced BC.
The peak flame temperature in 1D is slightly lower compared to the 2D prediction, but the peak HRR shows the opposite trend.
for DME diffusion cool flame with and without buoyancy for identical conditions (XDME= 0.587, UF = 62.3 cm/s, UO = 50.9 cm/s, a ~ 90 s-1, P = 1 atm)

findings.claim: Beyond single-component fuels, the group simulated isolated droplets of three Jet-A surrogate mixtures with the same global (fully pre-vaporised) combustion behaviour but very different distillation curves (n-decane/iso-octane/toluene; n-dodecane/iso-octane/1,3,5-trimethylbenzene; n-hexadecane/iso-octane/1,3,5-trimethylbenzene), with UNIFAC liquid-phase activity coefficients. For the first mixture, predictions agree with published drop-tower data for 550 um droplets in air once near-full internal mixing and sooting are included. Preferential vaporization depends strongly and non-linearly on initial droplet diameter and pressure: at low pressure and combustor-sized drops it is close to the frozen limit, while at practical pressures batch distillation dominates and chemical-property differences matter as much as physical ones. This is a ground (drop-tower) validation, not FLEX data.

sources.quote: The predictions using Mixture-1 are found to be in good agreement with previously published drop-tower experiments for 550 µm droplet combustion in air.
By comparing predictions for the three mixtures, preferential vaporization effects exhibit strong non-linear dependences on initial droplet diameter and ambient pressure.

However, at pressures typical of those found in applications, batch distillation dominates and preferential vaporization chemical property differences are found to become as significant as physical property effects in influencing combustion behaviors.

relevance.text: Suppression: the clearest operational result is that xenon, once considered as an agent, would support flames at very low O2 (LOI about 5% vs 21% for CO2 or He) and burn hotter and longer. It should not be used as a microgravity extinguishant. This was a model result, validated on one FLEX test. It also shows that diluent thermal diffusivity, not only heat capacity, governs inerting in the absence of buoyancy. Fundamental: in microgravity a liquid-fuel fire that appears extinguished, after radiative extinction of the visible flame, can keep burning as an invisible cool flame. It consumes fuel, releases partially oxidised species, and at elevated pressure or with He can re-ignite into hot burning (multi-cycle behaviour). Detection and post-extinguishment procedures should not assume that loss of visible flame means the end of reaction. Transferability: all results are for single, isolated, quiescent, spherically symmetric droplets of pure fuels. Ventilation flows, drift and multi-droplet or spray effects, the stated aim of this grant, are not covered by the deposited material.

habitat_conditions.text: Most n-alkane comparisons are in air (21% O2) at 0.5-5 atm (50.7-506.6 kPa), with selected He, CO2 or Xe dilution. The sub-atmospheric n-dodecane cases (0.5 and 0.75 atm = 50.7 and 76.0 kPa) bracket the pressure of a lunar habitat (O2 of 30% or more at 70.3 kPa or less). However, they used only 21% O2, so they are not at the higher O2 fraction expected there. The trend that cool-flame extinction diameter grows strongly as pressure falls (1.89 mm at 0.5 atm vs about 0.4 mm at 1 atm for n-dodecane) suggests low-pressure habitats shorten cool-flame burning. The effect of the higher O2 fraction is untested. No case approaches the spacesuit atmosphere (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa). The Earth reference is 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa.

earth_benefits.text: Better understanding and validated models of low-temperature (cool-flame) and NTC chemistry, relevant to engine knock, multi-stage autoignition, HCCI engines, efficiency and emissions. The dissertation also refined butanol transport parameters in a widely used kinetic model.

PSI-142.one_line: A ground study at Princeton, prompted by the surprising cool flames seen around burning droplets on the Space Station, used ozone-assisted counterflow burners and simulations to map when hot flames turn into low-temperature 'cool' and 'warm' flames and when those go out.
PSI-142.summary: This PSI-funded ground investigation (2016-2021) set out to explain the cool flames observed after radiative extinction of n-alkane droplets in the ISS Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX). Princeton researchers measured extinction limits of hot and cool non-premixed flames of n-heptane to n-tetradecane in an atmospheric counterflow burner, with and without ozone added to the oxidiser to boost low-temperature chemistry, probed multistage 'warm' flames with formaldehyde fluorescence, chemiluminescence and thermometry, and computed flame regimes for dimethyl ether up to elevated pressure. Without ozone, n-tetradecane cool flames survived at a fuel mass fraction near 0.32 at a stretch rate of about 83 1/s, versus about 0.55 for n-heptane at 78 1/s; ozone brought both to about 0.11 near 69 1/s. Hot-flame extinction occurred at fuel mass fractions of 0.04-0.055 for all fuels. Kinetic models overpredicted cool-flame extinction limits, and cool-flame reactivity scaled with oxygen mole fraction to a power of 1.5-2. Warm flames bridge cool and hot flames. For fire safety the work is fundamental: low-temperature flames can persist after visible flames go out.

question.text: Under what conditions does a hot diffusion flame turn into a cool flame (a self-sustaining flame at roughly 600-800 K driven by low-temperature peroxy chemistry), and how does the cool-flame flammable region relate to hot-flame flammability and extinction limits? FLEX on the ISS had shown n-alkane droplet flames that continued to burn as cool flames after the visible hot flame radiatively extinguished. The investigation hypothesised that oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convective transport control the transition, and aimed to (1) build a flammability diagram of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion and convection, (2) bridge hot- and cool-flame flammability and extinction limits, (3) verify phenomena seen in FLEX, (4) provide quantitative extinction, temperature and species data for kinetic and radiation model validation, and (5) extend the droplet results to a one-dimensional ground system (the counterflow flame).

sources.quote: Discipline Area:Combustion Science (FLEX flame extinction experiments)

physics.text: Hydrocarbons such as n-alkanes have two oxidation routes. Above roughly 1000 K, hot-flame chemistry is driven by H + O2 chain branching. Between roughly 600 and 800 K, low-temperature chemistry adds O2 to fuel radicals (peroxy chemistry), producing ketohydroperoxides that branch into radicals; this chemistry weakens as temperature rises (the negative temperature coefficient region) and so can sustain only a weak, low-temperature 'cool flame'. In the counterflow geometry, fuel and oxidiser jets meet at a stagnation plane and the flame residence time is set by the strain (stretch) rate a: high a extinguishes a flame by shortening residence time, while very low a (long residence time, as in microgravity droplets) lets radiative loss grow until the flame extinguishes radiatively. Large, slowly burning microgravity droplet flames reach this radiative limit, which is how FLEX produced cool flames. Adding ozone to the oxidiser supplies O atoms at low temperature, initiating low-temperature chemistry so that cool flames can be stabilised in a 1 g laboratory burner. Between cool and hot flames there is a 'warm' flame with two spatially separate reaction zones: a cool-flame stage on the fuel side and an intermediate-temperature stage on the oxidiser side.

sources.note: Two-stage hydrocarbon oxidation, negative temperature coefficient and strain/radiative extinction of counterflow flames are textbook combustion background.

sources.quote: It is found that there are three different flame regimes—hot flame, warm flame, and cool flame—which exist, respectively, at high, intermediate, and low temperatures. Furthermore, they are governed by three distinct chain-branching reaction pathways.
It was found that the warm diffusion flame has a two-staged double flame structure, with a leading diffusion cool flame stage on the fuel side and a second intermediate stage on the oxidizer side

equations.meaning: Global strain (stretch) rate of a counterflow flame (Seshadri-Williams form): V_O, V_F are oxidiser and fuel nozzle exit velocities (m/s), rho_O, rho_F their densities (kg/m^3), L the nozzle separation (m); a in 1/s. Its inverse is the flow residence time. Valid for plug-flow nozzles with the flame away from the nozzles; the investigators' exact strain-rate definition was not confirmed from the deposited files.

sources.note: Standard counterflow global strain-rate expression.

equations.meaning: Damkohler number: ratio of flow residence time (about 1/a, s) to chemical time tau_chem (s). Stretch extinction occurs at high a when Da falls below a critical value. Cool flames, with slow peroxy chemistry (long tau_chem), extinguish at much lower a or need more fuel than hot flames, which is why the cool-flame limits in data IDs 1-2 sit at larger Yf than the hot-flame limits in data ID 3. At very low a, radiative loss rather than Da sets the (radiative) extinction limit.

sources.note: Damkohler-number interpretation of flame extinction is textbook background.

equations.meaning: Empirical scaling reported by the investigators: cool-flame low-temperature reactivity of n-alkanes (n-heptane to n-dodecane) is proportional to oxygen mole fraction X_O2 to the power n = 1.5-2, inferred from non-premixed cool-flame extinction limits at atmospheric pressure in a counterflow burner. omega_LTC is a generic low-temperature reaction rate (symbol introduced here).

sources.quote: the cool flame low temperature reactivity of n-alkanes is proportional to nth power of oxygen mole fraction, [O 2 ] n , with n = 1.5–2.

apparatus.text: An atmospheric-pressure counterflow burner at Princeton (fuel vaporised and diluted on one side, oxidiser on the other), with ozone generated and added to the oxidiser stream; the PI's earlier counterflow cool-flame burner paper (Combust. Flame 166, 2016) is given as the hardware reference. Diagnostics included thermocouple thermometry, CH2O planar laser-induced fluorescence and chemiluminescence imaging. A micro-jet was used to impinge vortices on premixed double flames. Numerical work used 1-D counterflow and freely propagating flame codes (with arc-length continuation to trace extinction turning points) with detailed and reduced kinetic models, and 2-D transient simulations for the vortex study.

sources.quote: Multistage diffusion flames of n-heptane, n-decane, and n-dodecane are established in an atmospheric counterflow burner. Planar laser-induced fluorescence, chemiluminescence, and thermometry are used to probe the structures of such flames.
The transient interactions between double flames and impinging vortices are then investigated experimentally using a micro-jet and numerically in two-dimensional transient modeling.

procedure.text: For extinction limits, a flame (hot, or cool with ozone assistance) was established at a given fuel mass fraction Yf and the strain rate a was raised (or fuel reduced) until extinction; the extinction strain rates of cool flames (aCFE) and hot flames (aHFE) were recorded versus Yf for each n-alkane, with and without ozone, and compared with simulations using detailed and reduced kinetic models. Warm/multistage flames were mapped with CH2O PLIF, chemiluminescence and thermocouple profiles across the burner gap, at several fuel mole fractions and fuel inlet temperatures (550-650 K), with and without ozone. Computations explored (a) spark-assisted propagation of n-heptane/air, (b) 1-D freely propagating DME flames by arc-length continuation and (c) DME/air cool-flame regimes and burning limits up to 20 atm, under FLEX-like oxygen conditions. PSI's deposited data are the digitised figure data from eight published figures.

findings.claim: Kinetic models (detailed and reduced) predict hot-flame extinction adequately but scatter widely for cool flames and generally overpredict the measured cool-flame extinction limit for all n-alkanes; cool-flame heat release is spread over many reactions of large molecules, making reduced models hard to build. The same overprediction was found for DME/methane cool flames until the DME + OH H-abstraction rate, among others, was updated.

sources.quote: Although the different kinetic models adequately predict the extinction limits of the hot flames, a large scatter is present in the model results for cool flames, and a general overprediction of the measured cool flame extinction limit is observed for all of the fuels studied.
The measurements indicate that the original kinetic model significantly overpredicts the cool flame extinction limits.

findings.claim: Cool-flame reactivity of n-alkanes (n-heptane to n-dodecane) scales with oxygen mole fraction as [O2]^n with n = 1.5-2, a nonlinear dependence common to all fuels tested, attributed to multiple O2-addition steps and the negative temperature coefficient; a 'radical index' derived from the extinction data increases with carbon chain length.

sources.quote: the cool flame low temperature reactivity of n-alkanes is proportional to nth power of oxygen mole fraction, [O 2 ] n , with n = 1.5–2.

findings.claim: A self-sustaining multistage 'warm' diffusion flame exists between cool and hot flames at atmospheric pressure: a cool-flame stage on the fuel side and an intermediate-temperature stage on the oxidiser side with comparable heat release. Ozone strengthens the second stage without changing the structure; in the deposited thermometry, peak temperature rose from 657 K without ozone to 788 K with 4.5 mol% ozone. Hot flames can extinguish directly into warm or cool flames, so the warm flame is a bridge between regimes.

sources.quote: Finally, under certain conditions, a hot flame can extinguish directly into either a warm flame or a cool flame. Hence, the results suggest that the multistage warm flame can act as a critical bridge between cool flames and hot flames

findings.claim: Computed DME counterflow diffusion flames at elevated pressure and temperature, with and without radiation, give a general 'epsilon-shaped' (€) flammability diagram of hot, warm and cool flames versus oxygen mole fraction. A cool flame can form by radiative or stretch extinction of a hot flame, or stretch extinction of a warm flame. Raising oxidiser temperature, oxygen fraction or pressure shifts the cool-flame regime to higher stretch rates, and unlike hot flames cool flames cannot be scaled by pressure-weighted stretch rate.

sources.quote: It is also shown that the cool flame can be formed in several different ways: by either radiative extinction or stretch extinction of a hot flame or by stretch extinction of a warm flame.
Increases in oxidizer temperature, oxygen concentration, and pressure shift the cool flame regime to higher stretch rates and cause the warm flame to have two extinction limits.

findings.claim: Premixed DME/O2/O3 'double flames' (coupled cool and hot flame) occur near the hot-flame extinction limit. Measured hot-flame extinction equivalence ratio rose from 0.0876 to 0.1089 as strain rate rose from 59 to 107 1/s, and cool-flame extinction from 0.0664 (59 1/s) to 0.1149 (95 1/s). An impinging vortex can locally extinguish the near-limit hot flame, leaving a lone cool flame; extinguished holes, cool flames and double flames can coexist.

relevance.text: The work is fundamental combustion chemistry rather than spacecraft material testing. Its fire-safety relevance is that low-temperature (cool and warm) flames, which emit little visible light and run at roughly 600-800 K, can persist after a hot flame extinguishes radiatively, as FLEX showed for droplets in microgravity where long residence times favour them; the investigators note warm flames are particularly relevant to microgravity for this reason. A fire that appears extinguished may therefore still be oxidising fuel and producing partially oxidised species (e.g. formaldehyde). Transferability is limited: the fuels are n-alkanes, DME and dibutyl ether, not cabin materials; the laboratory flames are stabilised by ozone, which is absent in cabins; and most measurements are at 1 atm in 1 g counterflow geometry.

sources.quote: The multistage warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times.
the recent experimental and computational findings of cool flames in microchannels, microgravity droplet combustion, counterflow flames, and turbulent combustion environments are reviewed.

habitat_conditions.text: Experiments were at atmospheric pressure (comparable to the Earth sea-level reference, 101.3 kPa). Computations reached 20 atm and showed that higher oxygen fraction and pressure enlarge cool- and warm-flame regions, which qualitatively suggests enriched-oxygen atmospheres would not suppress cool flames; however, no tests were made at reduced-pressure, enriched-oxygen habitat conditions such as the 30%-or-more O2 at 70.3 kPa planned for the Moon, so no quantitative comparison is possible. The oxygen mole fractions of the extinction tests were not recorded in the deposited data.

earth_benefits.text: Cool and warm flames govern ignition timing, knock and emissions in advanced engines, many of which operate at 20-40 atm; the ozone-assisted counterflow cool flame is proposed as a platform for validating low-temperature chemical kinetic models of fuels.

PSI-159.one_line: Ground-commanded tests on the ISS burned ethane, propane and butane on a pea-sized porous sphere, both normally (fuel out of the sphere into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere) and inside-out (an oxygen-rich stream of up to 85% O2 out of the sphere into a fuel-filled chamber), and found the first spherical 'cool flames' of gaseous fuel.
PSI-159.summary: CFI-G, part of NASA's ACME project, burned spherical diffusion flames on a 6.35 mm porous burner in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack from March to October 2021. It ran 333 tests on 23 days. In normal flames, nitrogen-diluted ethane, propane or n-butane flowed into atmospheres of 18-40% O2 at 0.5-3 atm. In inverse flames, an O2/N2 stream of 12-85% O2 flowed from the burner into a chamber filled with fuel and nitrogen; the chamber held no oxygen. Of 280 hot flames, 189 extinguished radiatively. Fifteen were followed, after about 1 s, by a quasi-steady cool diffusion flame, the first observed for gaseous fuels. These occurred only for 30% n-butane flowing at 0.75-1.5 mg/s into 39-40% O2 at 2 bar, with burner temperatures above 515 K. The hot flames were 2.6 times larger than the cool flames that followed. All normal flames in about 21% O2 self-extinguished within 20 s. Inverse flames from 85% O2 self-extinguished in 41 of 43 tests at 2-3 bar but in 0 of 14 at about 0.5 bar. These are burner flames, not material flammability limits.

question.text: Cool diffusion flames, with peak temperatures of about 500-1000 K and governed by low-temperature (negative-temperature-coefficient) chemistry, were discovered in 2012 in ISS droplet experiments (FLEX, CFI). Droplets burn unsteadily and allow neither gaseous fuels, fuel dilution nor inverse flames. CFI-G set out to show, for the first time: steady cool diffusion flames on a spherical porous burner; cool flames of propane, n-butane and (as proposed) n-pentane over a wide range of stoichiometric mixture fraction $Z_{st}$, adiabatic flame temperature $T_{ad}$ and pressure; inverse cool flames; and cool flames that extinguish when the burner flow decreases and turn into hot flames when it increases. The data were meant to test and improve cool-flame kinetic mechanisms with CFD, and so to support more efficient engines. Because n-pentane's vapour pressure is too low for the CIR gas system, ethane replaced it.

sources.quote: it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate.
Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames.

physics.text: A diffusion flame sits where fuel and oxidiser meet in stoichiometric proportion. Around a porous sphere in microgravity, the flow is purely radial and weakens as $1/r^2$. A few burner diameters out, transport is by diffusion alone, so the flame is spherical and one-dimensional. On Earth, buoyancy breaks the symmetry. The investigators estimate a Richardson number of about 1300 in 1 g for this configuration. Reducing it well below 1 needs a gravity level about $10^{-4}$ g. The diffusion time $r^2/D$ at a 25 mm radius is about 30 s. Drop towers therefore cannot reach quasi-steady flames, still less observe their radiative extinction and any cool flame that follows. In a normal flame the fuel issues from the sphere and soot forms on the inside of the flame. In an inverse flame the oxidiser issues from the sphere, so the flame is inside out and soot forms on the outside. Microgravity flames grow slowly. They lose heat by radiation from soot and gas, and to the burner and its support tube. Many therefore extinguish radiatively after tens of seconds. Hydrocarbons such as n-butane have a negative-temperature-coefficient region in which low-temperature oxidation, producing formaldehyde, CO, H2O2 and H2O, can sustain a weak 'cool' flame at a few hundred kelvin above ambient. Such a flame can appear after the hot flame dies, provided the fuel stream and the burner surface are warm enough and the residence time is long. For fire safety, cool flames are a reminder that a mixture can keep reacting and can re-ignite after visible extinction.

The cool flame sits where $dT/dZ$ changes sign, so both the burner and the ambient must be cooler than the cool flame. As $T_s \to T_{cf}$ the cool flame collapses onto the burner. apparatus.text: Tests ran in the ACME chamber insert of the CIR, a windowed constant-volume chamber of about 83 L free volume. Burner flow raised the pressure and depleted the reactant during each day. The burner was a 6.35 mm sphere of sintered 316 stainless steel (10 micron media, about 41% porosity), sinter-bonded to a stainless supply tube. A fine type-K thermocouple was embedded up to about 1 mm into the sphere to measure burner temperature. Tests were terminated if the burner reached 723 K. Three crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers metered fuel, oxidiser and ISS nitrogen. Only one gas stream could be diluted with nitrogen on orbit at a time. CFI-G used a coiled Kanthal A-1 hot-wire igniter (0.32 mm wire) on a retracting arm. Cool flames were imaged by the intensified CFI camera, which had a formaldehyde (CH2O*) bandpass filter (390-490 nm) and ran at about 23 frames/s. Hot flames were also imaged by the ACME colour DataCam (12-bit, up to 30 fps, often about 1 fps with long exposures). The analog video was recorded on the ground. Other instruments: a CFI-G radiometer array with two fixed gains per sensor; a Schmidt-Boelter wide-angle radiometer at 154 mm radius (0.6-50 µm); three wide-angle PMTs (230-700 nm, 310 nm OH*, 430 nm CH*); thermocouple rakes; two thermocouples at 200 mm; and a chamber pressure transducer. On the far rake, thermocouple tips were at 45, 60, 100 and 100 mm from the burner centre. On the near rake they were at 13, 25, 50 and 100 mm. On each rake, the two innermost were type B (Pt/Rh) and the rest type K. The thin-filament pyrometry array had only 3 of its 5 SiC fibres (14 µm) left. Non-imaging data were logged at 125 Hz. The HiBMs camera with CIR backlight was rarely used: its IPSU failed on day 1 and was replaced on 18 May 2021.

procedure.text: The crew configured the hardware: they swapped bottles and MFCs, exchanged igniter tips and changed thermocouple rakes. All tests were then run from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center using pre-programmed scripts and parameter files. No tests used manual control, apart from ending a test after extinction or on burner over-temperature. Round 1 (29 Mar - 23 Jun 2021, 10 days) used normal flames: the chamber was filled with an O2/N2 atmosphere of nominally 18%, 21% or 40% O2 at 0.5, 0.93, 1, 2 or 3 atm, and fuel flowed from the burner at 0.1-3.2 mg/s. Round 2 (15 Jul - 4 Oct 2021, 12 days) used inverse flames: the chamber was filled with fuel/N2 at 0.5-3 atm, and an O2/N2 mixture of 12-85% O2 flowed from the burner at about 0.9-9.1 mg/s O2. An added 13th round-2 day (18 Oct 2021) repeated the cool-flame normal-flame conditions of 23 Jun (30% n-butane into about 40% O2 at 2 atm) using the near thermocouple rake. In each test the scripted sequence recorded pre-ignition data and images, ignited the flame with the hot wire and retracted it, then held constant flow. The flow timeout was typically 90-360 s, and 66 s on many inverse tests. Post-flame data followed. The burner-flow conditions in a scripted run were constant; dilution, flow rate, O2 fraction and igniter energy were changed between tests. Some round-1 tests tried to ignite cool flames directly with low igniter power, using 2-2.9 V for 10-20 s instead of the standard 3 V preheat and 3.75-4 V ignition. A twin safety timer limited each day's total limiting-reactant flow to 999 s. About 12 tests were run per day. The chamber was not vented between tests, so O2 (or fuel) fell and pressure rose during the day. The investigators estimated chamber composition after each test from the flows, assuming complete or no combustion. Since the cool flames of 23 Jun were found only afterwards, in data review, flow was kept on after radiative extinction in later tests.

psi_data.summary: PSI-159 holds 3,756 files, about 2.09 TB. Nearly all of the volume is raw imagery that has not been downloaded here: 986 zip archives (about 2.0 TB) of intensified-camera TIFFs, DataCam HOBJ images, converted images and HiBMs images, plus 336 ground-recorded analog video files (.ts, 81.7 GB). The most usable data are already local: 338 per-test 125 Hz CSV files (1.46 GB) of raw channel voltages, with matching mfcSetpoints CSVs. Channels include MFC flows, PMTs, thermocouples (rakes, 200 mm, burner), dual-gain radiometers and pressure transducers. Calibrations are given in the ACME Software Interface Design Document, which is not in PSI. Also local are about 1,000 small text files per test: as-run script parameters, timestamped test-point timelines, image-downlink comments and camera configurations. There are 22 daily operation logs, 24 'flow traces' PDFs with per-test narrative and parameters, and the two experimental-table CSVs, which give one row per test with conditions and outcomes. The CSVs feed tests.csv. Daily 'test sheets', 'test parameter notes' and 'daily test point log' PDFs are scans with no text. The final report (2022) and the ACME Engineering Implementation report are the only analysis documents. Acceleration (SAMS) data are not archived in PSI.

findings.claim: Fifteen spherical cool diffusion flames of a gaseous fuel were observed, the first such observation. All followed radiative extinction of a hot flame, after a dark interval of 0.7-1.1 s. The cool flames of four tests in June 2021 (21174 C3, C4, C6, F1) were quasi-steady for about 14 s and disappeared when the fuel flow stopped; in one test the radiometer and burner temperature were steady enough to suggest the cool flame would have lasted indefinitely. The ten cool flames of tests 21291 A1 and C1 instead ended by re-igniting into hot flames.

sources.quote: Of those that extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames.
For test points 21174C3, C4, C6, and F1, the cool flames lasted for approximately 14 s and disappeared as soon as the fuel flow stopped.
A similar delay, 0.7 –1.1 s, occurred for all 15 cool flames.
During the cool flame, the radiometer output and burner temperature were steady enough to suggest this flame would have lasted indefinitely with continued flow and an infinite domain.

findings.claim: Cool flames formed in a narrow window only: normal (not inverse) flames, n-butane (not ethane or propane) at 30% in N2 in the burner stream, flowing at 0.75-1.5 mg/s into 0.385-0.399 ambient O2 at 2.03 bar (about 203 kPa). Burner temperature also had to be above 515 K. None were seen below about 0.4 O2, below 2 bar, or for any inverse flame, including those fed with 85% O2.

sources.quote: These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% n- butane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s.
these cool flames were only observed for burner temperatures above 515 K
Cool flames were not observed for oxygen mole fractions below about 0.4, which is consistent with a limiting oxygen index for cool flames

findings.claim: No inverse cool flames appeared in 154 inverse tests. The investigators attribute this mainly to short residence times. The paper also states that inverse flames had low burner temperatures (below 500 K), against more than 515 K needed in the normal cool-flame tests. The PSI inverse table disagrees: 44 of 151 inverse tests with a reading had a peak burner temperature above 500 K, up to about 925 K (21242 A1). Hypothesis 4 (inverse cool diffusion flames) was therefore not demonstrated.

sources.quote: Cool flames were not observed for inverse burn- ing, primarily because of short residence times.
The inverse flames also had low burner temperatures (below 500 K), but droplet cool diffusion flames are observed with surface temperatures near 400 K.

sources.note: config = inverse; peak_temp_c + 273.15 > 500 K in 44 of 151 non-null readings (154 inverse tests); maximum 924.65 K at 21242 A1.

findings.claim: Cool flames were smaller than the hot flames that preceded them. Measured hot-flame radii were 12.4-17.7 mm and cool-flame radii 5.1-7.6 mm, a mean ratio r_hf/r_cf of 2.6 against 3.2 predicted by the investigators' Spalding-type partial-burning model. Fitting the model to the radii gives a cool-flame mixture fraction of 0.53 (fuel-rich side of Z_st = 0.20), a burner-surface mixture fraction of 0.75 and an inferred cool-flame peak temperature of about 869 K. A SiC filament placed in one cool flame did not glow, so its peak temperature was below the 950 K detection limit of thin-filament pyrometry.

sources.quote: The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large.
They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.
The mean measured r hf / r cf is 2.6 and the mean predicted by Eq. (12) is 3.2.
Finally, the mean T cf is found from Eq. (10) to be 869 K.
No glow was detected in the filament, indicating the peak temperature was below the TFP detection limit of 950 K

findings.claim: With a platinum-containing type-B thermocouple about 1 cm (13 mm radius) from the burner (18 Oct 2021 repeat day), each cool flame re-ignited into a hot flame within seconds. The thermocouple sat in the rich premixture left after hot-flame extinction and catalysed it once it reached 720-820 K. Test 21291C1 cycled through 6 hot and 5 cool flames, and 21291A1 also gave 5 cool flames, until the flow stopped at about 165 s. A catalytic surface near a flame-extinguished fuel/oxidiser mixture can thus repeatedly re-ignite a hot flame.

sources.quote: It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition.
The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons.

findings.claim: Of 280 hot flames, 189 extinguished radiatively (self-extinguished) and the rest at flow termination. In the experimental tables, 183 of 272 tests with a recorded outcome self-extinguished: 102 of 133 normal (77%) and 81 of 139 inverse (58%). By fuel the fraction was similar: normal ethane 30/40, propane 34/40, n-butane 38/53; inverse ethane 27/49, propane 24/37, n-butane 30/53. Median hot-flame burn time was 29.5 s for self-extinguished normal flames and 8 s for self-extinguished inverse flames. For flow-terminated flames it was 61 s (normal) and 66 s (inverse, the usual flow timeout). The longest burns were 304 s (normal) and 152 s (inverse).

sources.quote: Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated.

findings.claim: Normal flames in nominally 21% O2 (x_o2 below 0.25, mostly 0.21-0.22 with a few at 0.18 and 0.23; any pressure 0.5-3 atm, any fuel) were weak. Only 41 of 64 tests ignited. All 41 with a recorded outcome self-extinguished, with a median burn time of 8 s and a maximum of 20 s. At about 40% O2, 88 of 112 tests ignited. Only 60 of 89 self-extinguished (67%), with a median burn time of 49 s; the others ran until flow timeout or burner over-temperature. Heavily diluted fuel streams (burner fuel mole fraction below 0.05) ignited in only 14 of 40 tests. Most of those 14 burned for about 1 s.

findings.claim: Inverse flames fed with 85% O2 (burner stream; chamber of fuel + N2) showed a strong pressure effect. At 2.2-3.3 bar (221-331 kPa), 41 of 43 self-extinguished, with a median burn time of 11 s. At 0.55 bar (55 kPa), 0 of 14 self-extinguished: all ran to flow termination (median 66 s), several hitting the burner temperature limit. Across all inverse O2 levels, the self-extinguished fraction was 0/26 at 0.55 bar, 19/39 at 1.1 bar, 31/35 at 2.2 bar and 28/33 at 3.3 bar. Self-extinction (radiative extinction) of these inside-out flames is thus much more likely at elevated pressure, consistent with stronger radiative loss. This is an inference from outcome counts, not a measured radiation balance.

sources.quote: These oscillations grew in strength until the flame self-extinguished.

findings.claim: Raising the burner-stream O2 fraction made inverse flames easier to ignite. With 85% O2, 76 of 79 tests ignited (plus one momentary flash), and all 22 at 50% O2 ignited. With 21% O2, only 16 of 27 ignited. Below 20% O2 (0.12-0.19), 6 of 12 ignited, 5 more gave only a momentary flash, and the 0.12 O2 test did not ignite.

findings.claim: The flames approached radiative extinction through growing oscillations and local quenching that opened holes in the flame shell. Soot clusters escaping the flame added to the heat loss. A hole lets fuel and oxidiser mix directly, which the investigators note enhances flammability. Inverse flame size was set by the O2 flow, the limiting reactant: larger O2 flow gave a larger flame, while extra N2 at fixed O2 flow did not change the size.

sources.quote: The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame.
This hole allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, thereby enhancing flammability.
The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully extinguishes.
The flame size is dependent on the limiting reactant, which for inverse flames is the oxygen.
Flame size is determined by access to sufficient fuel to consume the oxygen, which was at the same flow rate in both cases.

findings.claim: Normal flames, especially at elevated O2 and pressure, were bright and sooty at ignition. In microgravity the soot stayed in the flame longer and formed clusters, some escaping outward. The soot then faded as the flame cooled radiatively before extinction. Inverse flames formed their soot just outside the flame, in the hot fuel-rich chamber gas. Imaging at the end of each day showed no soot build-up on the chamber windows.

sources.quote: Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters.
Therefore, in this test, the soot forms just outside the flame.
However, the end-of-day imaging did not appear to change over time, suggesting that the soot was not an issue for the chamber windows.

findings.claim: Burners and their supports heated strongly. Peak burner temperatures reached 532 °C (805 K) in normal flames (21088 F1, ethane, about 38% O2) and 651.5 °C (925 K) in inverse flames (21242 A1, 85% O2 into about 43% propane at 0.55 bar). 30 of 284 tests with a reading exceeded 450 °C (723 K), the stated termination limit. Longer hot-flame burns heated the burners further, hot burners enabled cool flames, while the cold support tube locally quenched flames.

These attempts either failed to ignite or produced hot flames. All 15 confirmed cool flames followed hot-flame extinction.
