findings.claim: A Spalding-type droplet-burning model extended to burner flames and the partial-burning regime predicts both hot and cool flame radii with one fitted property: assuming peak temperatures of 1400 K (hot) and 750 K (cool), rhoD = 0.0334 g/m/s at 300 K gives R^2 = 0.92 against the measured radii of the cool flames and of quasi-steady normal n-butane hot flames (X_O2 0.37-0.40, 0.5-2 bar). This is about 35% above the 0.0248 g/m/s measured for O2/N2 at 298 K.

relevance.text: CFI-G is a fundamental combustion study, not a materials or fire-response test, and its numbers are not flammability limits for spacecraft materials. Three results bear on fire safety. (1) Detection: after a hot gaseous flame extinguished radiatively, a nearly invisible cool flame could persist for as long as fuel kept flowing. It was detected only by an intensified formaldehyde-filtered camera and radiometers, and not by the operations video. The team did not notice the first cool flames until days later. Visible-light or flame-flicker detection would miss such a reacting zone. (2) Re-ignition: a hot platinum surface (a type-B thermocouple) in the rich mixture left after extinction repeatedly re-ignited the hot flame. Catalytic or hot surfaces near a leak that has 'gone out' can therefore restore a fire. A hot burner surface (above 515 K) was likewise needed to sustain the cool flame. (3) Prevention: oxygen enrichment strongly increased ignition success and burn duration. Normal flames in 21% O2 all self-extinguished within 20 s, while at 40% O2 a third of the flames survived until the flow was cut. Pressure had the opposite effect for inverse flames: oxygen-rich jets into fuel-laden gas self-extinguished at 2-3 atm but not at 0.5 atm. These trends concern small (mg/s) laminar gas flames on a 6 mm burner in a closed, quiescent 83 L chamber. They transfer qualitatively at most.

sources.quote: Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during testing.
an unwanted outcome was hot-flame reignition (from the cool flames) caused by catalysis from the platinum in the exposed type-B thermocouple closest to the burner.
residual heat in the porous burner re-ignited the flowing fuel as a steady spherical cool diffusion flame

habitat_conditions.text: Be precise about where the oxygen was. The 85% O2, the highest oxygen concentration in PSI, was only the oxidiser stream issuing from the burner in inverse-flame tests. During those tests the chamber atmosphere was fuel (about 6-43%) in nitrogen, with no oxygen. ACME limited the chamber atmosphere to 40% O2. In normal-flame tests the ambient was 18-40% O2 at 0.5-3 atm (about 51-304 kPa), with about 40% O2 tested at 0.5 atm (7.35 psia, about 51 kPa), 1 atm and 2 atm. That overlaps and exceeds the intermediate lunar-habitat atmosphere (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less). It brackets the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2, 101.3 kPa). The spacesuit condition (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa) was not tested: no ambient above 40% O2 and none below about 50 kPa. The inverse 85% O2 stream is better compared to an oxygen leak or jet into a fuel-rich region than to a cabin atmosphere. Cool flames were found only at about 39-40% O2 and 2 bar, a combination of oxygen fraction and total pressure higher than any planned habitat atmosphere. Flows were burner-driven only (no ventilation), with velocities of order cm/s at the flame.

sources.quote: ACME testing is limited to 40% oxygen in the combustion chamber
Chamber filled to 1 atm with ~30% ethane (balance N2)

earth_benefits.text: Cool-flame (low-temperature) chemistry governs autoignition, knock, and octane and cetane behaviour in engines. Most engine design models neglect it. The steady, spherical, one-dimensional ISS cool flames give clean validation targets (flame radii, burner and ambient boundary conditions, durations) for cool-flame kinetic mechanisms. The investigators argue this could help engines move toward ultra-lean, low-temperature combustion, with efficiencies they put at up to 60% against 38% or less today. The soot observations in normal and inverse flames also bear on soot control in oxygen-enriched combustion.

sources.quote: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry.

limitations.text: Cool flames were obtained under one narrow condition set only (30% n-butane, about 40% O2, 2 bar, 0.75-1.5 mg/s): 15 flames in 7 tests on 2 days. The first five were cut short because they were not detected in real time, and the later ones were disturbed by catalytic reignition on the type-B thermocouple. So no cool-flame extinction limit (in flow, O2 or pressure) was mapped.

sources.quote: hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion.

limitations.text: The burner was not spherically symmetric: more flow leaked through the sintered joint at the supply tube, and the tube itself was a heat sink. At high flows the flames became offset, ellipsoidal or parabolic and quenched locally near the tube. One-dimensional models therefore only approximate these flames.

sources.quote: At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape.

limitations.text: Mass flow controllers performed poorly below about 10% of full scale, so low-flow set points may differ from actual flows. The chamber was a closed volume, so O2 or fuel fraction fell and pressure rose through each day. Tabulated chamber compositions are estimates from flow balances, not gas-chromatograph measurements.

sources.quote: When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing
estimates of the chamber contents were computed assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized

limitations.text: 'Flow-terminated' does not mean the flame was stable. Flow was cut by scripted timeouts (often 66 s in inverse tests) or when the burner reached its temperature limit. Self-extinction fractions therefore depend on the chosen timeouts and are not burning-limit statistics.

sources.quote: Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated.

The HiBMs camera was unavailable for most of round 1. Some image data were deliberately deleted on orbit to meet daily downlink limits. Acceleration effects were not evaluated with SAMS data.

gaps: The PSI record has no start or end dates. Test dates (29 Mar - 18 Oct 2021) come from the final report and the tables.
The PSI record's hypothesis and objective still list n-pentane. Ethane replaced it because of n-pentane's low vapour pressure (final report p6, p17).

Only two publications are listed in the PSI record. The second (Waddell et al., Combust. Flame 254 (2023) 112852) is a normal-gravity n-heptane pool / stagnation-flow study with no ISS data. The ISS results are in Kim et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 39 (2023) 1647-1656 (doi 10.1016/j.proci.2022.07.015). Its accepted manuscript at par.nsf.gov was used for quotes. Other works found: M. Kim, MS thesis, U. Maryland 2022 (doi 10.13016/n8ln-uehb), and NASA NTRS 20210022542 (Stocker, JASMAC-33 ACME overview, which reports 'Observed the first spherical, quasi-steady, burner-supported cool flames!'). Raw-data PDFs 'test sheets', 'test parameter notes' and 'daily test point log' (21 of each, plus misspelled variants) have no text layer and were not read, as instructed.
Data check: the two flow-trace PDFs for 21222 ('flow traces etc.pdf' and 'flow traces etc-1.pdf') appear to be duplicates.

Data check: in tests.csv, x_o2 and fuel_fraction mean different things by config. For normal flames they are the ambient O2 and the burner fuel mole fraction; for inverse flames, the burner-stream O2 and the ambient fuel mole fraction. Any cross-config plot must keep these apart.

Data check: inverse-table pressures are 0.495, 0.552, 1.10-1.103, 2.207 and 3.310 bar. Fill pressures were nominally 7.35/14.7/29.4/44.1 psia (0.507-3.04 bar), and Kim et al. give 0.46-3.04 bar. The table values are about 9% higher at each level, and tests.csv inherits them (pressure_kpa up to 331).

Data check: tests.csv 'ignited' is null for 8 inverse rows whose 'Hot ignition' is 'flash' (momentary flame, about 1 s, marked SE). The Inverse Flames CSV has 861 empty trailing rows. Its 'Color' column holds 'limit' in 29 rows, apparently flagging the burner temperature limit rather than flame colour. 'Peak burner temp (K)' contains '#VALUE!' and 'Tad'/'Zst' contain '#DIV/0!' in some rows.

Data check: counts differ between sources. The report has 280 hot flames, 189 radiatively extinguished; the tables have 263 ignited plus 8 flashes, 183 SE and 89 FT. The difference is presumably reignitions within one test (for example 21291A1 and C1, each with several hot flames, recorded as one FT row).

Data check: report Table 3 lists '21174D13' while the CSV has '21174 D1'. Report Appendix D says the 18 Oct 2021 (GMT 291) tests used 30% C3H8, but Table 2, the 21291 flow-trace notes and the experimental table all say 30% n-butane.

Data check: 30 tests show peak burner temperatures above 450 °C (723 K), the stated termination limit (max 651.5 °C in 21242 A1). This is presumably overshoot after flow cut-off or lag, but it is not explained in the documents.
The Engineering Implementation report (dated 19 May 2022) still states inverse-flame tests 'have yet to be conducted'. This is stale text carried over from an earlier version.
Raw 125 Hz data files are in instrument voltages. The calibration document (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D) is not in PSI. SAMS acceleration data are not archived with the experiment.

The final report and engineering report contain a NASA staff phone number and e-mail; these were not copied. No credentials and no text addressed to an AI were found in the sampled raw notes (as-run parameter files, TP timelines, image comments, flow-trace PDFs).

Publications pass 2026-11-15: per-fuel outcome counts in the paper (Kim et al. 2023, Table 1; radiatively extinguished / flow-terminated) are normal ethane 30/10, propane 34/6, n-butane 46/17 and inverse ethane 25/22, propane 24/13, n-butane 30/23. tests.csv agrees for four groups but has normal n-butane 38 SE / 15 FT and inverse ethane 27 SE / 22 FT. The n-butane excess in the paper fits the hot-cool-hot tests 21291 A1 and C1 being counted as several hot flames; the 2 extra inverse-ethane SE rows in PSI are unexplained. The paper also states that normal propane flames above 1 bar were limited to X_O2 = 0.21.
